ci: Stories are shared in different ways.
lo: Imagining stories together; Ways stories are shared; Connecting with stories

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students bring their own story characters to life by animating them with voice and movement using Animating a Character with Adobe Express. This taps straight into 'imagining stories together', letting students see their ideas leap from page to screen in a magical way. Students swap characters with a classmate and give someone else's creation a new voice, exploring how stories shift when told by different people. The final artefact is a short animated clip?complete with the student's own recorded voice?that can be shared at assembly or emailed home to families. The 'Animate from Audio' feature lets students record their narration and see the character's mouth move in sync, making even the shyest storyteller feel like a movie director. Kids walk away buzzing with confidence, knowing their stories can travel far beyond the classroom walls.

Students dive into a global library of picture books and audio stories on Epic, discovering how tales are shared around the world. This experience connects beautifully with 'connecting with stories', as children listen to and discuss stories from different cultures and families. Invite students to become 'story detectives', hunting for similarities and differences in how people tell tales?then sharing their discoveries in a class story circle. Each child chooses a favourite story to recommend, recording a short audio message explaining why it spoke to them, which is then played for visiting parents or other classes. Epic's 'Read-To-Me' feature lets even pre-readers access rich stories independently and hear fluent narration. Students finish with a sense of belonging to a worldwide community of storytellers, ready to celebrate both their own voice and others'.

Children co-create a vibrant class picture book retelling a favourite family story, using Book Creator's voice recording and drawing tools to blend spoken word and hand-drawn illustrations. This hands-on storytelling adventure brings the line of inquiry 'connecting with stories' to life as each child hears about their classmates' traditions and memories. Students take on the role of 'story collectors', interviewing peers and weaving together many voices into one big shared book, celebrating the diversity in the room. The finished artefact is a multimedia eBook packed with colourful drawings, audio snippets of student narration, and even family greetings in different languages, ready to share with families and our school library. Book Creator's 'read-to-me' feature means every child?regardless of reading level?can listen back to the class stories, hear their friends' voices, and feel included in the magic. By seeing their own stories valued and published alongside others, students build confidence in their voice and pride in the many ways we express ourselves.

Students use Apple Clips to film and narrate their own imaginative stories, combining live video, voiceover, stickers, and animated text. Each child acts out or retells a favourite story or an original tale, using the app's creative effects to bring characters and settings to life. They can add sound effects and playful filters to enhance the mood or highlight key moments. The final product is a short, engaging video story that demonstrates how stories can be shared in many different ways. This process helps students connect with the idea of storytelling as performance and visual expression, not just words on a page. Finished stories are screened in a class 'story cinema' to celebrate diverse ways of sharing and imagining together.

Students use Tablet Magnifiers to closely examine illustrations, textures, and fine details in storybooks or classroom artefacts. They take magnified photos of interesting patterns, hidden elements, or unique features in the images, then discuss how these visual details help tell the story or set the mood. Working in small groups, students select their favourite magnified images and sequence them to create a 'zoomed-in' visual story. The class then guesses which story or scene each sequence belongs to, sparking conversation about how artists and authors use visual clues. This hands-on activity encourages observation, imagination, and collaborative storytelling. The final product is a gallery of magnified story moments, displayed digitally or as a printed class collage.

Students design and build their own mini shadowbox theatres using shoeboxes, coloured cellophane, paper cut-outs, and craft sticks to create characters and backgrounds from their personal or family stories. They then use a simple torch or LED puck light to project shadows onto the box 'stage', animating their tales with movement. To add a digital twist, students record short audio narrations of their stories on a classroom iPad, syncing their live shadow puppet show with their voices. This project celebrates imagination, sequencing, and diverse storytelling styles?helping students express identity and culture through both hands-on making and digital storytelling.

ci: Everyone has a role to play in the community.
lo: My communities; Contributing to the local community; Connections in my community

s.d: Let students become community helpers by programming Bee-Bots to travel around a giant floor map of the school, stopping at key locations like the library, office, and playground. This hands-on adventure brings to life the idea that everyone has a role to play in the community by letting children physically explore how staff and spaces connect. Students can take turns acting as 'tour guides', narrating the Bee-Bot's journey and explaining the importance of each stop to classmates. The final artefact is a lively, narrated video tour of the Bee-Bot's travels, captured on the iPad Camera and shared at assembly for families and staff. Using Bee-Bot's sequence-and-repeat function, students experiment with efficient routes and even create 'special missions' for different community roles. Kids walk away seeing themselves as active members of a bigger system, ready to contribute and collaborate.

Students create talking portraits of real school community members?like the principal, nurse, or gardener?by drawing their faces and using ChatterPix Kids to animate their voices. This activity makes the line of inquiry 'Who is in my community?' delightfully personal and memorable. Invite the actual staff members in to hear and respond to their digital doppelg?ngers, sparking giggles and real connection. The finished artefacts are a gallery of talking portraits that can be played in the foyer or at a school event to celebrate every role. ChatterPix's voice recording and mouth animation features let even shy students give a voice to their chosen character. Children discover the power of storytelling and empathy, seeing how every person matters.

Transform the classroom into a 'community soundscape' by wiring up Makey Makey boards so that touching different objects (like a lunchbox, a book, or a whistle) plays recorded sounds representing different school roles. This playful experiment explores 'Connections in my community' through the senses, as students match jobs to their signature sounds and actions. Bring in a local expert?like the school chef or crossing guard?to help students brainstorm what sounds represent their work, making the learning feel real and valued. The result is an interactive sound wall that visiting families or other classes can try, learning about school roles through touch and sound. Makey Makey's ability to turn everyday objects into touch sensors opens up creative possibilities for even the youngest learners. Students leave with a sense of pride in their own role as creators and connectors.

Students use Tablet Magnifiers to investigate everyday objects and materials found in their school and local community, such as coins, leaves, fabric, or classroom tools. They capture close-up images that reveal textures, patterns, and features not easily seen with the naked eye. Each student selects one magnified photo and creates a 'mystery object' challenge for classmates, describing its role in the community and why it is important. The class discusses how these objects help people in different roles, connecting the details to the broader idea of community helpers and shared spaces. This activity builds observation skills and sparks curiosity about the hidden details in our environment. The final product is a digital or printed 'community close-ups' gallery with student captions.

Students use Apple Clips to create short video interviews where they act as different community helpers or family members, using the app's stickers and live titles to identify roles. They record themselves answering questions about their responsibilities, how they help others, and what makes their role important. By layering in sound effects and playful visuals, students make their interviews engaging and easy to follow. These video interviews are then shared with the class to build a digital 'community wall' that celebrates the many ways people contribute. This activity helps students see the connections and diversity within their local community, while practising speaking and listening skills.

Students design and build a giant collaborative train set from recycled boxes, cardboard tubes, and craft materials, with each carriage representing a different person or role in the school community (like the Principal, Nurse, or Librarian). Using simple coding with Sphero Indi robots placed in the 'engine', students program routes along their handmade tracks to visit each carriage and learn about the connections between roles. This hands-on project blends creative construction with basic robotics, helping students visualise how everyone's contributions keep the school 'train' running smoothly. The design cycle guides them through imagining, planning, building, testing, and sharing their interactive school system model.

ci: Scientists follow a method to discover new things.
lo: The scientific process; Observing my world; Drawing conclusions

s.d: Prep scientists become real-world explorers by using the Seesaw app to identify and record living things they spot on a nature walk around the school grounds. This playful investigation brings the line of inquiry 'Observing my world' to life as children notice patterns and differences in the animals and plants they encounter. Students can imagine they are field researchers discovering a brand-new species, giving it a creative name and sharing their 'discovery' with a buddy class. Their final artefact is a class nature wall ? a collage of photos, student-drawn sketches, and fun facts about each living thing, ready to share with families and the school community. The app's 'Favourites' feature lets students build their own mini digital collection of local wildlife, making it easy to revisit and compare observations over time. Kids leave with the confidence to look closely, ask questions, and see themselves as scientists in their own backyard.

Students transform into junior astronomers by using the Sky Map app on iPads to explore the night sky during the day. They point their devices upwards to identify stars, planets, and constellations, learning how scientists use technology to observe things far away. Each child chooses a favourite constellation or planet, draws it on paper, and then uses the app to find where it appears in the real sky. The class creates a giant collaborative sky mural, with each student adding their drawing and a fun fact about their chosen celestial object. This hands-on activity encourages children to ask questions about patterns in the sky and notice how things change over time. By connecting digital exploration with creative art, students build curiosity about the universe and see themselves as real-world investigators.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Children bring a scientist character to life by animating their own voice and ideas using the 'Animate from Audio' feature in Animating a Character with Adobe Express. This activity connects directly to the central idea, showing that scientists use communication to share discoveries and ask questions. Students can swap roles and interview each other's animated scientists, asking what they do when experiments go wrong or how they make predictions. The final product is a collection of playful, talking scientist animations, ready to be showcased at assembly or emailed to families. The 'Animate from Audio' tool lets students turn their own voices into lively digital characters, making the science talk feel personal and fun. By the end, every child feels empowered to speak up, share their thinking, and see themselves as creative problem-solvers.

Prep students dive into a world of science-themed picture books and read-alouds using Epic, exploring stories about weather, seasons, and curious scientists. The teacher curates a digital bookshelf featuring titles like 'What Will the Weather Be?', 'Ada Twist, Scientist', and 'Snowy Day', encouraging children to notice how characters observe, predict, and experiment. After listening to or reading a story, students draw their favourite experiment or weather event and dictate a sentence about what surprised them most. The class then creates a digital gallery of their drawings and ideas, which can be shared with families or used as prompts for future investigations. Epic's read-to-me feature supports early readers and makes complex science ideas accessible through engaging visuals and narration. This activity builds scientific vocabulary, sparks wonder, and helps children connect storytelling with real-world inquiry.

Students become mini-scientists by coding a simple animated story that shows how they conduct a classroom experiment, such as testing which objects sink or float. This hands-on coding adventure mirrors the line of inquiry around sequencing the scientific process?predicting, observing, testing and drawing conclusions. With each student taking on the role of both scientist and storyteller, their digital investigations become playful narratives, ready to share with peers or even with a Year 1 buddy class. The final artefact is a lively sequence on the iPad where their character predicts, tests, and celebrates a science discovery, complete with speech bubbles and animated reactions. By using ScratchJr's tap-to-program blocks and the 'trigger on tap' function, students make their stories interactive?letting viewers choose the next step in the investigation. This empowers young learners to see themselves as curious investigators who can communicate real-world discoveries through imaginative technology.

Students design and build spinning weather wheels using cardboard circles, split pins, and craft materials to represent different weather types (sun, rain, wind, clouds, snow). They decorate each section with textured materials like cotton balls, foil, tissue paper, and felt to bring each weather type to life. Using a simple stop-motion app on iPads, students animate their wheels to show changing weather patterns and record short audio explanations of their predictions for each type. This hands-on project supports observation and communication skills, connecting scientific inquiry with creative storytelling and visual representation.

ci: Living things share our world and have an important role in nature
lo: The different living things around us; The roles living things play in nature; How humans and other living things share space

s.d: Students become family story reporters by using the Insta360 camera to film a 360-degree tour of a special place in their school or classroom that reminds them of home or family traditions. Working in small groups, they narrate what makes each spot meaningful, sharing memories or describing objects that connect to their personal histories. The immersive camera lets children capture every angle, so viewers feel like they are right there, exploring together. After filming, the class gathers to watch the virtual tours, pausing to discuss similarities and differences in what each child values. This activity sparks conversations about belonging and the unique ways families shape our sense of place. The final product is a collection of 360-degree video tours, ready for a virtual gallery walk with families or buddy classes.

Children become time travellers by using Stop Motion Studio to animate the story of their life so far, from babyhood to today. Each student brings in or draws pictures of key moments?like a first birthday, moving house, or a favourite holiday?and sequences them as frames in a stop-motion timeline. They add simple narration or captions to explain what is happening in each scene, practising oral storytelling and sequencing skills. The app's onion-skinning feature helps them smoothly animate transitions between events, making their personal history come alive. When finished, the class hosts a 'Life Stories Film Festival,' where students watch and celebrate each other's journeys. This project helps children see how their own story fits into the bigger picture of family and community.

Students become local explorers by using the Field Guide to Victoria app to investigate native plants and animals found around their school or neighbourhood. They search for species that might have been present when their families first arrived in the area, or that hold special meaning in family stories. Each child selects a favourite plant or animal, then draws or writes about how it connects to their own history or community. The app's detailed photos and maps help students compare past and present, noticing which species are still common and which have changed over time. Their work is compiled into a class 'Then and Now' nature scrapbook, blending personal memories with local biodiversity. This activity deepens students' sense of place and highlights the connections between people, history, and the natural world.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Children transform themselves into family storytellers using the Animate from Audio feature in Animating a Character with Adobe Express (https://new.express.adobe.com/home/tools/animate-from-audio). Each student draws a character representing themselves or a family member, then records a short story or memory?such as a favourite family celebration or a special tradition. The app automatically lip-syncs their voice to the character, creating a lively animated storyteller. Teachers guide the process, helping children rehearse their narration and choose expressive voices. The finished animations are shared in a digital 'Family Stories Cinema,' sparking conversations about similarities and differences in traditions. This activity builds oral language skills and celebrates the diversity of family experiences in the classroom.

Students use Freeform to create a collaborative digital timeline of their class community, mapping out important events, birthdays, and milestones from each child's life. They drag and drop photos, drawings, and icons onto the shared canvas, arranging them in chronological order to show how their stories overlap and connect. Children can add speech bubbles or voice notes to explain why each moment matters, practising sequencing and oral language skills. The flexible workspace lets students zoom in on individual journeys or zoom out to see the whole class story at once. As the timeline grows, students notice patterns?like shared celebrations or changes over time?and reflect on what makes their community unique. The final timeline is displayed on the interactive whiteboard for families to explore during open classroom events.

s.t: Family Heritage Homes: Miniature Memory Villages
s.d: Students design and build a miniature 'home' that represents something special about their family's heritage using cardboard boxes, fabric scraps, natural materials, and recycled bits. They decorate their homes with personal touches, then use Sphero Indi robots to 'visit' each other's creations, mapping a route between homes with coloured tiles and sharing stories as the robot travels. This hands-on project weaves together physical making, digital navigation, and storytelling, helping students celebrate identity and community while exploring how we all share and shape our planet together.

ci: Relationships impact our wellbeing.
lo: Developing relationships; How those around us impact our behaviours and interactions; Keeping ourselves healthy and safe

s.d: Children become 'friendship robots', programming Bee-Bots to travel along a giant floor map representing different places in their school where relationships are built?like the playground, classroom, and library. This playful journey lets students explore how developing relationships in various spaces affects their feelings and sense of belonging. Students work in pairs to give each other directions, learning that clear communication and teamwork are key to keeping everyone safe and happy. The final artefact is a photo story: each Bee-Bot stop is captured and captioned by students, then shared as a visual map with families to show how friendships grow at school. Bee-Bots' sequence-and-repeat function helps students design longer, collaborative journeys that mirror real-life interactions. Kids leave with the confidence to navigate new social spaces and the understanding that strong relationships are built step by step.

Students invent 'Feelings Boards' using Makey Makey, connecting playdough, foil, and everyday objects to trigger different sounds for emotions like happy, sad, or calm. This hands-on project brings the line of inquiry about recognising and expressing feelings to life in a tangible way. Each group becomes wellbeing designers, tasked with imagining which sounds or music might help a friend feel better or safer in the classroom. The finished artefact is an interactive emotions station, where classmates and even visiting Year 1s can press different objects to hear the sounds students have chosen to represent each feeling. Makey Makey's ability to turn almost anything conductive into a computer key lets students experiment wildly?using fruit, fabric, or even a puddle of water as part of their circuit. They walk away knowing they can use creativity and empathy to support themselves and others.

Students use ChatterPix Kids to bring their 'Feelings Friends' to life by drawing or photographing a character that represents an emotion?like a smiling sun for happiness or a gentle cloud for calm. Each child records a short message in their character's voice, sharing a tip for making friends or describing a time they felt included at school. The app animates the character's mouth to match the recording, creating a playful, talking avatar. These mini-movies are compiled into a class video gallery that can be shared with families or used as conversation starters during circle time. ChatterPix Kids' simple interface empowers even the youngest students to express themselves and listen to others' perspectives. Children finish with a sense of pride, knowing their voices and ideas help build a caring classroom community.

Prep students animate their own friendship stories in ScratchJr, coding characters to show how kind actions and words can change the day for someone else. This directly connects to the unit's focus on how relationships impact our wellbeing. Students swap storyboards and code each other's ideas, learning to see friendship from another person's shoes. The final artefact is a gallery of animated mini-movies, ready to be screened for parents or shared with a buddy class. ScratchJr's speech bubble and background switching features let students add dialogue and change settings, making each story richer and more personal. Children finish with the pride of being storytellers who can use technology to spread kindness.

Students will co-design a digital class friendship book, each contributing a page sharing their unique identity and what makes them feel happy and safe at school. This activity explores the line of inquiry 'how those around us impact our behaviours and interactions' by prompting children to notice what they value in friendships and caring relationships. Families are invited to add a short audio message to their child's page, creating a bridge between home and school voices. The final artefact is a vibrant multimedia eBook, complete with student drawings, voice recordings, and family messages, which can be shared on the big screen during a class celebration and emailed home to every family. Using Book Creator's 'read aloud' and easy audio embedding features, even emergent readers can confidently access and share their pages with peers. Every child leaves with a deep sense of belonging, pride in their identity, and the courage to celebrate the positive relationships that help them flourish at school.

s.t: Feelings Forest: My Emotion Explorer Map
s.d: Students design and craft their own 'Emotion Explorer' map using large sheets of paper, felt, cardboard scraps, and natural materials like leaves and twigs. Each student creates a unique forest path representing their feelings and important people in their lives, decorating their map with hand-drawn symbols, pop-up trees, and crafted emotion creatures. Using Bee-Bots, students program simple journeys along their map's path, stopping at key spots to share a story or feeling with classmates. This hands-on adventure helps students express their identity, understand emotions, and celebrate how different relationships shape who they are.

ci: Emotions can be expressed in different ways.
lo: Recognising our own and others' emotions; Responding to and interpreting our emotions; Different ways we express emotions

s.d: Students become emotion composers, using GarageBand to create musical soundscapes that express a single feeling?joy, sadness, surprise, or calm. This taps straight into the idea that emotions can be expressed in different ways, making feelings audible instead of just visible or spoken. Inviting the Year 6 music leaders in to guess which emotion each piece represents flips the usual classroom dynamic and gives real-world feedback from older student musicians. Their finished tracks turn into a playlist of feelings, which can be played for families at the next assembly or shared as a wellbeing resource across the school. GarageBand's Live Loops let even young students experiment with layers and mood-shifting changes, far beyond just tapping a beat. Kids leave knowing their feelings have a sound?giving them a fresh tool to show the world how they feel, even when words are tricky.

Students work in pairs or small groups to film short video skits using Apple Clips that depict specific emotions such as excitement, frustration, or nervousness. They use Apple Clips' stickers, filters, and animated text features to visually highlight each emotion and the ways people might respond to them. Each student narrates their character's feelings and models healthy emotional responses, creating expressive and relatable scenes. These videos capture both the emotional experience and appropriate reactions, helping students deepen their understanding of recognising and interpreting emotions. The final clips are compiled into a class 'Emotion Gallery' where students watch and discuss how emotions can be expressed differently. This creative process supports empathy and emotional literacy through engaging storytelling and multimedia expression.

Students turn the iPad into a giant collaborative feelings map using Freeform, sketching, doodling, and placing emoji to show how different emotions might look, feel, and even where in the body they are sensed. This creative brainstorm helps all students recognise their own and others' emotions in a playful, visual way. Bringing in a real artist via video call to share how professionals use mood boards to start their work gives a glimpse into how emotions drive creative careers. Their final artefact is a living wall-sized digital canvas?full of drawings, words, and images?that can be printed out and displayed around the school. Freeform's collaborative board feature means the whole class can build together in real time, layering their voices visually. Students leave with a sense of how their inner world can be mapped and celebrated, and that everyone's feelings are a vital part of creative expression.

Students design an interactive feelings detective book, where each page invites the reader to guess the emotion shown through a combination of student-drawn faces, voice-recorded clues, and gentle sound effects. This taps directly into recognising our own and others' emotions by challenging classmates and families to interpret nuanced expressions and vocal cues. To deepen empathy, students swap books and try to decode the emotions from someone else's perspective, then annotate responses inside the app. The finished artefact is a colourful, multimedia eBook that can be shared with Prep buddies or sent home as a digital conversation starter about emotional literacy. Using Book Creator's comic templates and embedded audio hotspots, students combine visual storytelling and oral language in one seamless format. Every student becomes a confident feelings communicator?empowering them to notice, express, and interpret emotions with creative flair well beyond the classroom.

Students use Teachable Machine to train a model that recognises different facial expressions representing emotions such as happiness, sadness, anger and surprise. They capture images of themselves or classmates making these expressions, teaching the model to classify each one. The final product is a digital emotion detector that can identify and label emotions in real time. This activity links directly to understanding how we express and interpret emotions through facial cues. Students compare their model's accuracy to real-world systems like accessibility tools and face-unlock features in devices, which also use image recognition to interpret expressions. They reflect on how technology can help people better understand emotions, especially for those with communication challenges.

s.t: Feelings Bot Parade: Emotions on Wheels!
s.d: Students design and craft expressive robot costumes using cardboard boxes, fabric scraps, paper plates, and art materials to represent different emotions (like joy, sadness, or excitement). They decorate Sphero Indi cars with their creations, then use simple color code tiles to program their 'Feelings Bots' on a parade route that tells a story of changing emotions. Along the way, students stop at 'emotion stations' to act out and discuss feelings, blending hands-on building, digital coding, and dramatic expression. This project helps students embody and communicate emotions through movement, art, and technology, making emotional literacy a joyful, memorable experience.

ci: Services are established to help the needs of people in the community.
lo: Local services; Why we need local services in our community; How services meet personal and community needs

s.d: Kick off by turning community helper photos into talking characters using ChatterPix Kids ? students snap a picture of a local postie, nurse or lollipop person, then make them 'speak' about their daily work. This instantly dives into 'why we need local services in our community' by letting the helpers explain it in their own words (well, students' voices!). For an added spark, students can interview a real helper or family member to gather true facts and fun stories before recording. Each child creates a 30-second talking portrait, then the class puts these together for a digital 'Meet Our Helpers' wall to share with families. The app's background and sticker effects help each helper shine with a burst of personality ? think nurse with a superhero cape or postie with a puppy sidekick. Kids walk away with a sense of pride in their community and the confidence to tell stories in creative ways.

Students program BeeBots to deliver 'packages' to map locations representing different local services ? post office, fire station, hospital, or library ? on a giant floor map of Elsternwick. By doing this, they explore how services are established to help people and what happens if one is missing. Students take on the role of town planners, puzzling out the most efficient routes to ensure everyone in the community gets what they need. Each team films a short video tour showing their BeeBot making the journey and narrating which service it's visiting and why. Using BeeBot's sequence-and-repeat function, students experiment with longer routes and discover how real systems need careful planning. The experience builds not just coding skills, but also a deeper appreciation for the invisible systems that keep a community running.

Students use Tablet Magnifiers to explore and document the fine details of objects and materials used by local services, such as uniforms, badges, tools, or vehicles. They take close-up photos of textures, symbols, or features that make each item unique to its service?like the reflective strip on a firefighter's jacket or the grooves on a key. Students then create a matching activity, pairing magnified images with the correct community service and explaining how each feature helps meet people's needs. This hands-on investigation builds appreciation for the design and purpose of everyday items. The final product is a digital matching game or poster that highlights the hidden details of community helpers' tools.

Challenge students to invent a 'help button' for a chosen community service using Makey Makey and everyday objects ? maybe a banana phone for the police, or a foil ambulance siren. This activity goes deep into 'how services meet personal and community needs' by asking 'How do people call for help, and what could make it easier?' Each group can demo their invention to a visiting grown-up, acting out a real-life scenario where someone needs to quickly reach the right helper. Their working prototype, filmed and explained in a short video, is shared at assembly or on the school website. Makey Makey's ability to turn almost anything conductive into a working input means even the wildest student ideas get a real-world test. Kids leave feeling like inventors who can solve real problems ? not just for themselves, but for everyone in their community.

Students use Apple Clips to create video tours of local services, such as the post office, fire station, or library. They record short clips explaining what each service does, who works there, and how it helps the community. Using live titles, stickers, and voiceover, students highlight the importance of these services and how they meet people's needs. The finished videos are combined into a digital 'Community Services Guide' that the class can watch together. This activity helps students understand the roles and systems that support their daily lives, while building confidence in speaking and presenting.

Students will design and build a 3D maze representing a miniature town using cardboard boxes, tubes, recycled containers, and craft materials to create roads, buildings, and local services (like fire stations, hospitals, and post offices). Using Sphero Indi cars, children program simple routes to 'respond' to community emergencies, navigating their crafted maze to reach different services. This hands-on project lets students explore how community helpers are organised and work together to meet needs, blending creative construction with basic coding and teamwork. It brings the theme to life as students imagine, build, and test their own organised community systems.

ci: Patterns help us to interpret the world around us.
lo: Patterns and cycles in our lives; Different patterns around us; How patterns can be created, interpreted and extended

s.d: Students will take their iPads outside and use Sky Map to hunt for repeating star patterns and constellations in the daytime sky. This sparks wonder about how natural cycles and patterns, like seasons and day-night, help us make sense of the world around us. Rather than just spotting stars, students play the role of junior astronomers, reporting their discoveries back to classmates as if they are the first to chart the sky. Each pair will snap a screenshot of their favourite constellation, add a voice recording describing its pattern, and post it on a class display for families to enjoy at home. The app's time-travel slider lets students fast-forward or rewind the sky, so they can see how patterns shift across different months. By seeing these invisible patterns come to life, students build confidence as real explorers who notice hidden cycles in the everyday world.

Children design colourful floor mazes and program Sphero Indi cars to drive in loops, zig-zags, and repeating sequences that mirror natural patterns like caterpillar-to-butterfly or day-to-night cycles. Exploring 'how patterns can be created, interpreted and extended', students become inventors, testing how different colour tiles change Indi's path. Students swap mazes and decode each other's patterns, learning to think like pattern detectives. The final artefact is a short video demonstration, with students narrating the pattern and its real-world inspiration for a school assembly video wall. Indi's speed and turn customisation features allow for complex, non-linear pathways and cycles beyond the basic forward-and-turn commands. Learners walk away seeing pattern-spotting as a playful superpower they can use to break down even the trickiest puzzles.

Students use Tablet Magnifiers to investigate patterns in nature and everyday classroom objects, such as leaf veins, shell spirals, fabric weaves, or fingerprints. They capture magnified images and identify repeating shapes, lines, or colours, discussing how these patterns help living things or objects function. Students then create a 'pattern gallery' by grouping their images into categories?natural, man-made, geometric, or organic. This activity encourages close observation and helps students recognise that patterns are everywhere, supporting their understanding of cycles and sequences. The final product is a digital or printed pattern collage with student labels and explanations.

Students become storytellers by scripting and recording their own mini-plays about life cycles?think frog spawn to frog or seed to flower?using Puppet Pals. This activity brings 'patterns and cycles in our lives' to life as students literally act out the repeating stages. Instead of just watching, students take on the role of science communicators, creating performances aimed at teaching little siblings or Prep students about how living things grow and change. Their finished work is a shareable animated show, complete with their own voices, character choices, and background scenes. Puppet Pals' custom character creator lets them snap photos of real objects or their hand-drawn art, blending classroom creativity with digital magic. By seeing their stories make sense to others, students realise they can teach real science through playful storytelling.

With Makey Makey kits, children turn ordinary classroom objects?like fruit, foil, or found leaves?into interactive pattern instruments, exploring the rhythms and sequences in music and nature. This hands-on investigation brings the idea of 'how patterns can be created, interpreted and extended' to their fingertips, literally turning patterns into sounds and actions. Students become inventors, challenged to create a repeating sound sequence inspired by a butterfly's wingbeats or the cycle of rain and sun, then perform for their buddy class. The final product is a touch-activated pattern 'music board', with each tap playing part of a pattern for friends and families to try. The advanced remapping tool lets students change which objects trigger which notes, offering endless combinations and pushing their sense of experimentation. After this, students walk away bursting with confidence as creative problem-solvers who can make patterns jump off the page.

s.t: Seasons Spinners: Cycle of Change Dioramas
s.d: Students design and craft a rotating diorama that shows how a tree or animal changes through the four seasons. Using cardboard circles, paper plates, felt scraps, recycled materials, markers, and child-safe fasteners, they build a spinner where each turn reveals a different seasonal scene. Students then use Sphero Indi (or similar simple robot) to 'travel' to each season, triggering their spinner to display the matching change. This hands-on project helps students visualize repeating patterns in nature and connects digital movement with tangible model-making, deepening understanding of cycles in the natural world.

ci: Plants are a life sustaining resource.
lo: Products derived from plants; Plants all around us; The interconnectedness of plants

s.d: Students embark on a digital plant hunt around the schoolyard using Field Guide to Victoria, capturing photos and recording observations of local plant species they discover. They create a class gallery where each student uploads their plant snapshot alongside a short, interesting fact they learned about that species. Using the app's compare feature, students investigate similar-looking plants, discussing differences and what this reveals about biodiversity in their environment. A guest botanist joins via video call to answer students' questions and view their live discoveries, deepening their understanding of plant life. This hands-on activity encourages students to think like plant detectives, noticing patterns and connections among plants growing nearby. The final gallery becomes a vibrant, interactive resource showcasing the variety and importance of plants all around them.

Students bring the world of plants to life by making their favourite fruit, vegetable, or flower talk using ChatterPix Kids. This playful activity connects directly to the line of inquiry about 'products derived from plants' as students explore everything from apples to cotton. Imagine a tomato explaining how it becomes sauce or a sunflower chatting about its journey from seed to snack ? it's a fresh way to flip the lesson and let the plants do the storytelling. Each student will share their creation with families at home, spreading plant appreciation beyond the classroom walls. The magic comes from ChatterPix's voice recording and drawing features, letting students add silly faces, captions, and personalities to their chosen plant. Suddenly, even the quietest student has a voice ? and a giggly, unforgettable way to teach others about the power of plants.

Students use Teachable Machine to build a simple plant part classifier by photographing leaves, stems, flowers and roots from classroom or local plants. They train the model to recognise each part, then test it with new plant images to see if it can correctly identify the structures. This hands-on activity deepens understanding of plant anatomy and the interconnectedness of plant parts. The process mirrors real-world plant identification apps and agricultural monitoring systems that use AI to classify plant features for research and farming. Students present their classifier's results and discuss how technology can support sustainable resource use and environmental stewardship.

Challenge students to create 'plant product journeys' using PicCollage, mapping out how everyday items ? like paper, bread, or clothing ? start as plants and end up in our homes. This activity shines a light on the unit's focus on 'products derived from plants' in a way that feels personal and relevant to young lives. Students become investigative reporters, interviewing family members or staff about their favourite plant-based products and how they use them. The finished digital collages can be printed or shared at assembly, showing colourful step-by-step stories of plants transformed into items we use every day. PicCollage's cut-out and background-removal tool lets students combine real photos, stickers, and text to invent creative, eye-catching journeys. Kids walk away with sharper digital storytelling skills and a new appreciation for the hidden plants in their world.

Students use the insta360 camera to create a virtual plant walk, recording 360-degree videos of different plants around the school or local area. Each group selects a type of plant?such as trees, flowers or edible plants?and films close-ups of leaves, stems and roots, as well as the plant's surroundings. The camera's immersive view allows students to show how plants are interconnected with their environment, including pollinators, soil and sunlight. After filming, students narrate their videos to explain the products derived from each plant and how plants sustain life. The finished virtual walks are shared with the class, who explore the videos on iPads and discuss the importance of plants in daily life. Teachers assess students on their ability to identify plant features and explain their significance in sustaining living things.

s.t: Rainmaker Robots: The Water Cycle Adventure Track
s.d: Students will design and build a vibrant 3D water cycle adventure track using cardboard, felt, blue cellophane, cotton balls, and recycled materials to represent clouds, rivers, rain, and sunshine. They will then program a Sphero Indi robot (or similar age-appropriate robot car) to journey through each stage of the water cycle, pausing at student-created stations that explain evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and collection. Along the way, students collaboratively decorate and label their track, using simple code cards or color tiles for navigation. This hands-on challenge helps students visualize natural cycles, fosters teamwork, and blends creative making with early robotics in an unforgettable, active learning experience.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Homes reflect our culture and environment.
lo: Different types of homes; Characteristics of a home; The importance of sustainable living spaces

s.d: Imagine students becoming global home detectives, using Epic to explore vibrant picture books and videos about houses from every continent. This activity brings the 'different types of homes' line of inquiry to life by letting students see igloos, treehouses, and desert tents through the eyes of children who live there. To spark empathy, students will each choose a home from another culture, then write or voice a short message introducing themselves as a child living in that home?ready to swap with a buddy. The final artefact is a digital 'pen pal' introduction, paired with an image from Epic, ready to be shared with families or displayed in a class gallery. Epic's 'Read-to-Me' feature lets every child access stories in their own way, even if they're not yet confident readers. Students walk away knowing their own home is just one of many wonderful ways people belong in the world.

Students become home designers, using PicCollage to create a visual blueprint of what makes a house a home. This taps into the 'characteristics of a home' line of inquiry, inviting students to look closely at materials, shapes, and special features. They will interview a grandparent, family member, or neighbour about their childhood home, then include a drawing or photo of that memory in their collage. The finished product is a digital poster blending old and new?photos, hand-drawn elements, text labels?that can be printed or shared at assembly. PicCollage's background remover tool lets students layer their own faces into historical or faraway homes, making the past feel personal. Students leave with new respect for the stories hidden in the walls around them.

Let students turn a recycled-materials model of a home into a talking tour guide using ChatterPix Kids. This activity links to 'the importance of sustainable living spaces' by giving each home a voice to explain its eco-friendly features. Students imagine their model is applying for a spot in a 'Greenest Homes of the World' exhibition, and must convince a panel why it deserves to be included. The final artefact is a short, funny video where the home's door or window 'mouth' shares its story, ready for a class film festival. ChatterPix Kids' custom stickers and filters let students add solar panels, gardens, or rainwater tanks right onto their photos. With every recording, students build confidence in speaking up for the planet?one tiny house at a time.

Students become local history explorers by using Field Guide to Victoria to investigate traditional and contemporary homes found in their own region. They will browse the app's collection of images and stories about Indigenous shelters, early settler cottages, and modern eco-houses, comparing how each type responds to the local climate and available resources. Each student selects one home style and creates a simple fact sheet with a drawing and three key features, such as materials used or ways the home stays cool in summer. The class then assembles these into a giant timeline mural, showing how homes have changed over time in Victoria. Field Guide to Victoria's visual galleries and location-based stories help students connect their own neighbourhood to the broader story of place and time. This activity grounds global perspectives in the familiar streets around them.

Students become sustainability engineers, programming Sphero Indi cars to navigate through a maze of model homes?choosing the most eco-friendly path. This activity brings the 'importance of sustainable living spaces' to life by asking students to think about energy use, waste, and clever design as they code their routes. Each team will explain their choices, debating which features matter most for a healthy planet. The final artefact is a filmed demonstration where the Indi car travels the chosen path, with students narrating their reasoning for a school-wide video showcase. Sphero Indi's colour tile sequencing lets students build in decision points?like solar panels or compost bins?that change the car's direction. Students finish with real coding skills and a sense of agency in designing a greener future.

Students will research and build miniature models of homes from different cultures and environments using recycled cardboard, fabric scraps, craft sticks, and natural materials. They'll integrate simple LED circuits (with coin cell batteries and copper tape) to add glowing 'lights' inside their homes, representing how people adapt to their surroundings and needs. Using age-appropriate apps like PicCollage on iPads, students will photograph their creations and digitally label unique features, linking each model to its place and time. The finished light-up village becomes a collaborative display, celebrating diversity, sustainability, and the creative ways people build homes around the world.

ci: The actions we take influence our safety and wellbeing.
lo: Safe environments; How our actions affect ourselves and others; Keeping our body and mind healthy

s.d: Students become health detectives by creating interactive digital books that guide readers through a 'choose your own adventure' journey about making safe and healthy choices. Each page presents a scenario?like deciding what to eat for breakfast, how to cross the road, or what to do when feeling worried?and students design two possible paths, using photos, drawings, and voice recordings to illustrate the outcomes. Book Creator's multimedia features let students embed sound effects for good choices and gentle reminders for risky ones, making each decision point engaging and memorable. As they build their books, students discuss with partners how different actions affect wellbeing, deepening their understanding of cause and effect. The finished books are shared in a class library, allowing peers and families to explore and discuss the impact of everyday decisions. This project empowers students to see themselves as authors of their own safety and wellbeing stories.

Students become storytellers by coding animated stories where characters make healthy or risky choices and see the consequences play out. This links directly to 'how our actions affect ourselves and others', giving students a playful way to experiment with cause and effect. Each student will swap their own story with a partner and remix it to show a different outcome, encouraging empathy and new perspectives. The final product is a short, interactive animation that can be shared with Prep buddies or uploaded to Seesaw for families to watch together. ScratchJr's 'trigger on tap' and 'endless loop' blocks let students create branching storylines and repeating healthy habits, like brushing teeth or stretching. By the end, students feel empowered to make positive choices and understand that their actions ripple out to those around them.

Students use Apple Clips to create safety and wellbeing video tips for their peers. They act out scenarios?such as crossing the road safely, making healthy food choices, or managing big feelings?and use the app's stickers, live titles, and filters to emphasise key actions. Students narrate their videos to explain why these actions matter for keeping themselves and others safe. The finished clips are compiled into a class 'Wellbeing Video Wall', which can be revisited during health and safety discussions. This activity empowers students to take ownership of their wellbeing and share practical strategies with others.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students become animated health experts by using the Animate from Audio feature in Adobe Express (https://new.express.adobe.com/home/tools/animate-from-audio) to create talking characters that explain how different body systems keep us safe and healthy. Working in small groups, students record their voices as they describe the role of the heart, lungs, or skin, then select a character?such as a friendly doctor or a superhero organ?to deliver their message. The app automatically lip-syncs the character to their narration, making the information engaging and memorable. Each group shares their animated explainer with the class, sparking questions and connections about how our bodies work. The finished artefact is a short, lively video that can be shared with families or embedded on the class blog. This activity helps students build confidence in communicating scientific ideas and deepens their understanding of how our bodies protect and support us every day.

Students become wellbeing artists, using Brushes Redux to create digital posters that celebrate healthy habits and positive actions in their daily lives. This connects to 'keeping our body and mind healthy', encouraging students to notice and promote the small choices that make a big difference. Students will swap posters and add a new layer?showing what happens when someone forgets or ignores the healthy habit, building empathy and reflection. The final artefact is a vibrant digital gallery displayed on the class screen or printed for the school corridor, sparking conversations with peers and visitors. Brushes Redux's layering and transparency tools allow students to create before-and-after scenes or highlight hidden details, adding depth to their messages. Students leave with creative confidence and the drive to inspire others to look after themselves.

Students design and build a vibrant obstacle course that represents a 'day in the life' of a healthy person, using cardboard, popsticks, fabric scraps, recycled containers, and markers. Along the track, they create interactive stations (like brushing teeth, eating fruits, exercising, and resting) with moving parts or flaps. Using Sphero Indi cars, students program simple routes to guide their cars through each healthy habit station, reinforcing cause-and-effect and the importance of daily routines. This hands-on project helps students physically map out and share their understanding of how healthy choices keep our bodies and minds strong.

ci: Artistic appreciation and expressions inspire our imagination and creativity.
lo: Forms of expression; Expressing thoughts and ideas; Understanding and appreciating art

s.d: Students bring famous artworks to life by giving them voices and personalities using ChatterPix Kids. This playful approach lets them embody different forms of artistic expression, deepening their understanding of how ideas and emotions are communicated through art. They can even adopt the role of 'artwork ambassadors' and perform their creations for a younger class, sparking cross-year conversations about creativity. The final product is a gallery of talking masterpieces?each artwork introducing itself, sharing its story, and inviting viewers to think about how it inspires imagination. By layering in background sounds or music with ChatterPix Kids' sound effects feature, students explore how voice and tone can transform meaning. Kids leave feeling fearless about experimenting with art and technology, realising their own ideas deserve to be heard.

Students curate their own digital exhibition of creative writing, visual art, and music using Book Creator. This presses right into the line of inquiry about expressing thoughts and ideas in imaginative ways. As classroom curators, they write artist statements and even include 'behind-the-scenes' pages revealing their process, inviting families and the school community to tour the finished eBook. Each child publishes a personal art anthology, complete with audio poetry readings, scanned artwork, and embedded music. Book Creator's comic templates and audio recording features let them blend text, speech, and images into a rich multimedia showcase. They finish the unit feeling like real authors, excited by the power and possibility of self-publishing.

Students experiment with digital painting on Brushes Redux and reimagine a classic work of art in a brand-new style. This connects directly to forms of artistic expression, as they discover how colour, texture, and brushstroke choices can dramatically change a piece's mood or message. They become 'art remixers', debating whether changing the original artwork adds or takes away meaning, and share their thinking in a class critique. The end result is a digital art gallery with side-by-side comparisons: students' reinterpretations displayed alongside the originals, open for the school to view and discuss. Brushes Redux's advanced layering tool lets them build complex compositions, try out bold changes without fear, and even add hidden details. The experience empowers them to see themselves as artists who can play, remix, and push boundaries.

Students compose and record their own original soundtracks in GarageBand, using music to express a feeling or tell a story inspired by a piece of visual art. This explores the link between music and expressing thoughts and ideas, inviting students to consider how sound and rhythm can change our response to what we see. They might even swap soundtracks with another class, challenging their peers to guess which artwork each piece of music matches, sparking lively debate about interpretation. The culminating artefact is a playlist of student-generated tracks, each paired with a visual artwork and a short artist statement explaining the creative choices. By experimenting with GarageBand's live loops and sound library, students discover how layering and mixing transform simple melodies into rich soundscapes. They finish the experience tuned in to how music shapes our feelings and more confident to create their own.

Students design interactive, choose-your-own-adventure stories in Delightex, where readers make decisions that affect the outcome of an artistic journey. This pushes deep into the idea of understanding and appreciating art by inviting others to step into the shoes of the artist or character. They take on the role of 'imagination guides', building stories that encourage empathy and let classmates experience art from different perspectives. Each finished project is an interactive storybook, complete with student-created art, branching paths, and audio narration, ready to be played by the wider school community. Delightex's path-branching feature lets students weave multiple endings and hidden surprises, making every reading a new adventure. By the end, they see themselves as storytellers and inventors, ready to take creative risks and put their ideas into the world.

Students work in teams to design and build colourful mini 'forts' or 'tunnels' using big cardboard boxes, fabric scraps, recycled materials, and child-safe art supplies. Inside their creations, they place a simple iPad with the Voice Memos app, recording and playing back their own poems, songs, or stories about feelings and imagination. Each fort is decorated to express an emotion or idea (like 'joy', 'curiosity', or 'peace'), blending artistic choices with physical construction. This project lets children express themselves through both building and audio storytelling, sharing their creative spaces and messages with classmates.

ci: Marketplaces reflect the needs and wants of communities.
lo: Needs and wants; The changing needs of communities; The design process

s.d: Students step into the shoes of local shoppers to design an interactive virtual marketplace, choosing stalls and products that reflect the real needs and wants of the Elsternwick community. This hands-on task brings to life the idea that marketplaces mirror what people value and require, as explored through real-world examples. Students work in teams and invite a parent or school staff member to 'shop' in their virtual market, then reflect on what surprised their guests and themselves about what was in high demand. The final artefact is a 3D interactive market map, complete with clickable pop-ups that explain which goods are needs and which are wants, ready to showcase at a family open afternoon. Delightex's Hotspot tool lets students embed audio stories and persuasive sales pitches for each stall, making every corner of their marketplace come alive with student voices. By tackling real-world choices and seeing how different groups prioritise, students build empathy and understand how communities shape ? and are shaped by ? their markets.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students use Animate from Audio (https://new.express.adobe.com/home/tools/animate-from-audio) to bring marketplace characters to life, recording their voices as shopkeepers, customers, or community helpers explaining why certain goods are needs or wants. The teacher guides students through choosing a character and recording a short persuasive pitch or story about a product or service that helps the Elsternwick community. For example, a student might voice a baker explaining why bread is essential, or a toy seller making a case for their latest game. The tool automatically lip-syncs the character to the student's voice, creating a lively animated video. These clips are compiled into a digital 'Marketplace Gallery' that can be shared with families or displayed on the class screen. This activity deepens understanding of community priorities and gives every student a voice in the conversation about what matters most.

Students design a digital survey using Microsoft Forms to collect data on what classmates, teachers, and family members consider needs versus wants in their daily lives. They brainstorm and craft clear, age-appropriate questions, such as 'What is something you cannot live without?' or 'What is something you like to have but do not need?' After distributing the survey, students analyse the responses using Forms' automatic charts and graphs, identifying trends and surprises. Each group creates a summary poster with key findings and a reflection on how different perspectives shape what communities prioritise in marketplaces. This data-driven approach helps students connect maths skills with real-world decision-making and sparks rich discussion about empathy and responsibility.

Students snap photos of everyday objects found in local shops or at home, then use ChatterPix Kids to animate these items as if they could talk. Each object 'speaks' about whether it is a need or a want, and why it matters to people in the community. For example, a loaf of bread might explain its importance for families, while a soccer ball might share how it brings joy but is not essential. Students record their voices and add fun stickers or backgrounds to personalise each talking object. The final collection of animated clips is assembled into a class video wall, sparking conversations about how we make choices in marketplaces. This playful activity builds persuasive language skills and helps students see everyday goods from new perspectives.

With Puppet Pals, students storyboard, voice, and animate short skits where they role-play marketplace designers solving a tricky problem for their community. This brings the design process to life, letting students think like inventors as they brainstorm, prototype, and pitch imaginative stalls or services that help meet changing needs. Teams swap scripts so another group can 'remix' their story from a different perspective ? for example, from the viewpoint of a new family moving to Elsternwick or an elderly resident. The final artefact is a set of playful video skits that can be shared with the Prep classes or uploaded to Seesaw for families to enjoy and comment on. Puppet Pals' custom character maker lets students upload photos of real market spaces and add themselves as digital puppets, giving their stories a unique local flavour. By collaborating and adapting each other's ideas, students learn that great community solutions often come from seeing problems through many different eyes.

Students design and build their own mini marketplace stalls using recycled boxes, fabric scraps, and craft materials, representing different community needs and wants (e.g., food, clothing, toys). Each group creates physical 'goods' for their stall, then codes a Bee-Bot or Sphero Indi to visit other stalls following a marketplace map they draw and decorate. Along the way, students practice exchanging 'needs' and 'wants' tokens and reflect on how their choices impact the community. This project blends creative building, basic robotics, and real-world marketplace concepts, making the design cycle hands-on and meaningful.

ci: Forces and motion are all around us.
lo: Forces around us; Scientific laws of motion; Innovations in technology

s.d: Imagine students transforming the classroom into a living map of motion, where they code Sphero Indi robots to demonstrate push, pull, and the invisible grip of friction. This playful investigation launches the unit's core idea?forces and motion are all around us?by letting learners become inventors of the very obstacles and ramps they want to test. Students take on the role of playground engineers, designing a course inspired by their own playground, then inviting a neighbouring Prep class to race through and predict the outcomes. Each group creates a time-lapse video of their robot's journey, annotated with spoken student reflections about what slowed Indi down or sped it up. The activity comes alive through Indi's advanced colour sensor tiles and the challenge of sequencing moves and repeats?students must debug to achieve the smoothest course. They leave with hands-on proof that scientific thinking can be playful, inventive, and totally in their control.

Students become inventors and scientific storytellers by creating an interactive ebook that explores the everyday wonders of push, pull, gravity, and friction. The project dives into the scientific laws of motion, encouraging students to record their own experiments and turn observations into bite-sized, illustrated explanations. To tie in a fresh angle, students interview a family member or community elder about how simple machines or playground equipment have changed since they were a child?discovering how innovations in technology shape lives. The final product is a multimedia science mini-book that mixes photos, recorded audio, videos, and child-made diagrams, ready to be published on the class blog or shared with families at a community science night. Book Creator's comic templates and embedded audio hotspots let students layer voiceovers and labels onto their images, making the science leap off the page. Young authors walk away with the confidence to explain forces in their own words and the thrill of being published scientists.

Students use Seek by iNaturalist to investigate how different materials and surfaces in the playground or classroom affect the movement of small living things, such as ants or beetles. They observe and identify these creatures, noting which surfaces they prefer and how their bodies help them move. Students then create a comparison chart showing which insects or bugs were found on which materials, linking their findings to the concept of forces and motion. This hands-on investigation helps students connect scientific laws of motion to real-world examples in nature. Teachers can facilitate a discussion about how living things adapt to their environments and how technology can help us study them. The comparison chart can be shared in a class science display.

Students select everyday objects like a soccer ball, seesaw, or backpack and use ChatterPix Kids to animate them with talking mouths and recorded voices. They write and record short scripts explaining the forces acting on their chosen object, such as pushes, pulls, friction, or gravity. Using the app's mouth animation and sound effects, students bring scientific concepts to life by giving objects personalities that describe how forces influence their motion. They create a series of engaging, fact-filled videos that demonstrate their understanding of forces and motion in real-world contexts. These videos are compiled into a digital gallery and shared with peers during assembly, encouraging students to communicate science creatively. This activity blends storytelling with scientific explanation, helping students articulate how forces shape everyday experiences.

Students use Teachable Machine to create a model that recognises different types of movement?such as rolling, sliding, or bouncing?by recording short videos or images of objects in motion. They train the model to classify each movement type, then test it with new examples from classroom experiments. This supports the investigation of forces and motion, helping students make connections between scientific principles and real-world applications. The activity parallels how sports coaching apps and physiotherapy tools use AI to analyse movement for feedback and improvement. Students share their findings and reflect on how technology can help us understand and innovate in the field of motion and forces.

s.t: Marble Run Mayhem: Forces in Action!
s.d: Students will design and build their own wild marble runs using cardboard tubes, recycled boxes, popsticks, paper plates, and masking tape. They will explore forces like gravity, push, pull, and friction as they experiment with different ramps, tunnels, and obstacles. Using iPads and the free 'Stop Motion Studio' app, students will film their marbles in action, creating short movies that highlight how their inventions work. This project brings the science of forces and motion to life through creative engineering, hands-on building, and digital storytelling.

ci: Taking care of our Earth starts with the choices we make.
lo: Earth's resources; How our actions affect the environment; Ways we can care for our planet

s.d: Students program BeeBots to navigate a giant classroom map of Earth's resources, guiding their robots to different stations representing water, forests, soil, and minerals. This hands-on journey sparks thinking about how our choices can help or harm these precious resources?right at the heart of taking care of our Earth. Each group takes on the role of 'planet protectors,' racing to collect and deliver 'resource tokens' to spots where they are most needed, just like real environmental stewards. The final showcase is a lively, interactive floor map with BeeBots zipping between resource zones, which families and other classes are invited to visit. By using the sequence-and-repeat function, students create more efficient routes, learning how smart planning can reduce waste and save energy. They finish with a sense of agency, realising that even small, thoughtful actions can make a big difference for the planet.

Students become eco-reporters, snapping photos of good and bad environmental choices around the school?litter, recycling bins, gardens, and more?then assembling them into persuasive digital posters. This activity gets students thinking deeply about how their actions affect the environment, one of the unit's key lines of inquiry. They interview staff and peers to include different perspectives on how the school community cares for the planet. Their finished products are vibrant, annotated posters that can be displayed around campus or shared with families to spark real change. PicCollage's background removal tool lets students creatively superimpose themselves into their posters as 'Earth Guardians', making their message pop. Students walk away as confident advocates, ready to spot and solve environmental problems wherever they go.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students work with their teacher to create animated eco-heroes using the Animate from Audio feature in Adobe Express (https://new.express.adobe.com/home/tools/animate-from-audio). Each child records their voice sharing a tip for protecting Earth's resources?such as 'turn off the tap while brushing your teeth' or 'put rubbish in the right bin'?and watches as their chosen character lip-syncs the message. The teacher guides students through selecting a character and background that matches their environmental tip, making the process accessible for Year 2. These short, animated clips are compiled into a class video and shown at assembly or shared with families. The activity turns sustainability advice into memorable, student-voiced animations that feel like real TV ads. Students see their ideas come to life and feel empowered to be everyday planet protectors.

Students compose and record catchy jingles or raps about recycling, water saving, or reducing waste using GarageBand, turning environmental action into music. This connects to the idea that taking care of our Earth starts with the choices we make, making sustainability memorable through rhythm and rhyme. They perform their songs for younger classes, sparking a ripple effect of positive action across the school. The finished tracks are shared as a digital album for families and played over the school PA system during Earth Week. GarageBand's Live Loops feature lets students layer sounds and experiment with textures, making even beginners feel like real music producers. By performing for an authentic audience, students gain the courage to use their voices for change.

Students document their personal eco-challenges?like packing a waste-free lunch or turning off lights at home?by creating daily photo or video diaries in Seesaw. This brings the central idea to life, showing how everyday choices add up to real impact. They invite family members to join in and reflect together, sparking conversations beyond the classroom. The final artefact is a week-long digital portfolio, complete with captions and reflections, which can be shared with the whole school community. Seesaw's voice annotation tool allows students to narrate their thinking and share their feelings about the changes they've made. They finish empowered, knowing that their small steps can inspire others and create a greener future.

Students design and build miniature animal habitats using recycled materials like cardboard boxes, fabric scraps, bottle caps, and natural elements such as twigs or leaves. They then program a Sphero Indi robot (or similar age-appropriate robot) to navigate between the habitats, 'delivering' eco-friendly solutions?like tiny recycling bins or water drops they've crafted?to each one. This project lets students explore how caring for different environments supports life on Earth, encouraging creative problem-solving and teamwork while linking local actions to global environmental responsibility.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Landmarks and places of significance tell stories about our history.
lo: The significance of places to different people and cultures; The connection between landmarks and identity; How landmarks and symbols represent our history

s.d: Students use Delightex to design interactive virtual tours of significant Australian and Indigenous landmarks, layering in their own narration and digital artefacts. They begin by selecting a site such as the Birrarung (Yarra River), Uluru, or a local monument, then upload photos, draw symbols, and embed short audio stories that explain the site's meaning to different communities. Delightex's hotspots feature lets students add clickable facts, Dreaming story snippets, or questions for viewers to ponder as they navigate the tour. Each student curates a guided journey that weaves together history, culture, and personal reflection, creating a digital experience for peers and families to explore on iPads. This approach transforms students into digital custodians, blending storytelling and geography in a way that feels immersive and student-led. The final tours can be showcased at a class exhibition or shared with partner schools to spark cross-cultural dialogue.

Students create an animated retelling of a Dreaming story or local Australian landmark legend using Puppet Pals, casting themselves as storytellers and cultural custodians. Exploring how landmarks and symbols represent our history, students immerse in the voices and perspectives of both Indigenous and contemporary communities. They take on the role of travelling storytellers, crafting short puppet show episodes for younger classes and families to spark intergenerational conversations. The final artefact is a vivid digital puppet show, rich with student-recorded narration, character movement, and hand-drawn backgrounds that bring significant places to life. By layering multiple scenes and importing their own art directly into Puppet Pals, students unlock advanced animation flow and creative control beyond the basic features. Through this process, students discover their own power as custodians of place and story?making history meaningful, memorable, and alive for others.

Students will act as 'history detectives', capturing oral histories from family members or community elders about places of significance using Seesaw's audio and video recording tools. This activity explores how personal memories shape our understanding of place, as students discover the connections between landmarks and identity. To add a real-world angle, students curate a digital time capsule?collecting stories, photos, and artefacts that reflect the diversity of their class and neighbourhood. The final product is a multimedia journal entry for each student, published to a private class blog where families can listen, comment, and add their own stories. Seesaw's drawing and annotation tools allow students to highlight special features on photos or maps, making each entry interactive.
