Students leave with a sense of pride in their own heritage and the skills to preserve stories for future generations.

Students will become junior explorers, using the Field Guide to Victoria app to discover and document local Indigenous and Australian landmarks right from the school grounds or on a neighbourhood walk. This hands-on investigation brings the significance of places to different people and cultures to life as students connect real places to stories and meaning. To deepen empathy, students compare their own experiences of these places with those of Traditional Owners, discussing whose stories are told and whose are missing. Each student creates a digital 'Landmark Fact Card' with images, species sightings, and a short story about the place, ready to be shared in a class exhibition for families and community members. The app's built-in species identification and location tagging features help students link natural and cultural landmarks in surprising ways. By seeing their local area through new eyes, students gain a sense of belonging and the confidence to ask powerful questions about place and history.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students will use the Animate from Audio feature in Animating a Character with Adobe Express (https://new.express.adobe.com/home/tools/animate-from-audio) to bring the stories of Australian and Indigenous landmarks to life. Working in small groups with teacher guidance, students record their voices telling a Dreaming story or sharing a legend connected to a significant place, such as the Birrarung (Yarra River) or the Twelve Apostles. They select or design a character?like a river spirit, animal guide, or historical figure?and watch as their narration is lip-synced to the animated character. The final product is a short, engaging video that can be shared at assembly or in a class showcase. This process helps students connect oral storytelling traditions with digital creativity, making the stories of place memorable and meaningful. By animating their voices, students gain confidence in public speaking and a deeper appreciation for the stories embedded in the land.

Students will choose an Australian or Indigenous landmark, then craft a 3D diorama using recycled boxes, tissue paper, and natural materials (like stones, sand, and leaves) to recreate its landscape and features. They'll embed a simple battery-powered LED (with adult help) to illuminate a 'story stone'?a decorated rock that symbolizes the site's unique story or Dreaming. Using iPads, students will record a short audio narration about their landmark's significance, then attach a QR code to their lightbox so visitors can listen to the story. This project combines hands-on building, storytelling, and digital skills to celebrate the connection between place, culture, and history.

ci: Our relationships with others impact our lives.
lo: Importance of relationships; Developing and maintaining healthy relationships; The impact of relationships on wellbeing

s.d: Let students become relationship detectives by curating a digital bookshelf on Epic filled with stories about friendship, belonging, and empathy. As they explore the importance of relationships, each child picks one book that moved them and explains why to the class, connecting their own life to what they read. To deepen the impact, invite students to recommend books for a Prep buddy who might need advice about making new friends. The end result is a living, student-driven library of wisdom, each book annotated with a quick video or audio review using Epic's built-in recording feature. Leverage the platform's Classroom Collections to make personalised shelves visible to both families and future year levels. Suddenly, students aren't just readers?they're curators and guides for others seeking strong, healthy relationships.

Have students code short animated stories in ScratchJr where two characters navigate a friendship challenge, like sharing or apologising after a misunderstanding. This directly explores how we develop and maintain healthy relationships, turning abstract PSPE concepts into concrete, playful dilemmas. Flip the usual classroom dynamic by having students swap iPads, so everyone tries solving a classmate's story challenge from a fresh perspective. Each project is a mini-movie with dialogue, movement, and a genuine problem to resolve?ready for a class 'film festival' showcasing every student's scenario. Tap into ScratchJr's layering and background change features so characters can move through different settings as their relationship evolves. Students walk away as digital storytellers, able to model empathy and problem-solving beyond the playground.

Students work in small groups to explore familiar outdoor spaces like schoolyards, parks or gardens, using Seek by iNaturalist to identify plants, insects and birds they find. They capture photos and use the app's identification feature to learn about each species' name and characteristics. Each group compiles their findings into a digital field guide that highlights common, rare or surprising living things in their environment. Students then discuss how these natural elements influence their wellbeing and social connections, such as favourite play areas or calming spots shared with friends. This hands-on investigation helps students understand how their natural surroundings shape their relationships and daily experiences. The class combines all group guides into a shared display, including reflections on how nature supports healthy relationships.

Invite students to design a 'Feelings Soundboard' using Makey Makey, where pressing different everyday objects triggers audio recordings about experiences with friends?happy, tricky, or supportive moments. This playful project helps students unpack the importance of relationships and how emotions can be managed or shared with others. Cross into music and art by letting students select objects that symbolise friendship, then decorate them to match their stories. The final product is an interactive station for classroom visitors to explore, each touchpoint playing a unique voice message recorded by the creators. Use Makey Makey's mapping of multiple keys to objects so students can represent a whole spectrum of feelings and scenarios. Kids become confident communicators, ready to express their emotions and listen to others in creative ways.

Challenge students to illustrate 'relationship snapshots'?digital paintings that capture a moment of kindness, conflict, or teamwork?using Brushes Redux. As they reflect on how relationships change over time, each child tells a visual story about a friendship's ups and downs, blending art with social-emotional learning. Invite students to act as gallery curators, writing short artist statements and arranging the class's digital exhibition for families and other year levels to explore. The final gallery is an animated slideshow where each artwork slowly reveals itself stroke by stroke, thanks to Brushes Redux's playback feature. Encourage use of layered backgrounds and texture brushes to evoke different moods in each scene. Students discover that every relationship, like every artwork, is unique, layered, and worthy of reflection.

Students work in teams to design and construct colourful 'Friendship Bridges' from cardboard, craft sticks, yarn, and recycled materials, representing the connections between people. Next, they decorate simple Sphero Indi cars as 'Emotion Bots', coding them with coloured tiles to travel across each bridge, pausing at 'emotion stations' where students add hand-drawn emoji signs or calming textures. As the bots journey, classmates explain how different feelings and actions can strengthen or weaken relationships, making the abstract idea of connection tangible. This playful project blends physical building, basic robotics, and social-emotional storytelling to help students understand and reflect on the bridges they build with others.

ci: Celebrations and traditions shape the culture of a community.
lo: The ways personal and cultural events are celebrated; Our appreciation of the diversity of cultures; How celebrations shape community identity

s.d: Students become roving reporters, creating a podcast series that explores how celebrations and traditions shape the culture of a community. This taps directly into the line of inquiry about the ways personal and cultural events are celebrated, as students interview classmates, family members, and staff about their most meaningful traditions. Imagine the buzz as students step into the role of cultural detectives, uncovering hidden stories and amplifying voices that might otherwise go unheard. The final artefact is a polished audio episode?complete with theme music and student-led narration?shared with families and even featured at a school assembly. By using multi-track recording and sound layering, students can weave in music, ambient sounds from real celebrations, and even language snippets from around the world. Students finish with a sense of pride as cultural ambassadors, confident in their ability to capture and celebrate diversity through the power of storytelling.

The teacher creates a Wise Discussion Chatbot using the Character Interview scenario and sets the bot's role as Ava, a community celebration organiser explaining why particular traditions matter to different families. The topic is "How We Express Ourselves: Celebrations and traditions shape the culture of a community.". Students chat with the bot to explore a named perspective through guided questioning rather than general research; for example, they ask "How does this celebration show what your community values?" and "What might outsiders misunderstand about this tradition?". After the chat, students produce a question bank plus a short perspective-and-evidence summary that compares the chatbot responses with unit sources linked explicitly to How We Express Ourselves.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students create animated characters that retell a favourite family or cultural celebration, using their own recorded voices to bring the story to life. This connects beautifully with the line of inquiry about how celebrations shape community identity, as students reflect on what makes their traditions meaningful. They get to flip the script by animating not just their own stories, but also those of classmates?swapping scripts and learning to see celebrations through someone else's eyes. The finished artefact is a collection of short, animated videos where each character's mouth moves in sync with the student's voice, ready to be premiered at a multicultural film festival for the year level. Animating a Character with Adobe Express's lip-syncing and custom character creation tools make each video feel truly personal and dynamic. Students walk away with creative confidence and a deeper empathy for the stories that shape their community.

Students build a living digital wall of celebrations, pinning photos, recipes, artefacts, and stories from their own families and cultures. This directly supports the investigation into the ways personal and cultural events are celebrated, as students see firsthand the rich tapestry of traditions within their classroom. To deepen the experience, students invite family members or community guests to contribute posts or voice notes, turning the Padlet into a true community collaboration. The final artefact is a dynamic, multimedia Padlet board?organised by celebration or region?shared with the wider school community during Harmony Week. Padlet's map view lets students place celebrations on a world map, visually connecting traditions to their places of origin. Students leave with a sense of global citizenship and the joy of seeing their own heritage valued alongside others.

Students become cultural historians, creating interactive explainer videos that compare how two different cultures celebrate the same event (like New Year or harvest festivals). This activity links to the line of inquiry about how celebrations shape community identity and encourages students to notice both similarities and differences. Students are tasked with designing their video as a teaching tool for next year's Year 3 cohort, making their explanations clear, lively, and engaging. The final artefact is an interactive Explain Everything video?complete with voiceover, animated drawings, and clickable hotspots for bonus facts or quizzes?that can be shared on the school's digital showcase. Using Explain Everything's live collaboration feature, students can co-create scenes in real time, adding layers of creativity and teamwork. Students finish with the skills to break down complex ideas and the satisfaction of leaving a legacy for future learners.

Students will work in teams to design and build vibrant 3D 'towers' representing a celebration or tradition from their own or another culture. Using cardboard, fabric, recycled materials, clay, LED tea lights, and decorative craft supplies, they will construct physical towers featuring key symbols, artifacts, and elements of their chosen celebration. Then, students will embed simple programmable micro:bit messages or sound bites (recorded on micro:bit or Makey Makey soundboards) into their towers, sharing stories or greetings in different languages. This project fuses hands-on making with digital storytelling, encouraging students to express cultural identity and diversity in a memorable, interactive way.

ci: The rights and responsibilities of citizens are determined by the rules and laws of a community.
lo: The differences between rules and laws; People responsible for enforcing rules and laws; Rights and responsibilities of citizens; The consequences when rules, laws and rights are not met

s.d: Students will step into the Minecraft: Active Citizen world (https://education.minecraft.net/en-us/lessons/active-citizen) to explore how Nobel Peace Laureates shaped communities by standing up for rights and responsibilities. As they journey through stories of real change-makers, students grapple with the difference between rules and laws and the ripple effects of challenging or upholding them. Each student becomes a reporter, interviewing in-game characters and reflecting on how their own choices might impact their community. The final artefact is a digital scrapbook created in Minecraft, filled with screenshots, in-game journal entries, and 'citizen action plans' for their own school or neighbourhood. Students will use Minecraft's Book & Quill tool to record and export their reflections, combining text and images in a way that feels like real-world reporting. By seeing their ideas come alive in a 3D world, students gain the confidence to imagine themselves as active citizens beyond the classroom.

Students will design an interactive 'Guide to Rules and Laws' as a digital book, breaking down tricky concepts for younger students at Wesley. This links directly to the line of inquiry about the differences between rules and laws, as students must clarify and illustrate examples from both school and society. Students will include 'What if?' scenarios?inviting readers to imagine communities without certain rules or laws, and to debate the consequences. The finished product is a vibrant, clickable eBook featuring student-drawn comics, audio explanations, and branching choices for the reader. Book Creator's comic templates and audio hotspots allow students to blend storytelling, visuals, and voice in a way that feels like an interactive adventure. By teaching others, students realise they can break down complex ideas and make a real difference in their community.

Students use Dollar Street to compare how rules, laws, and responsibilities are experienced in homes from different countries and income levels. They explore the platform's photo galleries and family stories, focusing on images that show daily routines, safety measures, and community participation. Students select two or three families and create a visual comparison chart highlighting similarities and differences in how rules are followed or enforced at home, such as curfews, chores, or access to education. This connects directly to the inquiry into how rights and responsibilities are shaped by community context. As a real-world parallel, Dollar Street's AI-driven categorisation of household features mirrors how social researchers use image recognition to analyse living conditions globally. Students present their comparison charts and reflect on how context shapes the rights and responsibilities of citizens.

Students will become quizmasters, designing a fast-paced Kahoot challenge titled 'Rights, Rules and Real-Life Consequences' for their peers. This sharpens their understanding of what happens when rules, laws, and rights are ignored or upheld, directly tying into the unit's focus on consequences. Students must include real-life news stories or school scenarios, prompting classmates to debate what should happen next. The final artefact is a live, student-led Kahoot session, where the whole year level competes and discusses the trickiest questions together. By using Kahoot's 'Puzzle' question type, students can create questions that require sequencing events or matching causes to effects, not just picking the right answer. Running the quiz builds students' confidence as communicators and helps them see the real-world impact of choices in their own and others' lives.

Students will program Sphero BOLT robots to navigate a custom-built 'Community Board Game', where each square represents a rule, law, or citizen right. Linking to the unit's exploration of rights and responsibilities, students must code their Sphero to react differently when landing on spaces?sometimes advancing, sometimes pausing, sometimes solving a challenge. For a new angle, teams can swap board designs and try to adapt their code to handle unexpected rules, sparking conversations about fairness and adaptability. The final artefact is a filmed robot run-through, with students narrating the journey and reflecting on how the rules shaped their robot's fate. Sphero's sensor-triggered actions and custom LED animations let students make their robots 'react' to different board spaces in creative ways. Students walk away with hands-on coding skills and a fresh appreciation for how systems and rules shape real-world outcomes.

s.t: Rule City: Build & Govern Your Own Mini-Town
s.d: Students work in teams to design and construct a model town using cardboard, recycled boxes, craft sticks, and fabric scraps, creating roads, buildings, parks, and community spaces. Once built, each group invents a set of town rules and laws (displayed on hand-made signs), then programs a Sphero Indi or Bee-Bot as a 'citizen' to navigate common scenarios?like crossing streets or visiting the library?while following these rules. Teams test, revise, and reflect on how their rules shape daily life in their town, connecting physical making with digital problem-solving and the real-world impact of systems, laws, and citizenship.

ci: Humans use their understanding of scientific principles to take action.
lo: The work of scientists; The process of learning; How science brings about new understandings and changes

s.d: Students will step inside a virtual sustainable building using Minecraft Education's 'It's Good To Be Green' lesson (https://education.minecraft.net/en-us/lessons/its-good-to-be-green), exploring how scientific principles shape eco-friendly design. This directly brings alive the line of inquiry about how science sparks new understandings and changes in the world around us. Students become environmental consultants, critiquing the building's features and suggesting improvements for real spaces at Wesley College. Their final artefact is a narrated Minecraft tour video, guiding families through the virtual building and pitching their own sustainable upgrade ideas. They'll use Minecraft's in-game camera and book-and-quill to collect evidence and annotate their discoveries, then screen-record their walkthroughs for a polished presentation. Students walk away empowered to see themselves as changemakers, ready to spot?and fix?sustainability challenges in their own community.

Students become science detectives, using Explain Everything to record and annotate their own fair-test experiments on energy transformation or states of matter. This activity brings the process of learning and the scientific method to life, showing how scientists test and refine their ideas. Each group takes on the challenge of explaining a common misconception (like 'cold is a thing' or 'bigger objects fall faster') to a younger class, using diagrams, voiceovers, and step-by-step explanations. The final product is a dynamic, interactive video lesson that can be shared with Year 2 students or uploaded to the school website as a 'myth-busting' mini-series. Students harness Explain Everything's infinite canvas and layering tools to zoom in, annotate, and even animate tricky science concepts?far beyond a basic slideshow. By teaching others, they build real confidence in their scientific reasoning and communication skills.

Students will create a digital science biography using Book Creator, spotlighting a scientist whose work has changed the world. This taps into the line of inquiry about the work of scientists and the impact of their discoveries. Students will write from the scientist's point of view, crafting journal entries that reveal not only what they discovered but also the obstacles and failures along the way. The finished artefact is an interactive ebook, complete with voice recordings, photos, and clickable timelines, ready to be showcased at the Year 3 science fair and shared with families online. They'll use Book Creator's comic templates and audio hotspots to bring the scientists' stories vividly to life. By stepping into the shoes of real scientists, students see that discovery is messy, exciting, and always within reach.

Students become energy detectives, building and programming Micro:bit devices to monitor and display real-time classroom energy use. By investigating energy transformation as part of the scientific method, they learn how data can spark meaningful change. Students take on the role of sustainability advisors, using their findings to persuade the school community to adopt smarter energy habits. Each group creates a digital energy dashboard on their Micro:bit, with scrolling messages and animated icons that visualise both the problem and their proposed solution?ready for display at assembly or on the classroom door. The project leverages the Micro:bit's data-logging and radio communication features, allowing live comparisons between different rooms or teams. Through this hands-on mission, students discover how young scientists can use technology, data, and persuasive communication to take action for a more sustainable world.

Students will produce a short animated explainer using Adobe Express, unpacking how a key scientific principle (like insulation or energy transfer) solves a real-world problem. This activity highlights the central idea that humans use science to take meaningful action. Students take on the role of science communicators, scripting and animating their message for a real audience?like local council members or sustainability leaders. Their final artefact is a punchy, voice-animated video (using 'Animate from Audio') that can be shared on the school website or emailed to community partners. They'll dive into Adobe Express's 'Animate from Audio' feature to bring their narration to life with custom characters and motion. Students leave knowing their voices?and their science?can spark real change beyond the classroom.

Students design and build a spectacular Rube Goldberg-style chain reaction machine that demonstrates different types of energy transformation (e.g., potential to kinetic, motion to sound). Using recycled cardboard, marbles, dominoes, balloons, string, plastic bottles, and more, teams prototype each step and connect them for a dramatic final effect. They record their machine in action using an iPad, then use the Clips app to add voiceovers explaining each energy change and how scientific principles make their carnival contraption work. This hands-on challenge immerses students in the design cycle and links scientific understanding to creative problem-solving and real-world innovation.

ci: Adaptation and sustainability ensure the survival of living things in changing environments.
lo: Adaptations and structural features of living things; Roles of living things in an ecosystem; Actions that benefit or harm ecosystems

s.d: Students use Seek by iNaturalist to observe and identify living things in their local environment, such as insects, plants or birds in the schoolyard or nearby park. Working in pairs, they photograph and log their findings, using the app's identification features to learn about adaptations and roles in the ecosystem. Each pair selects one organism to research further, focusing on its unique adaptations and how it contributes to ecosystem balance. Students then create a short profile card for their chosen species, including a photo, key adaptations, and a description of its role. This hands-on investigation deepens understanding of how living things survive and thrive in changing environments. The class assembles a collaborative wall of local species, highlighting the importance of biodiversity and sustainability.

Students take on the role of ecosystem detectives, using National Geographic MapMaker to build interactive maps that track how living things interact and depend on each other across different biomes. This activity dives into the line of inquiry about 'roles of living things in an ecosystem' by mapping out food webs, migration routes, or habitat boundaries. To make it real, students choose a local or global ecosystem and imagine they are advising a team of conservationists on where to focus their efforts. Their finished map is a digital, annotated masterpiece with layers, icons, and pop-up facts, ready to be shared in a virtual gallery walk for the school community. MapMaker's custom drawing and annotation tools let students add their own shapes, lines, and notes?so every map tells a unique story. Students walk away seeing the world as a network of connections, empowered to think spatially about how every action can ripple through an ecosystem.

Students use Dollar Street to investigate how families around the world adapt their homes and daily lives to different environments. They browse photos and stories, focusing on adaptations in clothing, shelter, and food storage across various climates and ecosystems. Students select two families living in contrasting environments?such as a tropical region and a desert?and create a side-by-side poster or digital display showing how each family's adaptations help them survive and thrive. This activity links to the unit's focus on adaptation and sustainability. Dollar Street's AI-powered tagging of household features is similar to how environmental scientists use image classification to study adaptation strategies in diverse communities. Students share their displays and discuss how adaptation supports sustainability in changing environments.

The teacher creates a Wise Discussion Chatbot using the Project Ideation scenario and sets the bot's role as Leo, a student sustainability coach helping teams turn inquiry questions into realistic action projects. The topic is "Sharing the Planet: Adaptation and sustainability ensure the survival of living things in changing environments.". Students chat with the bot to test and refine possible inquiry actions or design ideas before committing to one plan; for example, they ask "What small change could our class actually test this week?" and "How will we know if our action helped?". After the chat, students produce a one-page project proposal naming the chosen idea, success criteria, resources, first prototype/action step and how it connects to the unit linked explicitly to Sharing the Planet.

Students use Padlet to create a collaborative debate wall where they post arguments and perspectives from different living things within an ecosystem, such as pollinators like bees, predators like owls, or plants competing for sunlight. They design posts that include text, images, and links to research, representing each organism's adaptations and survival needs. Using Padlet's threaded comments, students respond to peers with evidence-based counterarguments or support, simulating real ecosystem interactions and conflicts. This interactive platform helps students explore the roles and relationships of living things while practising communication and critical thinking. The final Padlet wall becomes a dynamic, visual ecosystem dialogue that can be shared with parents and other classes. Through this, students deepen their understanding of how adaptations and actions affect ecosystem balance and sustainability.

Students will design and build a unique animal using clay, recycled materials, and craft supplies, inventing imaginative adaptations to help it survive in a chosen ecosystem. Next, they'll construct a matching 3D habitat diorama using cardboard, fabric scraps, and natural elements, ensuring it includes features that support their animal's needs. Using Sphero Indi robots, students will code a simple 'migration' route for their creature?laying out coloured tiles and obstacles within their habitat diorama to simulate real-world challenges like finding food or shelter. This cross-disciplinary project brings adaptation and sustainability to life, connecting creativity, coding, and hands-on making to the big ideas of Sharing the Planet.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Exploration leads to new discoveries that can shape and change society.
lo: The factors that motivate exploration (Causation); How people reflect on discoveries from the past to inform change (Change); How exploration brings about change and new understandings for people, places and society (Change)

s.d: Let your students step into the shoes of famous explorers and changemakers in 'Meet and Greet!' from the Minecraft Education library. This immersive activity brings the central idea to life by letting students build a 3D timeline and interact with figures whose discoveries have shaped society. Students take on the role of museum curators, choosing which Australian or global explorers to feature and debating whose journeys most changed the world. Their final artefact is a virtual museum filled with custom-built exhibits and interactive signs that can be toured by families or other classes. Students will use Minecraft's NPC (non-player character) and sign features to create dialogue and information for each explorer, making the experience truly interactive. They'll walk away with a sense of how exploration sparks new ideas?and the confidence to see themselves as future discoverers.

Students use Dollar Street to explore how exploration and discovery have shaped societies by examining the homes and possessions of families from different countries and time periods. They select families from regions historically impacted by exploration and compare items such as maps, tools, and means of transport. Students create a timeline or annotated collage that illustrates how discoveries?like new foods, technologies, or materials?have influenced daily life. This connects to the inquiry into how exploration brings about change. Dollar Street's AI-driven organisation of household artefacts is similar to how museums use digital cataloguing to track the evolution of everyday objects. Students present their collages and explain how exploration has changed societies over time.

Students use Teachable Machine to create a model that recognises different types of exploration artefacts?such as maps, compasses, or navigation tools?by uploading images or taking photos. They train the model to classify each artefact, then challenge classmates to test the model with new items or images. This activity connects to the study of exploration and how discoveries are made and recorded. The process mirrors how museum cataloguing systems and digital archives use AI to identify and sort historical objects. Students present their classifier's results and discuss how technology can help us preserve and learn from the past.

Students become filmmakers as they use Stop Motion Studio to animate a pivotal moment of exploration?like the arrival of the First Fleet or a dramatic encounter between explorers and Indigenous Australians. This activity brings the line of inquiry about how exploration brings about change and new understandings to life through visual storytelling. Students are challenged to show both excitement and conflict, or to imagine how the event might have unfolded differently with more dialogue and empathy. Their finished stop-motion films can be screened at a school film festival or shared with a partner class overseas. They'll experiment with Stop Motion Studio's onion-skinning and voiceover features, adding layers of movement and authentic narration. Students leave with creative skills and a new appreciation for how stories of discovery can be told in many ways.

Students become cartographers tasked with mapping the journeys of famous explorers who shaped Australian history and global understanding. By tracing real routes and annotating key turning points, they dive into the line of inquiry on how exploration brings about change and new understandings for people, places and society. Each group must step into the perspective of an explorer or Indigenous community, debating in-character about the impacts and motivations behind these journeys. Their finished artefact is an interactive digital map layered with annotated routes, historical context, and reflective voice notes, ready to be shared with families and displayed in a year-level showcase. MapMaker's layer and annotation features let students overlay Indigenous place names and pre-colonial geography, revealing how discovery is shaped by perspective. Through this process, learners gain an active sense of agency in interpreting history and appreciate the power of maps to tell many stories, not just one.

Students will design and build their own 'exploration rovers' using recycled materials, wheels, and craft supplies, then program Sphero Indi robots to navigate a giant collaborative map representing different historical exploration routes (like the First Fleet or Indigenous trade paths). Along the journey, students will create and hide miniature 'time capsule artifacts' inside their rovers?handmade items or messages representing discoveries or moments in history. As they test and refine their rovers' journeys using the Design Cycle, students reflect on how exploration changes societies and what messages or objects might matter to future generations. This project fuses hands-on building, digital navigation, and historical imagination, making learning about past explorations a memorable adventure.

ci: An inquiry into the nature of the self; beliefs and values; personal, physical, mental, social and spiritual health; human relationships.
lo: Lines of inquiry to be confirmed once planner is uploaded

s.d: Students use Seek by iNaturalist to investigate living things around the school grounds or a nearby park, capturing photos and identifying species such as native plants, insects, and birds. In small groups, they collect data on at least five different organisms, using the app's identification badges and observation features to record details. Each group researches how their chosen species supports human health and community wellbeing, focusing on roles like pollination, air purification, or cultural significance. Students then design a digital poster or slideshow using their photos, species facts, and personal reflections on how nature influences mental and social health. This activity deepens their understanding of biodiversity's role in wellbeing and encourages thoughtful connections between people and the environment. The final presentations are shared in a class gallery walk to inspire discussion about personal and community health through nature.

Students become resilience coaches by designing interactive scenarios in Delightex, where classmates face digital 'choose your own adventure' challenges about friendship, setbacks, and staying safe. This hands-on activity brings to life the central idea of how we respond to setbacks and manage change, letting students test strategies in a safe, playful way. By swapping scenarios and giving each other feedback, they see firsthand how different choices can shape outcomes and relationships. Their finished artefact is an interactive story or simulation that classmates?and even younger grades?can play through, sparking real discussion about what works and what doesn't. Delightex's branching scenario builder lets students weave in multiple paths and consequences, pushing them to think beyond right and wrong answers. Students leave with the confidence to tackle tricky situations, knowing they've practised and reflected on what it means to bounce back.

Students dive into Epic's digital library to curate a 'Resilience Reads' collection, hand-picking picture books, comics, and articles that show characters overcoming obstacles and building healthy friendships. This ties directly to the inquiry into personal responsibility and positive relationships, as students analyse how fictional and real people handle setbacks. They take on the role of book reviewers, creating video or audio recommendations for their classmates and even for the school newsletter. The final artefact is a multimedia reading guide?complete with student reviews and suggested discussion questions?shared with families to encourage resilience conversations at home. Epic's built-in annotation and quiz features let students highlight powerful moments and pose thought-provoking questions to their peers. By the end, students see themselves as reading mentors and critical thinkers, ready to inspire others to grow through challenges.

Invite students to compose 'soundtracks of resilience' in GarageBand, crafting original music that expresses the emotions felt when facing challenges or celebrating supportive friendships. This creative process taps into the unit's exploration of mental and social health, helping students reflect on how music can shift moods and build community. Students collaborate with another class to swap tracks and guess the stories or feelings behind each composition, sparking empathy and deeper listening. The final product is a class album?complete with liner notes explaining each track's inspiration?shared at assembly or uploaded for families to enjoy. GarageBand's Live Loops and multi-track layering allow students to experiment with complex textures and moods, far beyond basic recording. Students finish with a new way to express themselves and a toolkit for using music to boost their own and others' wellbeing.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students use Adobe Express's Animate from Audio feature (https://new.express.adobe.com/home/tools/animate-from-audio) to create animated characters that role-play challenging friendship scenarios and safe online interactions. They write scripts exploring empathy, boundaries, and respectful communication, then record their voices to bring these characters to life with natural lip-syncing. Each student produces a short animated dialogue that models positive responses to common social challenges, such as resolving conflicts or asking for help. This activity deepens their understanding of personal and social health by practising perspective-taking and communication skills. Students share their animations in small groups to spark discussion about healthy relationships and digital citizenship. The finished animations become a resource for peers to reflect on managing emotions and interactions both online and face-to-face.

s.t: Resilience Road: Build Your Own Journey Board Game
s.d: Students design and construct a 3D board game that represents a journey through life's challenges and triumphs, using cardboard, recycled materials, clay, and craft supplies for pathways, obstacles, and character tokens. They integrate simple interactive elements with Makey Makey or micro:bit to trigger sound effects or messages when players land on key spaces, blending physical making with digital creativity. Each game space features scenarios about overcoming setbacks and building friendships, encouraging students to reflect on their own strategies for resilience and safety. By inventing and playing their unique games, students collaboratively explore growth mindset and positive relationships in a memorable, hands-on way.

ci: Technology transforms how we create and share ideas.
lo: How technology expands creative possibilities; The evolution of communication tools; The impact of technology on expression

s.d: Students become digital storytellers by remixing the history of communication?each group picks a key invention, from the printing press to social media, and animates its impact using Explain Everything's interactive whiteboard. This launches a hands-on exploration of how technology constantly expands creative possibilities for sharing ideas. To shake things up, students reimagine how people might have expressed themselves if their chosen technology existed centuries earlier, sparking wild, cross-era mashups. The finished artefact is a narrated, animated timeline where students' voices and drawings bring the evolution of expression to life, ready to be showcased to families at a Communication Through the Ages gallery. By mastering Explain Everything's advanced animation paths and interactive hot spots, students can make their timelines dynamic and clickable. Suddenly, they don't just learn about history?they get to rewrite it, and see themselves as inventors shaping how communities connect.

Unleash creativity by having students compose original theme music and sound effects that capture the mood of different forms of digital expression?imagine the 'ping' of an email vs. The warmth of a handwritten letter. This dives deep into the impact of technology on expression, using sound as a universal language. Students swap roles with media producers: their compositions will become the soundtrack for real communication tool exhibitions created by Year 2s, who will curate artefacts with the soundscapes playing in the background. The final product is a playlist of student-made tracks, each labelled with the communication tool and emotion it's meant to evoke?shared with the school community via QR codes at the gallery. GarageBand's Live Loops let students layer beats, voices, and even environmental sounds for rich, textured audio. Along the way, they discover how sound transforms a message's meaning, and they gain the confidence to express ideas in ways that words alone can't.

Students step into the shoes of future designers by building immersive 3D scenes in Delightex that imagine the next leap in communication?think hologram postcards or empathy-boosting message pods. This directly explores how technology can expand creative possibilities, challenging students to invent what comes after today's smartphones and social media. By presenting their visions to an expert panel of local tech mentors (in-person or via video), students get real feedback and see their ideas as part of a bigger conversation. The class creates a virtual exhibition of these speculative worlds, opening it up online for families, peers, and even guest visitors to 'walk through' and vote on the most inspiring concept. Delightex's scene-linking and interactive object features let students build explorable interconnected environments, not just static dioramas. Students experience the thrill of turning blue-sky ideas into virtual reality, ready to imagine themselves as tomorrow's innovators.

Students become communication detectives, curating a living, interactive timeline of communication tools using Padlet's timeline view?tracking everything from ancient smoke signals to the latest emojis. This brings the line of inquiry on the evolution of communication tools to life in a format students can keep updating as new inventions emerge. Students add a 'future forecast' section: they must predict and justify what might come next, inviting their families to contribute ideas from home. The result is a collaborative, multimedia timeline filled with student-drawn images, voice clips, and even short video interviews with grandparents about technologies from their childhoods. Padlet's audio and video commenting features allow for rich, layered discussion and feedback that bridges generations and perspectives. Students walk away seeing themselves as historians and visionaries, able to spot patterns and wonder what's possible next.

The teacher creates a Wise Discussion Chatbot using the Project Ideation scenario and sets the bot's role as Kai, a project coach who helps students narrow broad inquiry ideas into one practical proposal. The topic is "How We Express Ourselves: Technology transforms how we create and share ideas.". Students chat with the bot to test and refine possible inquiry actions or design ideas before committing to one plan; for example, they ask "Which idea best connects to our central idea?" and "What resources, success criteria and next steps do you need?". After the chat, students produce a one-page project proposal naming the chosen idea, success criteria, resources, first prototype/action step and how it connects to the unit linked explicitly to How We Express Ourselves.

s.t: Wearable Message Makers: Light-Up Expression Bands
s.d: Students will design and craft their own wearable 'expression bands'?wristbands or headbands made from felt, recycled fabric, and cardboard?that light up to share a personal message or mood. Using simple circuits with LEDs and coin cell batteries, they'll integrate their chosen symbols, words, or emojis into the band, learning about both creative self-expression and basic electronics. Students will sketch, prototype, and refine their designs using the Design Cycle, then share how their wearable tech communicates ideas in new, interactive ways. This project brings together technology, hands-on making, and the evolving ways we express ourselves to others.

ci: Systems connect us.
lo: Human systems; The interconnections that exist within and across systems; The influence of systems on communities

s.d: Step into the bustling world of Minecraft's Sustainable Food Production lesson (https://education.minecraft.net/en-us/lessons/sustainable-food-production), where students trace the journey of food from farm to table and back again through waste and recycling. This immersive simulation lets students see first-hand how human systems?like farming, packaging, and waste management?are all interconnected and shape communities. As they move through virtual farms, recycling centres, and grocery stores, students take on the role of sustainability detectives, asking tough questions about what makes a system fair or sustainable for everyone. Their final portfolio is a digital map and photo-journal, created in-game, that follows a single item through every step of the system, highlighting the invisible connections that keep everything running. The in-game camera and book-and-quill features let students capture, annotate, and export their discoveries for a class exhibition or family showcase. By the end, students see themselves as part of the system?and start spotting opportunities to make real change in their own world.

The teacher creates a Wise Discussion Chatbot using the Project Ideation scenario and sets the bot's role as Leo, a student sustainability coach helping teams turn inquiry questions into realistic action projects. The topic is "How We Organise Ourselves: Systems connect us.". Students chat with the bot to test and refine possible inquiry actions or design ideas before committing to one plan; for example, they ask "What small change could our class actually test this week?" and "How will we know if our action helped?". After the chat, students produce a one-page project proposal naming the chosen idea, success criteria, resources, first prototype/action step and how it connects to the unit linked explicitly to How We Organise Ourselves.

With Lego Spike Prime, students engineer and code their own working models of everyday systems?like a rubbish sorting machine or a traffic light network. This hands-on build gets students deep into the nuts and bolts of 'interconnections that exist within and across systems', making abstract ideas tangible. Students swap roles as engineers, testers, and system 'hackers', trying to break or improve each other's designs to see how resilient and adaptable real systems need to be. Their final artefact is a filmed demonstration and pitch, where they show off their model in action and explain what happens when one part is tweaked or removed. Advanced coding blocks?like sensor feedback and conditional loops?let students create systems that respond to real-world changes, not just follow a set sequence. By the end, they see themselves as inventors who can spot problems and design better solutions for their community.

Students use Dollar Street to investigate how different human systems?such as transport, communication, and sanitation?are represented in homes around the world. They browse the platform's photo galleries, focusing on images that show infrastructure like water sources, toilets, and kitchens. Students select three families from different continents and income levels, then create an illustrated infographic comparing how each family accesses basic systems. This links to the inquiry into how systems connect communities. Dollar Street's AI categorises household features in a way similar to how urban planners use image data to assess infrastructure needs globally. Students share their infographics and discuss how access to systems influences quality of life.

Students become community researchers by designing and running a survey in Microsoft Forms to uncover how different people experience and rely on systems at school or home. This inquiry dives into the influence of systems on communities, letting students collect real data and spot patterns they might not expect. Students compare responses between different groups?like students, teachers, and parents?to see whose voices are heard most and whose might be missing. Their final artefact is an interactive data dashboard, where they visualise the results and pose questions for action or improvement. Microsoft Forms' branching logic feature lets students create adaptive surveys that respond to answers, making the research more personalised and meaningful. By the end, students see themselves as changemakers who can use data to spark conversations and shape better systems.

s.t: Eco-Systems in Motion: Sphero Smart City Challenge
s.d: Students design and build a vibrant miniature cityscape using recycled cardboard, bottle caps, fabric scraps, and natural materials, mapping out roads, parks, and key 'system' zones like recycling centres and compost stations. Working in teams, they code Sphero robots to represent 'waste trucks', programming routes to collect and deliver materials through their interconnected city systems. Along the way, they must troubleshoot breakdowns or blockages, redesigning physical features or code to keep their city running smoothly. This hands-on project highlights how human-made and natural systems interact, and empowers students to creatively explore sustainability and organisation in their own community.

ci: Changes to the Earth impact environment and communities.
lo: The causes of geological change over time; How extreme environments cause natural disasters; The impact of natural events on communities

s.d: Students use Teachable Machine to train a model that recognises images of different natural disasters?such as earthquakes, floods, and bushfires?by uploading photos or drawings. They teach the model to classify each event, then test it with new images to see how accurately it identifies disasters. This activity supports the investigation of geological change and the impact of natural events on communities. The process is similar to how emergency response systems use AI to quickly identify disaster types from satellite or drone imagery. Students evaluate their model's strengths and limitations, reflecting on how technology can support disaster preparedness and response.

Students become disaster detectives, creating interactive maps that trace the paths and impacts of real bushfires, floods, and earthquakes using National Geographic MapMaker. This mapping mission ties directly to exploring how natural events shape communities and environments over time. As a challenge, students compare a local Victorian event with a global disaster, asking: how do different communities prepare, respond, and rebuild? Their final product is a detailed, annotated digital map with custom markers, photos, and embedded notes, ready to be displayed on the big screen at assembly or shared with families via QR code. The tool's drawing and annotation layers let students overlay evacuation routes, damage zones, and before-and-after satellite imagery for a truly immersive map. Students finish with a geographer's eye for patterns and a sense of how mapped information can drive real-world action.

Students direct and film stop-motion disaster stories, using clay, Lego, or found objects to re-enact the chain of events in a bushfire or earthquake. This creative filmmaking connects to the line of inquiry about the causes and effects of geological change, as students break down complex processes into visual sequences. To deepen empathy, students are challenged to tell the story from the perspective of a community member, an animal, or even the land itself. The finished film is a short, soundtracked stop-motion movie, ready for a school film festival or to be sent to local emergency services as a thank-you. Stop Motion Studio's onion-skinning and time-lapse features empower students to create smooth, professional scenes that highlight both chaos and recovery. They leave as confident storytellers, able to communicate big scientific ideas through small, powerful visuals.

The teacher creates a Wise Discussion Chatbot using the Project Ideation scenario and sets the bot's role as Leo, a student sustainability coach helping teams turn inquiry questions into realistic action projects. The topic is "How the World Works: Changes to the Earth impact environment and communities.". Students chat with the bot to test and refine possible inquiry actions or design ideas before committing to one plan; for example, they ask "What small change could our class actually test this week?" and "How will we know if our action helped?". After the chat, students produce a one-page project proposal naming the chosen idea, success criteria, resources, first prototype/action step and how it connects to the unit linked explicitly to How the World Works.

Students design and build interactive surveys and quizzes using Microsoft Forms to explore community responses to natural disasters. They create scenario-based questions that ask peers to choose how they would react as scientists, emergency responders, or local residents during events like floods or bushfires. Using Forms' branching logic, students craft different pathways that reflect the consequences of each decision, allowing respondents to experience multiple perspectives. The final product is a dynamic, student-created decision tree quiz that captures diverse viewpoints on disaster management and environmental change. This activity deepens understanding of how communities respond to geological and extreme environmental events by simulating real-world choices. Students analyse response data and present insights on common strategies and challenges faced by affected communities.

s.t: Disaster-Proof Dream Homes: Shake, Splash & Blaze Challenge
s.d: Students design and build model houses using cardboard, craft sticks, foil, and recycled materials, then test their resilience against simulated natural disasters. Using Dash robots equipped with attachments (like a 'shaker' arm, fan, or water sprayer), students create mini earthquakes, floods, and bushfires to challenge their constructions. Teams iterate on their designs using the Design Cycle, learning about scientific principles behind disaster-resistant architecture and community safety. The project connects engineering, creativity, and real-world problem-solving, making the science of natural disasters unforgettable.

ci: Country, language and community are significant to the lives of First Nations people.
lo: The diversity of First Nations people; The importance of community, family and kinship; The importance of Country to First Nations people

s.d: Students become digital explorers, using the Field Guide to Victoria app to investigate the native plants and animals that have shaped First Nations connections to Country. This hands-on discovery ties directly to the unit's focus on the importance of Country to First Nations people, revealing the living knowledge behind every landscape. Students become local wildlife detectives, sharing their findings with a real environmental group or inviting a community Elder to discuss how these species feature in oral histories. Each student curates a digital field journal, complete with their own photos, species notes, and reflections on how these living things connect to culture and language. The app's built-in audio calls and Indigenous language names let students listen to animal sounds and learn the traditional names for each species?bringing language and land together in a way that's unforgettable. By the end, students see their own neighbourhood through new eyes and understand that Country is alive, storied, and deeply cared for.

The teacher creates a Wise Discussion Chatbot using the Character Interview scenario and sets the bot's role as Dr Maya Chen, a wildlife ecologist advising the class about local habitats. The topic is "Sharing the Planet: Country, language and community are significant to the lives of First Nations people.". Students chat with the bot to explore a named perspective through guided questioning rather than general research; for example, they ask "Which adaptation would help this species survive a hotter summer?" and "What human action is putting this habitat under pressure?". After the chat, students produce a question bank plus a short perspective-and-evidence summary that compares the chatbot responses with unit sources linked explicitly to Sharing the Planet.

Students become radio hosts, producing a short podcast series where they interview local First Nations community members or share stories inspired by Indigenous literature. This activity brings to life the unit's inquiry into the importance of community, family, and kinship by capturing real voices and lived experiences. Students work in teams as producers, scriptwriters, and sound editors, learning how to ask thoughtful questions and create episodes that truly listen. The final podcasts, complete with intro music and sound effects, are published for the school community and even pitched to local radio or libraries. Using the podcast equipment's multi-track recording feature, students layer in ambient sounds?like birdsong or clapsticks?to create an immersive listening experience. By becoming storytellers and listeners, students build empathy and learn the power of giving others a platform.

Students create a living digital mural on Padlet, mapping out the many First Nations languages spoken across Australia and highlighting their unique stories. This collaborative investigation deepens understanding of the unit's focus on the significance of language to identity and belonging. Students become language detectives, reaching out to family members or community language experts to add personal connections and rare words to the board. The Padlet grows into a vibrant, interactive map filled with voice notes, images, and short video clips, which is shared at assembly or with partner schools. By using Padlet's map view, students can pin languages to their traditional regions and see the breathtaking diversity at a glance. The experience empowers students to see language as a living treasure, and to champion its preservation.

Students design immersive virtual galleries using Delightex, curating artefacts, artworks, and stories that showcase the importance of kinship and tradition in First Nations cultures. This creative challenge ties to the unit's inquiry into the importance of community, family, and kinship, letting students step into the shoes of museum curators. Students consult with local artists or Elders (in person or via video), ensuring their galleries reflect real voices and respectful storytelling. The final galleries are shared as interactive 3D spaces, which classmates and families can explore online?each artefact annotated with student research and audio explanations. Delightex's branching scenario feature lets students create choose-your-own-path journeys, so visitors can experience different perspectives and stories as they move through the gallery. Students finish with a sense of pride in curating culture, and a toolkit for sharing stories in new and respectful ways.

s.t: Story Stones & Talking Maps: Ancestral Pathways Quest
s.d: Students design and craft 3D landscape maps using recycled cardboard, clay, natural materials (leaves, stones, sand), and fabric to represent significant places and features from local First Nations stories or global Indigenous cultures. Using Ozobot robots, students program journeys along 'paths' they create, with each stop marked by hand-painted 'story stones' that share language words, symbols, or short audio recordings (via QR codes) about the site's cultural significance. The hands-on process blends digital coding, map-making, and tactile art, helping students explore the importance of land, language, and storytelling in connecting communities and sharing the planet. The project culminates in a guided walk-through where peers 'travel' the map, learning about diversity and respect through interactive storytelling.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Human migration is a response to challenges and opportunities
lo: The reasons people migrate; Migration throughout history; Effects of migration on communities, cultures and individuals

s.d: Step into the shoes of a migrant during the Australian Gold Rush with the Minecraft: Gold Rush library lesson (https://education.minecraft.net/en-us/lessons/australian-gold-rush2), where students journey from England to the goldfields of Victoria. This experience brings 'the reasons people migrate' to life, letting students discover firsthand the push and pull factors behind historical migration. Students become time-travelling diarists, using the in-game camera and book and quill to capture daily life, hardships, and hopes as if they were real gold seekers. The finished artefact is a vivid digital diary packed with images and stories, ready to be shared at a family history night or published as an eBook for the school community. The teleportation and interactive dialogue features in this Minecraft lesson let students jump between key locations and access extra historical sources, making their journey feel authentic and immersive. By the end, students see migration not as a distant concept, but as a series of personal choices and challenges that shaped communities.

Students become migration detectives by mapping the journeys of real families displaced by bushfires, floods, or earthquakes using National Geographic MapMaker. This hands-on activity dives deep into 'migration throughout history', showing how environmental disasters have shaped where people live. Students choose a real-world case study and annotate their map with photos, quotes, and news clippings, then analyse how the landscape and community changed before and after the event. The final product is a digital, annotated migration map that can be displayed in the school foyer or presented to local emergency services. MapMaker's layering and annotation tools let students compare historical and current migration routes, adding a level of insight far beyond drawing lines on paper. Students walk away with the power to visualise big stories and make sense of how places and people are always changing.

Students use Dollar Street to examine the impact of migration on families by exploring photo stories from households that have moved due to challenges or opportunities. They identify visual clues?such as packed belongings, new housing styles, or changes in family routines?that signal migration experiences. Students create a digital scrapbook or storyboard that traces the journey of one family, highlighting reasons for migration and the effects on their daily life. This directly supports the inquiry into why people migrate and how it shapes communities. Dollar Street's AI-driven sorting of migration-related features is similar to how humanitarian organisations use image analysis to track displacement patterns. Students present their storyboards and reflect on the personal and societal impacts of migration.

Students design and code a 'migration warning system' using Micro:bit, simulating the real-life alerts that help communities respond to bushfires, floods, or earthquakes. This activity directly addresses 'how changes to the Earth impact environments and communities', making the science of natural disasters practical and urgent. Students take on the role of inventors, brainstorming how technology can support people facing sudden displacement and then testing their device in a classroom simulation. The final artefact is a working prototype that flashes, beeps, or displays a warning message?demonstrated at an assembly or shared with a local SES volunteer. By using Micro:bit's sensors and radio communication features, students can experiment with real-world data and even send alerts across the classroom network. They gain hands-on coding skills and see how digital solutions can make a real difference in times of crisis.

Students become documentary producers, filming a three-minute report that compares how communities prepare for and recover from bushfires, floods or earthquakes. Within IMovie, they combine student-recorded footage, voice-over narration, titles and maps or photographs captured directly for their project. Each documentary explains the disaster's causes and processes before tracing effects on homes, habitats, transport and community wellbeing. Students use split-screen, picture-in-picture and cutaway features to compare places before and after an event, while captions identify evidence and sources. They refine pacing, sound levels and transitions so that facts, firsthand perspectives and practical safety messages remain clear. The completed mini-documentaries form a class film festival about resilience, environmental change and community response.

s.t: Rescue Rover Rally: Navigating Nature's Obstacles
s.d: Students design and construct 3D models of landscapes affected by different natural disasters (like bushfire-scorched forests, flooded towns, or earthquake-crumbled roads) using cardboard, fabric scraps, clay, and recycled materials. They then code and decorate a Sphero Indi or similar programmable rover to navigate rescue routes through their handmade terrains, simulating emergency response journeys. Along the way, students must problem-solve real-world challenges, like blocked bridges or unstable ground, and iterate on both their physical models and robot code. This project brings systems thinking to life, showing how environments and communities adapt to change, while blending digital skills with hands-on creativity.

ci: Leaders shape communities.
lo: Roles and responsibilities of effective leadership; The purpose of leadership in communities; Qualities of influential leaders

s.d: The teacher creates a Wise Discussion Chatbot using the Character Interview scenario and sets the bot's role as Ava, a community celebration organiser explaining why particular traditions matter to different families. The topic is "Who We Are: Leaders shape communities.". Students chat with the bot to explore a named perspective through guided questioning rather than general research; for example, they ask "How does this celebration show what your community values?" and "What might outsiders misunderstand about this tradition?". After the chat, students produce a question bank plus a short perspective-and-evidence summary that compares the chatbot responses with unit sources linked explicitly to Who We Are.

Students design and host a live Kahoot quiz show called 'Who Leads?,' using questions they've researched about famous and unsung leaders from around the world. This taps into the line of inquiry about the qualities and impact of influential leaders while making the learning social and surprising. Flipping roles, students become quizmasters and even challenge teachers or parents to see who knows the most about leadership. The final product is a competitive, high-energy quiz event broadcast to the year level or during a school assembly. Kahoot's question randomisation and team mode features let students craft tricky questions and spark team-based debate, not just rapid-fire recall. Learners walk away with pride in their expertise and see how fun it is to lead and challenge others in a positive, inclusive way.

Students become leadership campaigners by creating a digital poster series in Canva, each spotlighting a different leadership strength?like empathy, courage, or listening?that's often overlooked. This directly explores the unit's focus on the sometimes invisible qualities that make leaders influential in their communities. Building on visual arts, students remix famous leadership quotes and their own reflections, then campaign around the school by displaying their work in key spaces or sharing digitally with families. The final artefacts are eye-catching, professionally styled posters using Canva's Magic Write and Remove Background features for truly original messaging. Magic Write lets students spark their own campaign slogans or calls to action, making each poster unique and powerful. Students gain the creative confidence to advocate for the kind of leadership they believe in, knowing their ideas can shift thinking in their community.

Students produce a podcast mini-series titled 'Leadership Stories from Year 4,' where they script and record episodes exploring school and community leadership from unexpected perspectives. This brings the purpose of leadership alive by having students act as reporters, interviewing classmates, staff, or even student leaders from other schools. Students also record 'what if' segments?imagining what would happen if leaders made different choices or faced harder challenges. The finished work is a polished audio series, edited with intro music and sound effects, and published for families, other classes, and even the local community to tune in. Using the podcast equipment's audio mixing and multitrack editing features, students experiment with layering voices, soundscapes, and authentic storytelling. By publishing their own voices, students step into the public space as young thought leaders, realising their stories and questions matter.

Students use Padlet to create a collaborative debate wall where they post arguments, counterarguments and evidence about the roles and responsibilities of effective leaders in communities. They design posts that include text, images and links to biographies or speeches of influential leaders, encouraging peers to respond with thoughtful questions or alternative viewpoints using threaded comments. This interactive platform allows students to investigate leadership qualities and dilemmas by engaging in respectful online discussions, simulating real-world community decision-making. They curate a rich digital dialogue that highlights different leadership styles and challenges, then summarise key insights in a final reflection post. The Padlet wall becomes a dynamic resource showcasing diverse perspectives on leadership and how leaders shape communities.

Students work in teams to design and build imaginative miniature communities from recycled cardboard, craft materials, and LEGO figures, each representing different leadership roles (mayor, coach, captain, etc.). They then program simple Ozobot robots to follow custom-drawn paths through their community, stopping at key 'leadership stations' where students place interactive signs or mini-challenges that showcase leadership qualities in action. The project blends hands-on construction with basic robotics, encouraging students to reflect on how leaders guide and shape the places we live. This creative journey lets every child bring their vision of leadership to life?both in what they build and how they direct their LeaderBot through it!

ci: People can create or manipulate messages to target specific audiences.
lo: The devices used to target audiences; Critical evaluation of messages; How we know we have been influenced

s.d: Students use Dollar Street to analyse how advertising and persuasive messages are tailored to different audiences by examining household items, media devices, and branded products in homes from various countries and income levels. They select images that show advertisements, packaging, or media consumption, then create a gallery walk with annotated captions explaining how marketing targets specific needs or aspirations. This activity connects to the inquiry into how messages are crafted to influence audiences. Dollar Street's AI-powered categorisation of product types mirrors how marketing analysts use image recognition to study consumer behaviour. Students present their annotated galleries and discuss how advertising strategies vary across cultures and economic backgrounds.

Students become 'message detectives' by creating interactive case files in Book Creator, analysing a selection of real advertisements, pop songs, and viral images to unmask the tricks used to target young audiences. This ties in powerfully with examining the devices used to target audiences and the critical evaluation of messages. Students publish their detective files as a digital exhibition for parents and younger students, teaching them how to spot manipulation in everyday media. Each student's case file contains annotated images, audio 'clue' explanations, and clickable hotspots revealing where and how persuasive language or visuals do their work. Book Creator's built-in comic templates and audio hotspots transform ordinary analysis into an engaging, multimedia experience. Students finish as confident analysts, ready to decode?and even outsmart?the messaging swirling around them.

Students use Teachable Machine to train a model that can recognise and classify persuasive techniques in media messages?such as emotional appeals, statistics, celebrity endorsements or loaded language?by uploading or recording short video or audio samples. They curate examples from advertisements, social media clips or news segments, then label and train the model to identify each technique. The resulting classifier is tested by classmates, who submit new samples to see if the model can accurately detect the persuasive device. This activity directly supports critical evaluation of messages and helps students understand how they are influenced by targeted communication. The process mirrors how social media platforms and advertising agencies use AI to automatically flag or categorise persuasive content for moderation or targeted marketing. Students reflect on the strengths and limitations of their model in a short written analysis.

The teacher creates a Wise Discussion Chatbot using the Character Interview scenario and sets the bot's role as Ava, a community celebration organiser explaining why particular traditions matter to different families. The topic is "How We Express Ourselves: People can create or manipulate messages to target specific audiences.". Students chat with the bot to explore a named perspective through guided questioning rather than general research; for example, they ask "How does this celebration show what your community values?" and "What might outsiders misunderstand about this tradition?". After the chat, students produce a question bank plus a short perspective-and-evidence summary that compares the chatbot responses with unit sources linked explicitly to How We Express Ourselves.

Students use Explain Everything to create interactive digital whiteboard presentations where they design and record persuasive messages aimed at specific audiences. They combine drawing tools, text annotations, voice recordings, and imported images to build layered explanations that reveal how different devices like emotional appeals or repetition influence viewers. For example, students might annotate a commercial, political ad, or social media post to highlight bias and persuasive techniques. They then record their own voiceover reflections explaining how the message targets its audience and whether it changed their thinking. This process helps students critically evaluate messages by making their reasoning visible and audible. Finally, presentations are shared for peer feedback, encouraging discussion about how messages shape opinions and influence behaviour.

s.t: Persuasion Pinball: Build & Code Your Message Machine
s.d: Students design and construct interactive pinball machines from cardboard, recycled materials, and craft supplies, embedding key persuasive messages or advertisements throughout the playfield. Using micro:bit boards and simple sensors, they program sound or light effects that trigger when the ball hits specific targets, reinforcing their intended message to the player. Each group selects a target audience and crafts both the physical and digital elements to maximise impact, blending creativity, engineering, and persuasive communication. This hands-on project lets students critically explore how design, technology, and messaging work together to influence audiences.

ci: Entrepreneurs have a responsibility to develop, market and sell sustainable products and services.
lo: The power of giving back; How our environment is impacted by the products we create; Sustainable business practices

s.d: Invite Year 5 students to step into the shoes of eco-entrepreneurs as they explore sustainable buildings in Minecraft: Its Good To Be Green (https://education.minecraft.net/en-us/lessons/its-good-to-be-green). This digital adventure brings alive the central idea that entrepreneurs must design and market products and services that truly care for our planet. Students become sustainability consultants, critiquing and redesigning virtual spaces to minimise waste and maximise positive environmental impact. Their final showcase is a guided video tour of their improved Minecraft building, pitched to a real-world audience of parents and local business owners. Using Minecraft's Book & Quill feature, students annotate their builds with sustainability tips and business ideas directly inside the world.
