They finish with the confidence to see themselves as real change-makers, ready to build a greener future both online and off.

Students become inventors by designing a prototype of a sustainable product?think reusable packaging, water filters, or solar-powered gadgets?using Tinkercad's 3D modelling tools. This hands-on project connects directly to the unit's focus on how entrepreneurs develop products that reduce environmental harm. To spark real-world thinking, students pitch their designs to a panel of local community members or parents, gathering feedback and fresh perspectives. The final artefact is a digital 3D model, complete with an annotated walkthrough video explaining its sustainable features. Tinkercad's 'Send to 3D Print' feature lets students see their creations leap from screen to reality, ready for display at the market stall event. They walk away with practical design skills and the thrill of seeing their own ideas take shape in the real world.

Transform students into financial analysts as they use Microsoft Excel to track costs, sales, and environmental impacts of their sustainable business ideas. This activity ties straight into the line of inquiry about responsible business practices, challenging students to balance profit with positive impact. By comparing their own data with real-world companies' sustainability reports, students wrestle with the tough choices entrepreneurs face. Their final product is a colourful, interactive dashboard with graphs showing profits, carbon savings, and even 'giving back' donations. Excel's conditional formatting and pivot tables help students visualise patterns and spot opportunities for improvement. They gain the power to make data-driven decisions?an essential skill for any future entrepreneur or changemaker.

Students become sustainability storytellers by producing a podcast episode using Canva's podcasting features, interviewing local entrepreneurs or community members about giving back. This creative task links to the unit's exploration of the power of giving back and how businesses can inspire positive change. Students take on the role of real journalists, crafting questions and editing their recordings for a school-wide audience. The finished artefact is a polished podcast episode, complete with original cover art and show notes, ready to be shared on the school website or at the market event. Canva's 'Magic Write' tool helps students script compelling introductions and memorable episode titles. They leave with the confidence to use their voices to spark conversations and action in their community.

Challenge students to build and code a working model of an eco-friendly factory or recycling machine using Lego Spike Prime. This STEM-rich activity dives straight into how our environment is impacted by the products we create, making sustainability a hands-on engineering challenge. Students work in teams as real-world problem-solvers, consulting with a local waste management expert or parent volunteer for feedback on their designs. Their final artefact is a moving, sensor-powered model that sorts or processes materials, demonstrated live at the market stall event. Spike Prime's data logging and advanced sensor integration let students test and refine their machines for real efficiency gains. They finish with the technical know-how and teamwork skills to tackle big challenges in the world around them.

Students design and build miniature market stall 'pods' from recycled cardboard, fabric scraps, and upcycled plastics, creating both the physical stall structure and display elements for their sustainable product. They integrate a simple micro:bit or Makey Makey circuit to add an interactive feature ? such as a light-up sign, movement sensor, or sound effect that activates when a customer 'visits' their stall. This project brings entrepreneurship to life as students prototype, iterate, and test both their stall's design and customer experience, closely mirroring real-world market innovation and sustainable business practices. It ties directly to the unit by blending hands-on making, digital technology, and systems thinking about ethical production and marketing.

ci: Design processes enable people to respond creatively to challenges in the natural world.
lo: The nature and impact of natural hazards (Causation); How design processes are used to generate and test solutions (Function); The ethical and practical considerations in human responses to natural challenges (Responsibility)

s.d: Students bring natural hazards to life by designing interactive 3D models of bushfires, floods, or earthquakes using Merge Cubes. This hands-on experience lets them explore the nature and impact of natural hazards from every angle, making the concept of causation truly tangible. Imagine students stepping into the shoes of disaster scientists, presenting their hazard models to a panel of local emergency services experts invited virtually or in person. The final artefact is an augmented reality model that can be held, rotated, and annotated, ready to be shared at a school expo or with families via a QR code. Using Merge EDU's layered annotation feature, students embed voice explanations and real-time data overlays directly onto their 3D models. They leave with a sense of creative power, knowing they can explain?and even help solve?real-world challenges in ways that grab attention.

Students will design and 3D model a deployable emergency shelter that could be used after bushfires, floods, or earthquakes in Australia. This hands-on challenge brings to life the line of inquiry about how design processes are used to generate and test solutions to natural hazards. Students will pitch their shelter concepts to a panel of local emergency services volunteers, gathering real feedback on practical and ethical considerations. Their final artefact is a detailed, annotated 3D shelter prototype?complete with labelled features and a virtual walk-through?that can be shared with the school community and local stakeholders. Tinkercad's collaborative editing mode enables teams to co-design, iterate, and leave digital feedback directly on each other's models in real time. By becoming inventive problem-solvers who address real-world needs, students see themselves as designers with the power to shape safer, more resilient communities.

Students become real-world risk mappers by plotting the locations and impacts of recent natural hazards in Australia and around the globe using National Geographic MapMaker. This directly explores the nature and impact of natural hazards, making abstract disasters concrete and local. Students take on the role of local council advisors, mapping not just the hazards but also the communities, wildlife, and infrastructure affected?then proposing priority zones for action. Their final artefact is a layered, annotated digital map, complete with custom symbols, data overlays, and embedded student recommendations, which can be printed for the school foyer or shared online with a community partner. They harness MapMaker's drawing and annotation tools to create custom icons and colour-coded hazard zones, moving well beyond the basic pin-drop. Students finish with the know-how to advocate for smarter, fairer responses to natural disasters in their own backyard.

Students become disaster tech innovators by programming Micro:bits to create simple early-warning devices for natural hazards, such as flood alarms or earthquake shakers. This activity brings to life the ethical and practical considerations in human responses to natural challenges, as students weigh whose safety should come first and how to make their devices accessible for all. To push their thinking, students interview a local SES volunteer or disaster expert (in person or via video) and use their insights to refine their prototypes. The final artefact is a working device with code and a short video pitch, ready to be shown to families or at a school STEM night. Students use the Micro:bit's sensor inputs (like tilt or water detection) and radio communication features to simulate real-world alert systems. They leave as confident problem-solvers, ready to use technology for good in their community.

The teacher creates a Wise Discussion Chatbot using the Character Interview scenario and sets the bot's role as Dr Maya Chen, a wildlife ecologist advising the class about local habitats. The topic is "How the World Works: Design processes enable people to respond creatively to challenges in the natural world.". Students chat with the bot to explore a named perspective through guided questioning rather than general research; for example, they ask "Which adaptation would help this species survive a hotter summer?" and "What human action is putting this habitat under pressure?". After the chat, students produce a question bank plus a short perspective-and-evidence summary that compares the chatbot responses with unit sources linked explicitly to How the World Works.

s.t: Disaster-Proof Dream Homes: Shake, Rattle & Rebuild!
s.d: Students design and construct model houses using recycled cardboard, balsa wood, fabric, and a variety of everyday materials, aiming to withstand simulated natural hazards like earthquakes, floods, or bushfires. They use a micro:bit with sensors (e.g., accelerometer, moisture sensor, or temperature sensor) embedded in their structures to test and record how their designs perform under stress?such as shaking platforms, water spray, or heat lamps. Guided by the design thinking cycle, students iterate on their prototypes, analyze real hazard data, and reflect on how their innovations could help communities stay safe. This hands-on challenge connects STEM concepts to real-world resilience, ethical design, and sustainability.

ci: Finding peaceful solutions to conflict can make a difference in the world.
lo: Types of conflict; Causes and impacts of conflict; Conflict resolution

s.d: Students use Dollar Street to explore how conflict and its resolution are experienced in households across different cultures and economic backgrounds. They examine photo stories and images that reveal signs of conflict?such as security measures, shared spaces, or family routines?and identify strategies families use to maintain peace. Students create a comparative chart or visual map showing examples of conflict and resolution from three different families. This links to the inquiry into types and impacts of conflict. Dollar Street's AI-driven tagging of household features is similar to how peacebuilding organisations use image analysis to understand community needs. Students share their charts and reflect on how peaceful solutions can make a difference globally.

Students become peacemakers through music by composing original soundtracks in GarageBand that reflect the emotional journey of conflict and reconciliation. This creative process explores the impact of conflict on wellbeing, blending the unit's focus with music and emotional literacy. By collaborating in small groups, students each contribute a musical motif representing a different perspective?turning disagreement into harmony. The final piece is a layered audio track, performed at assembly or published online for the school community. GarageBand's Live Loops feature lets students experiment with structure and mood, giving their compositions a professional edge. They gain confidence expressing complex ideas through sound and learn that peaceful solutions can be heard as well as seen.

Students use Teachable Machine to create a model that recognises different types of conflict scenarios?such as personal, community or global conflicts?using short video role-plays or audio recordings. They script and record examples, label them by conflict type, and train the model to classify new scenarios. This process deepens understanding of conflict causes and resolution strategies by requiring students to analyse and categorise real-life situations. The activity mirrors how AI in customer service or online moderation tools detects and classifies conflict or escalation in communications. Students present their model and a reflection on how technology could support peaceful solutions in society.

Students become filmmakers, using Stop Motion Studio to animate stories of conflict and peaceful resolution inspired by literature, history, or their own lives. This hands-on project dives deep into the causes of conflict and the creative possibilities for resolution. Students are challenged to retell a classic story from the perspective of the 'villain,' encouraging empathy and critical thinking. Their final product is a polished stop-motion film, ready to premiere at a lunchtime film festival or on the school website. Stop Motion Studio's onion skinning and voiceover features allow students to layer dialogue and subtle gestures, bringing their characters' emotions to life. They leave with storytelling skills and a new sense of how powerful it is to see the world through someone else's eyes.

Students become conflict resolution researchers, designing and distributing a Microsoft Forms survey to gather data on how classmates, teachers, and even family members handle disagreements. This activity explores the unit's focus on the causes and impacts of conflict, while giving students a real-world reason to practise respectful questioning and data analysis. By comparing responses across generations, students uncover surprising trends and spark conversations about how peaceful solutions have changed over time. The final artefact is a dynamic data dashboard, which can be presented to the school leadership team as a catalyst for new wellbeing initiatives. Microsoft Forms' branching logic lets students tailor follow-up questions based on answers, making their survey feel personal and insightful. They finish with real research skills and the knowledge that their voices can help shape a kinder school community.

s.t: Peace Pathways: The Conflict Resolution Board Game Lab
s.d: Students design and build their own large-scale, 3D board games that explore conflict and peaceful solutions, using cardboard, recycled materials, clay, and craft supplies for game pieces, pathways, and obstacles. They integrate Makey Makey kits or micro:bit sensors to add interactive elements?such as sound effects or digital 'chance' cards triggered by landing on special spaces?bridging physical play with simple coding. Each game challenges players to navigate real-world-inspired scenarios, encouraging empathy, perspective-taking, and creative problem-solving. Teams follow the Design Cycle to brainstorm, prototype, test, and refine their games, making learning about peacebuilding both hands-on and memorable.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Colonisation has shaped society.
lo: The impact of colonisation; Colonisation stories; The effects of colonisation ? past, present and future

s.d: Step into the shoes of a goldfield explorer with Minecraft: Australian Gold Rush (https://education.minecraft.net/en-us/lessons/australian-gold-rush2), where students journey through the Victorian goldfields, documenting daily life and choices. This immersive experience brings the impact of colonisation to life, letting students grapple with the hopes, hardships, and cultural collisions that shaped society. As they teleport between ship, settlement, and dig site, students encounter stories from multiple perspectives?including Indigenous voices and migrants?sparking rich questions about fairness and legacy. Their final artefact is a digital diary, crafted with the in-game book and quill and illustrated with Minecraft camera snapshots, ready to be published as an eBook or shared in a school exhibition. The teleportation feature and interactive non-player characters allow students to explore branching narratives and make decisions that affect their story path. Students leave with a deeper empathy for the people who built Australia and the confidence to question whose stories are told?and whose are missing.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students bring a historical figure or community member from a colonised society to life by animating their story using Adobe Express's Animate from Audio feature (https://new.express.adobe.com/home/tools/animate-from-audio). This creative approach dives into colonisation stories, encouraging students to voice firsthand accounts and imagine how individuals navigated change. They can flip the script by animating both a coloniser and an Indigenous perspective, then compare the tone, choices, and emotions expressed. The final product is a short, shareable animated video that can be screened for families or published on the school website. Adobe Express's Animate from Audio tool transforms students' recorded voices into expressive, moving characters?making empathy and voice central. Students walk away empowered to use digital storytelling as a way to amplify voices from the past and make history feel personal.

Students will curate a living digital museum of colonisation stories using Padlet's map view, plotting real-world locations where key events unfolded and adding perspectives from both colonisers and First Nations communities. This directly probes the line of inquiry around 'Colonisation stories' by making visible the diversity of voices across time and place. Each group adopts the role of historical curators, responsible for investigating, verifying, and ethically presenting stories that challenge single narratives. The final artefact is an interactive global map, with multimedia posts (audio retellings, archival images, diary snippets, and poetry) that can be explored by families and the wider school community. Padlet's map view allows students to geotag content, embed video or audio, and enable moderated commenting for peer-to-peer empathy-building. Beyond empathy, students gain the agency to amplify marginalised voices and question how history is mapped?and who gets to be remembered.

Students become investigative journalists, producing a podcast episode that uncovers a lesser-known colonisation story from Australia or another part of the world using Podcasting using Canva (https://www.canva.com). This project tackles the impact of colonisation by encouraging students to interview community members, historians, or even classmates role-playing as historical figures. To deepen the experience, students can create a 'then and now' segment, comparing the lasting effects of colonisation on communities today. Their podcast, complete with intro music and sound effects, will be shared at a school assembly or uploaded for families to listen at home. Canva's podcasting tools allow students to mix interviews, narration, and ambient sounds for a professional finish. They leave with the skills to ask tough questions, listen deeply, and share stories that matter.

Students design interactive branching scenarios with Delightex, where choices made by colonisers and Indigenous people lead to different outcomes for society. This activity brings the effects of colonisation?past, present and future?to life by letting students experiment with alternative histories and ethical dilemmas. By inviting peers or parents to play through their scenarios, students spark real conversations about cause, effect, and responsibility. The final artefact is a clickable digital scenario, ready to be showcased at a school expo or embedded in the class blog. Delightex's scenario-mapping feature lets students build complex, multi-path stories with images, audio, and decision points. Students finish with a sense of agency, seeing how small choices can ripple through history?and how imagining alternatives can inspire action today.

s.t: Time Capsule Storyworlds: Augmented Diorama Adventures
s.d: Students design and build immersive dioramas representing a location before, during, and after colonisation, using cardboard, fabric, clay, natural and recycled materials. Each diorama includes hidden QR codes or AR markers created with CoSpaces Edu or AR Makr, which, when scanned with iPads, overlay student-made digital stories, Indigenous perspectives, or imagined future scenarios onto the physical scene. The project fuses hands-on model-making with interactive digital storytelling, encouraging students to think critically about change over time and diverse viewpoints. This tactile-tech hybrid brings history to life and empowers students to reflect on place, memory, and the ongoing impact of colonisation.

ci: People's choices are influenced by their beliefs and values and can impact others.
lo: How values and beliefs impact choices; How people's choices and actions impact others; Responsible decision-making

s.d: Students create an immersive 360-degree 'decision room' that places viewers inside moments when beliefs and values influence a community. They stage and film scenarios such as including an isolated classmate, responding to unfairness or balancing a personal preference with collective wellbeing. Because the Insta360 camera captures every direction, each group carefully positions contrasting reactions around the scene so viewers must turn and notice multiple perspectives. Students replay the footage, identify visible consequences and refilm after improving how clearly each choice communicates responsibility. The finished guided virtual experience includes spoken prompts inviting viewers to consider whose values shaped the decision and who was affected. Classmates explore each scene and discuss how changing one action could alter the outcome for everyone.

Students use the Field Guide to Victoria app to investigate local community values and beliefs by exploring stories, images and interviews about diverse people and places in their region. They collect digital field notes and photos that capture examples of how individuals' choices reflect their values and impact others, such as environmental care or cultural traditions. Using the app's annotation tools, students create a multimedia digital journal that documents their observations and reflections on responsible decision-making in their own neighbourhood. This hands-on exploration deepens their understanding of how beliefs shape actions in real life, linking to natural and social systems around them. They then present their journals in small groups, discussing patterns and differences they discovered, fostering empathy and critical thinking about community impact.

The teacher creates a Wise Discussion Chatbot using the Character Interview scenario and sets the bot's role as Ava, a community celebration organiser explaining why particular traditions matter to different families. The topic is "Who We Are: People's choices are influenced by their beliefs and values and can impact others.". Students chat with the bot to explore a named perspective through guided questioning rather than general research; for example, they ask "How does this celebration show what your community values?" and "What might outsiders misunderstand about this tradition?". After the chat, students produce a question bank plus a short perspective-and-evidence summary that compares the chatbot responses with unit sources linked explicitly to Who We Are.

Students transform the classroom into a podcast studio and use Podcasting using Canva (https://www.canva.com) to interview family members or community leaders about beliefs and values that have shaped important choices. Acting as investigative journalists, they plan open questions and listen for stories involving courage, kindness, fairness or difficult responsibility. Canva's audio recording, timeline editing and music library allow each group to assemble a polished episode with an introduction, edited interview highlights and a reflective conclusion. Students trim clips, balance voice and music levels, and sequence contrasting perspectives to show how one decision can affect other people. Each episode concludes with the students explaining what surprised them and how their own viewpoint changed. The class hosts a listening gallery and offers feedback on empathetic questioning, evidence and responsible storytelling.

Turn Padlet into a living tapestry of beliefs by having students anonymously post sticky notes about choices they've made and the values behind them, then invite classmates to respond with empathy or curiosity. This activity links directly to 'how values and beliefs impact choices', making invisible motivations visible and sparking honest, respectful dialogue. To shake things up, students can invite another Year 5 class or even parents to add their own stories, weaving a web of perspectives across generations. The final artefact is a vibrant, interactive wall of stories, questions, and replies, rich with connections and surprises. Padlet's 'timeline view' lets students map out how one choice can lead to unexpected consequences over time, visually tracing the journey from belief to impact. Students leave with a toolkit for respectful discussion and a sense that their classroom is a safe space for real conversations.

s.t: Identity Automata: The Choice & Consequence Chain Reaction
s.d: Students design and build elaborate chain reaction machines (inspired by Rube Goldberg devices) that visually represent how personal choices, shaped by beliefs and values, ripple out to affect others. Using cardboard, recycled materials, marbles, popsicle sticks, and LEGO gears, students craft each segment to symbolize a decision point or value (e.g., honesty triggers a positive domino effect, while selfishness creates an obstacle). They integrate BBC micro:bit sensors or Makey Makey to trigger sounds or lights at key moments?bridging the physical with the digital. The process encourages deep reflection on cause and effect in decision-making, while celebrating the diversity of each student's identity and the collective impact on their community.

ci: Thinking beyond ourselves empowers us to act.
lo:
How we evidence our process
How taking action helps us grow our understandings
How we provoke others to make meaningful change

s.d: Students create immersive 3D virtual galleries where they curate exhibits that showcase persuasive messages for causes they are passionate about, directly addressing 'How we provoke others to make meaningful change'. The act of designing these digital spaces places students in the role of activist-artist, exploring how their beliefs and values can influence others through atmosphere, layout, and interactive storytelling. Inviting families and the local community to 'tour' the virtual gallery, students become hosts, sparking real conversations about agency and social impact. Each student crafts a themed room, complete with embedded videos, artworks, and written provocations designed to persuade and inspire action around their chosen issue. Using Delightex's collaborative design feature, groups build and edit their spaces together simultaneously, allowing for authentic teamwork and creative negotiation. Students leave empowered with the understanding that their voices, when amplified through digital creativity, can reach and move audiences they might never otherwise meet.

Students design and run live Kahoot quizzes that challenge peers to spot bias, evaluate media claims, and identify persuasive techniques in real-world advertisements. This playful competition directly explores 'How we evidence our process', as students must defend their quiz choices by referencing analysis strategies and critical thinking steps. By swapping quizzes with other classes or even teachers, students learn to anticipate misconceptions and teach critical literacy skills beyond their immediate circles. The final artefact is a classroom tournament, with each team hosting a session and collecting real-time feedback on which questions provoked the most debate or reflection. The advanced 'Puzzle' and 'Type Answer' question types push students to craft nuanced, open-ended challenges rather than only relying on multiple choice. Students walk away as more discerning, media-literate citizens, ready to question and decode persuasive messages in everyday life.

Students compose sonic identity tracks?short, powerful audio logos or theme tunes that encapsulate the mood and message of their media campaigns. Composing music for the purpose of 'How taking action helps us grow our understandings', they experiment with how sound can influence emotion and drive engagement in advocacy. Collaborating as a creative studio, each team pitches their track to a real-world NGO or school leader, arguing how their chosen beats and melodies evoke a specific call to action. The final product is a portfolio-ready, polished audio file used as the 'sound signature' for campaign videos, podcasts, or digital posters. Leveraging GarageBand's extensive library of loops, students layer, remix, and automate effects?learning to shape atmosphere as well as content. This empowers students not just to communicate with words, but to harness the emotional power of sound to move an audience.

Students build a collaborative digital 'Action Wall' on Padlet, mapping out real change-makers, media campaigns, and their own evolving ideas about advocacy. This activity deepens 'How we provoke others to make meaningful change', as students crowdsource inspirations and critique the effectiveness of different persuasive strategies. By inviting guest contributors?parents, local activists, or alumni?to comment or add resources, students connect their inquiries to authentic voices and expertise. The final Padlet becomes a curated, multi-modal resource board, filled with annotated articles, campaign videos, infographics, and original reflections that can be shared with the entire school. Using Padlet's timeline or shelf view, students visually organise the development of their own action projects and spark discussion on trends in persuasion. Students gain the insight that knowledge grows through dialogue and collective curation, not just solo research.

Students storyboard, record, and edit dynamic video explainers that peel back the layers of iconic persuasive campaigns?breaking down techniques, storytelling structures, and ethical choices. Investigating 'How we evidence our process', they become media detectives, annotating real campaign footage with live drawings, voiceovers, and interactive callouts. As the class assembles a shared library of explainers, students critique and build upon each other's work, simulating a professional media studio environment. The final artefact is a collection of annotated videos that can be shared at assembly or online, equipping younger students with the tools to spot manipulation in media. Explain Everything's infinite canvas lets students blend live video, sketches, embedded web content, and collaborative editing in a single seamless workflow. Students take away not just the skills to dissect media, but the confidence to pull back the curtain and teach others how persuasion really works.

s.t: Persuasion Pinball: Build & Code Your Message
s.d: Students design and construct their own interactive pinball machines from cardboard, recycled materials, rubber bands, and marbles, each themed around a social issue or cause they care about. Using micro:bit or Makey Makey kits, they add digital sound effects or LED scoreboards that trigger when targets are hit, reinforcing key messages or slogans. This hands-on project lets students express persuasive ideas through both physical design and simple coding, creatively blending media, engineering, and advocacy. The final machines become playable campaigns, inviting others to experience, reflect on, and be influenced by their messages.

ci: Student-led exhibition (PYPEX) ? Students develop and present their own units of inquiry.
lo: Student-led transdisciplinary themes; Approaches to learning; Research and presentation skills

s.d: The teacher creates a Wise Discussion Chatbot using the Project Ideation scenario and sets the bot's role as Kai, a project coach who helps students narrow broad inquiry ideas into one practical proposal. The topic is "How We Organise Ourselves: Student-led exhibition (PYPEX) ? Students develop and present their own units of inquiry.". Students chat with the bot to test and refine possible inquiry actions or design ideas before committing to one plan; for example, they ask "Which idea best connects to our central idea?" and "What resources, success criteria and next steps do you need?". After the chat, students produce a one-page project proposal naming the chosen idea, success criteria, resources, first prototype/action step and how it connects to the unit linked explicitly to How We Organise Ourselves.

During their PYP Exhibition, students use Teachable Machine to build a custom classifier that recognises key artefacts, images or sounds from their chosen inquiry topics?such as endangered species, renewable energy devices or cultural symbols. They collect and label media relevant to their research, train the model, and demonstrate its use as an interactive element in their exhibition booth. This activity supports research and presentation skills, and mirrors how museum apps and educational kiosks use AI to help visitors identify and learn about objects. Students include a reflection on the classifier's accuracy and how AI can support public education.

Students design and run a school-wide survey to investigate what values matter most to different age groups?democracy, fairness, freedom, or something else entirely? This hooks into the transdisciplinary theme of values and systems, but puts students in charge of authentic data collection and analysis. Instead of just reporting back, students must compare the results to what they've learned about Australian government and ask: is our political system a true reflection of our community's priorities? The final artefact is a dynamic data dashboard, with charts and insights displayed for the whole school to see during Exhibition. Using Microsoft Forms' branching surveys and live analytics (not just the basic quiz), students can dig into patterns by year level or gender, surfacing stories hidden in the numbers. They'll leave knowing how to use data to tell a persuasive civic story?and maybe spark a real debate about what should change.

Students team up as law-makers and engineers to design, build, and code a simple automated voting machine using Lego Spike Prime. This directly supports the inquiry into the processes of government, giving students a hands-on experience with voting systems and the challenges of fairness and accuracy. To keep things real, the teams must debate and justify their design choices?should their machine allow for secret ballots, what happens if someone tries to vote twice, and how do they handle a tie? The finished project is a working prototype that runs a mock classroom election, with parents and peers invited to try it out during PYPEX. Advanced use of Spike Prime's custom sensors and colour detection allows the machine to verify ballots and tally votes instantly. Students finish with a deep respect for the invisible systems behind democracy?and the technical know-how to build them, not just talk about them.

Students design an interactive 3D Museum of Government Systems in Delightex, building separate galleries for democracy, monarchy and dictatorship. They populate each scene with buildings, symbols, labelled objects and information panels that reveal how leaders are selected, laws are created and citizens participate. Using Delightex's scene editor, object animations and CoBlocks coding, students create clickable exhibits that trigger explanations or show how a decision moves through each political system. Every gallery includes a fictional civic dilemma, such as funding a park, restricting protests or responding to a natural disaster. Visitors follow the virtual tour and compare how values such as fairness, freedom, authority and equality influence each response. Students finish with a curator's statement that justifies which system best protects citizens' rights and why.

s.t: Govern-Bot City: Build & Code Your Own Nation
s.d: Students design and construct a miniature nation using recycled cardboard, popsticks, and craft materials to create government buildings, courtrooms, and community spaces. They then program Sphero robots to act as 'citizens', navigating the city according to rules and laws collaboratively designed by the class?experimenting with different systems (e.g., democracy, monarchy, dictatorship). Through iterative prototyping and coding, students physically experience how values, structures, and laws shape the daily life and fairness within their nation. This hands-on simulation makes the abstract concepts of governance and civic organisation tangible, memorable, and fun.

ci: Energy may be converted, transformed, and used to support human progress.
lo: Different forms of energy and how they are used; The impact of different energy sources on the planet; Sustainable energy practices

s.d: Students will step into the world of Minecraft: Alternative Energy (https://education.minecraft.net/en-us/lessons/alternative-energy) to explore, build, and compare hydropower, wind power, and waste-to-energy plants. They will see first-hand how different forms of energy are converted and used, and how these choices impact communities and the planet. Acting as city planners, students must weigh the needs of a growing population against environmental concerns, debating tough decisions about energy sources. Their final creation is a virtual sustainable city, complete with annotated energy facilities and a video tour explaining their design decisions for a real-world audience. Using Minecraft's in-game camera and Book & Quill, students will capture and narrate their process, combining visuals and explanations in a digital portfolio. By the end, they will see themselves as innovators who can design for both progress and sustainability.

Students use Dollar Street to compare how families from different countries and income levels use energy in their daily lives. They explore photos of kitchens, lighting, and appliances, noting the types of energy sources?such as firewood, solar panels, or electricity?used in each home. Students create a comparative infographic that highlights the environmental impact and sustainability of each energy choice. This directly connects to the inquiry into energy use and sustainable practices. Dollar Street's AI-driven tagging of energy-related features mirrors how environmental agencies use image recognition to monitor global energy consumption. Students share their infographics and discuss how access to energy shapes human progress and environmental outcomes.

Students use Teachable Machine to train a model that classifies images or sounds of different energy sources?such as solar panels, wind turbines, fossil fuel plants and hydroelectric dams. They gather and label media, then train the model to distinguish between renewable and non-renewable sources. This activity supports inquiry into forms of energy, their uses and impacts on the planet. The process is similar to how environmental monitoring systems use AI to identify and track energy infrastructure from satellite images or field recordings. Students present their classifier and a reflection on how AI can support sustainable energy practices.

The teacher creates a Wise Discussion Chatbot using the Character Interview scenario and sets the bot's role as Dr Maya Chen, a wildlife ecologist advising the class about local habitats. The topic is "How the World Works: Energy may be converted, transformed, and used to support human progress.". Students chat with the bot to explore a named perspective through guided questioning rather than general research; for example, they ask "Which adaptation would help this species survive a hotter summer?" and "What human action is putting this habitat under pressure?". After the chat, students produce a question bank plus a short perspective-and-evidence summary that compares the chatbot responses with unit sources linked explicitly to How the World Works.

Students will engineer and code working models of hydroelectric dams or wind turbines using Lego Spike Prime, exploring how mechanical energy is converted into electricity. This hands-on robotics challenge deepens their understanding of how energy may be transformed and used to support human progress. Working in teams as 'renewable engineers', students will test and refine their builds, racing to see whose design generates the most power or lifts the heaviest load. Their final artefact is a live demonstration and a time-lapse video of their build, which can be shared with families or featured in a science expo. By programming sensors and motors with Spike Prime's advanced block coding, students can measure output and tweak their machines for maximum efficiency. They leave with real-world engineering skills and the thrill of seeing their ideas come to life.

Students design and build a working model of an amusement park ride (such as a Ferris wheel, carousel, or roller coaster) powered by their choice of renewable energy, like solar, wind, or hand-crank. Using recycled cardboard, wooden skewers, plastic bottles, gears, and motors, teams prototype their ride, integrating a micro:bit or Makey Makey to monitor energy input or trigger ride movement. Learners apply the design cycle to test, refine, and showcase how energy is converted and transformed to create motion and fun, drawing real-world links to sustainable engineering. This collaborative project challenges students to creatively solve problems while making energy concepts tangible and memorable.

ci: Communities interact with the environment in different ways.
lo: How community values shape the management of the natural environment; The need for sustainable practices; Taking action for environmental stewardship

s.d: Students become energy detectives, using Micro:bit's data logging to track and investigate real energy usage around Wesley College and at home. This hands-on inquiry dives into how community values shape our choices about energy and the environment. Imagine students presenting their findings to campus decision-makers, suggesting ways the school could save energy and reduce its environmental footprint. Their final artefact is a set of interactive data visualisations and a short action proposal, ready to be shared with the Facilities team and families. The real magic comes from Micro:bit's built-in data logger, which lets students gather, process, and analyse live energy data?no guesswork, just real numbers. Students leave empowered with the skills and voice to champion practical, sustainable change in their own community.

Students become environmental storytellers, producing a podcast series that explores local and Indigenous perspectives on caring for the land. This creative project connects directly to the line of inquiry about how different community values influence environmental management. Students can invite guest experts, interview classmates who attended Camp Mallana, or even record soundscapes from local parks to bring their episodes to life. The final product is a polished, multi-episode podcast published for the school community and families, sparking real conversations about stewardship. By using Canva's podcasting tools (https://www.canva.com), students can mix interviews, music, and sound effects for professional-quality episodes. They finish with the confidence to use their voices and technology to inspire change far beyond the classroom.

Students become global explorers, creating interactive maps that compare sustainable practices in different communities around the world. This activity shines a spotlight on the need for sustainable practices by inviting students to investigate and annotate real-world case studies?from Indigenous fire management in Australia to urban farming in Singapore. Students are challenged to consider what makes a practice 'sustainable' and how geography, culture, and resources shape community choices. Their finished artefact is a digital map layered with their own annotations, images, and case study summaries, ready to be shared at assembly or with partner schools. National Geographic MapMaker's custom annotation and layering tools let students build rich, multi-dimensional maps that tell compelling stories. Students walk away with a global mindset and the mapping skills to visualise solutions to environmental challenges.

Students become environmental advocates, designing digital action books that inspire others to take up the challenge of stewardship. This project connects to 'taking action for environmental stewardship' by having students research a local issue and propose creative, practical solutions. Students can collaborate in pairs, take on roles as journalists or campaigners, and even include interviews with community members. The final book?complete with interactive elements, audio, and video?can be published online and shared with families, local council, or feeder schools. Book Creator's comic templates and embedded multimedia features allow students to craft engaging, persuasive stories that jump off the (digital) page. By the end, students have the tools and confidence to turn their ideas into real-world advocacy.

Students become virtual ecologists, building 3D models of local ecosystems or sustainable innovations that can be explored in augmented reality using Merge Cubes. This immersive experience ties directly to the central idea of how communities interact with their environment in diverse ways. Students are invited to swap cubes and step into each other's shoes, seeing the world from the perspective of a river, a tree, or even a waste treatment plant. Their final product is a set of interactive AR models, complete with narrated explanations, that can be shared at a student expo or with younger year levels. Merge Cubes' object annotation and layered AR features let students add voiceovers and clickable hotspots for a truly interactive experience. Students leave not just with technical know-how, but with empathy for the living systems they're striving to protect.

Students will design and build wearable tech accessories?such as wristbands, badges, or hats?using recycled materials, conductive thread, and simple circuits (LEDs, coin cell batteries, sewable microcontrollers). Each wearable will visually represent a chosen environmental issue or Indigenous stewardship practice, lighting up or changing color to communicate key messages. Students prototype their designs, solder or sew in electronic elements, and use digital drawing apps to create stencils or logos. This project challenges students to combine hands-on making with digital design, advocating for conservation and responsible action in a creative, memorable way.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Significant events shape a place
lo: What is a significant event; Why these events occurred; Impact of significant events

s.d: Step into the shoes of a goldfields explorer with Minecraft: Gold Rush (https://education.minecraft.net/en-us/lessons/australian-gold-rush2), where students relive the journey of hopeful miners arriving in Victoria. By experiencing firsthand why the Gold Rush was such a significant event, students unpack the forces that shaped Melbourne and its communities. As they write diary entries and snap in-game photos, students grapple with whose voices are remembered and whose are left out of history. Their final artefact is a digital diary?complete with images and immersive storytelling?ready to be shared with families and displayed at a school history showcase. The lesson's teleportation feature lets students jump between historical locations, deepening their understanding of cause and effect across different settings. By the end, students see themselves as time travellers?confident in their ability to connect personal stories to the bigger picture of how events shape a place.

Students become migration cartographers by using National Geographic MapMaker to plot the journeys of families and communities across continents and generations. Exploring what makes an event 'significant', they visually map out migration routes, settlement patterns, and the ripple effects on local culture. By inviting parents or community members to contribute their own migration stories, students gain a richer, multi-perspective view of Melbourne's evolving identity. The final product is an interactive digital map annotated with personal stories, photos, and key historical events?perfect for sharing at an open evening or on the class blog. MapMaker's layering and annotation tools let students overlay historical events, population changes, and cultural landmarks for true depth. Students walk away as mapmakers with a sense of belonging and a toolkit for seeing how movement shapes the world around them.

Transform your students into history podcasters as they script and record interviews with 'witnesses' of Melbourne's significant events?real or imagined?using Podcast Equipment. Delving into the question of why events occurred, students step into the roles of journalists, activists, or community elders to explore motivations and consequences. By collaborating with a local historian or inviting family members to share their stories on-air, students see how history is a living conversation. Their finished artefact is a polished podcast episode, complete with intro music and sound effects, ready to broadcast to the school community and beyond. Using the podcast mixer's live EQ and multi-track recording, students can layer voices, music, and archival audio for a professional touch. They finish the project with the confidence to ask big questions and the skills to amplify voices from the past and present.

The teacher creates a Wise Discussion Chatbot using the Character Interview scenario and sets the bot's role as Ava, a community celebration organiser explaining why particular traditions matter to different families. The topic is "Where We Are in Place and Time: Significant events shape a place". Students chat with the bot to explore a named perspective through guided questioning rather than general research; for example, they ask "How does this celebration show what your community values?" and "What might outsiders misunderstand about this tradition?". After the chat, students produce a question bank plus a short perspective-and-evidence summary that compares the chatbot responses with unit sources linked explicitly to Where We Are in Place and Time.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students bring Melbourne's history to life by animating a character who witnessed a significant event, using Animating a Character with Adobe Express. As they retell why a particular event happened, students give voice to someone often overlooked?a child on the goldfields, a recent migrant, or a market stallholder. By sharing their animations with a Year 3 buddy class, students practise empathy and see how stories can bridge generations. The final artefact is a short animated video where their chosen character narrates the event's causes and consequences, ready for sharing on the school's digital channels. The Animate from Audio feature lets students turn their own recorded voices into expressive, lip-synced animations in minutes. They finish with creative confidence and a knack for making history feel personal and real.

Students design and construct a large, interactive 3D board game that traces the journeys of different migrant groups through history. Using recycled cardboard, craft sticks, fabric scraps, and paint, teams build detailed landscapes and landmarks representing significant places and moments along migration routes. They then integrate programmable Ozobots or Sphero Indi robots as 'travellers,' coding them to navigate the maze according to historical challenges, choices, and events. This hands-on project immerses students in the experience of migration, helping them understand how significant events shape communities and places over time.

ci: Personal changes and influences contribute to our evolving sense of self.
lo: Physical, social, emotional and intellectual changes that occur throughout life; Influences that shape our identity; Developing a sense of self

s.d: Students use Merge Cubes to create an interactive 3D 'Identity Cube' that brings their evolving sense of self to life. Each face of the cube features a different aspect of identity?such as family, culture, passions, challenges, and dreams?represented through student-created 3D models, images, and short audio reflections. Using the Merge EDU app, students program hotspots that trigger pop-up stories or voice notes, allowing viewers to explore the layers of their journey. This augmented reality artefact invites peers to rotate and tap the cube, uncovering hidden influences and personal milestones. The process encourages students to think spatially about how identity is multi-faceted and ever-changing. The finished cubes are showcased in a virtual gallery, sparking conversations about belonging and individuality.

Students use Teachable Machine to create a model that recognises changes in physical appearance, posture or voice tone to represent different stages of personal growth?such as childhood, adolescence and adulthood. They record or photograph themselves acting out scenarios that reflect social, emotional or intellectual changes, then label and train the model to classify each stage. This activity links to the unit's focus on how influences shape identity and self-concept. The process mirrors how physiotherapy and sports-coaching apps use AI to track developmental changes and provide feedback. Students share their classifier and a reflection on how recognising change can support self-awareness.

Students use Adobe Express to craft a digital visual timeline, capturing key personal changes and milestones from childhood to the present day. This directly brings the line of inquiry about 'physical, social, emotional and intellectual changes that occur throughout life' to life, as students annotate each moment with reflections and questions. Each timeline is reviewed by a Year 3 buddy, sparking inter-age conversations about how change feels and what is still to come. The result is a multimedia sequence?photos, scanned drawings, voice notes and text?showcasing each student's evolving self, which can be shared with families via QR codes at open night. By tapping into Adobe Express's Animate from Audio feature, students can record themselves narrating a memory and have an avatar bring their story to life. Students take away both technical storytelling skills and a sense of pride in how much they have grown.

Students become identity detectives, curating a collaborative Padlet wall where they collect and analyse representations of identity from books, films, sports, and their own lives. This connects to the line of inquiry around 'developing a sense of self' by challenging students to examine how identity is portrayed, constructed, and sometimes misunderstood in the wider world. Each student adopts the role of a guest curator, writing short reviews or counterpoints to posts?fostering respectful debate and new perspectives. The final Padlet is a living gallery, shared with the school library and updated throughout the term as new influences and examples arise. Padlet's comment and voting features allow students to spark discussion and highlight the most thought-provoking artefacts. Students leave with digital curation skills and a sharper eye for the stories and stereotypes that shape who we think we are.

Students become documentary filmmakers, using iMovie to record and edit 'One Change, Many Stories'?short films interviewing family, teachers or peers about a change that shaped their identity. This brings the central idea alive by letting students see firsthand how personal influences ripple through different generations. Students are challenged to edit in a 'what if?' moment: how might life have unfolded if that change never happened? The final films use iMovie's split-screen and picture-in-picture features to showcase real interviews alongside creative reimaginings, and are premiered at an evening film festival for the school community. Leveraging iMovie's green screen effect, students layer themselves into historical or future backgrounds, making the journey through change visually unforgettable. Students finish not just with slick editing skills, but with empathy for the many ways people grow and adapt.

Students design and construct a personalised 'totem tower' that visually and interactively represents key aspects of their evolving identity. Using recycled cardboard tubes, fabric, found objects, LEDs, and conductive tape, each section of the tower symbolises a different influence or change in their life (e.g., family, hobbies, beliefs, dreams). Students embed simple circuits or micro:bit-powered elements to bring their stories to life?lighting up or playing sounds when touched. This hands-on project fuses artistic self-expression with digital making, helping students reflect on 'who we are' while learning about circuits and storytelling through physical design.

ci: Emotions influence our wellbeing.
lo: How our feelings and emotions affect us; How feelings and emotions are interpreted; How our emotions and behaviour affect relationships

s.d: Children become emotion storytellers by creating short stop-motion animations that show how feelings change in everyday situations. Using Stop Motion Studio, students stage simple scenes with clay figures or classroom toys?such as a character feeling left out on the playground, then cheered up by a friend. They capture each movement frame by frame, experimenting with facial expressions and body language to convey happiness, frustration, or surprise. The app's onion-skinning feature helps them line up each shot for smooth transitions, while simple voiceover or sound effects can be added to match the mood. The finished artefact is a series of playful emotion stories, ready to screen for classmates and families. This hands-on filmmaking process helps children see that emotions are dynamic and can be expressed through movement as well as words.

Students will compose and record their own 'feelings soundtracks', using GarageBand to turn emotions into music. This activity brings to life how our feelings and emotions affect us, letting children explore the sounds of happiness, sadness, and excitement. Imagine the class as young composers creating a playlist for the school wellbeing team to use during mindfulness time. The final artefact is a collection of short, emotion-inspired audio tracks, each with a title and a short voice introduction by the student explaining the feeling. GarageBand's Live Loops feature lets even the youngest students layer beats and melodies to match the mood they want to express. Kids discover that their feelings can be shared and understood in ways that go far beyond words.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Children become voice actors by recording themselves expressing different feelings, then use Animate from Audio in Adobe Express (https://new.express.adobe.com/home/tools/animate-from-audio) to bring a digital character to life. Each child chooses a character template?such as a friendly monster, animal, or robot?and records a short message like 'I feel excited when I play with my friends!' or 'Sometimes I feel nervous on the first day of school.' The tool automatically lip-syncs the character to their voice, making the emotion visible and engaging. Students watch each other's animated clips and guess the feeling being expressed, sparking discussion about how tone and words help us understand emotions. The final artefact is a gallery of animated emotion clips, ready to share with families or play during circle time. This playful process helps children see that feelings can be expressed in many creative ways.

Students will collaborate on a giant digital feelings mural using Freeform, drawing, doodling, and adding stickers to represent all the emotions they know. This creative activity explores how our emotions and behaviour affect relationships, as students see how their feelings mix and interact with others' on the same canvas. To shake things up, the mural will be displayed at assembly and parents will be invited to add a digital 'sticker' of their own emotion, making it a true community artwork. The finished piece is a vibrant, layered digital mural that grows over the week and can be printed as a poster for the classroom. Freeform's infinite canvas and collaborative mode let every child contribute at once, with live drawing and image import for maximum creativity. Kids experience the joy of making something bigger together and learn that everyone's feelings matter in the group.

Children will become 'emotion detectives', using Epic to hunt for characters in stories who show strong feelings and collecting them in a digital 'Emotions Scrapbook'. This taps into how feelings and emotions affect us by helping students notice how characters' emotions change the story. Students will take on the role of book reviewers, recommending a story to another class based on how well it shows big feelings. The final artefact is a digital scrapbook with screenshots, emojis, and one-sentence reflections for each character they spot. Epic's search and collection features let students quickly gather their favourite books and characters into a shareable library. Kids leave with sharper eyes for feelings in stories?and maybe in real life too.

Students design and craft their own unique 'Mood Monster' hand puppets using socks, felt, buttons, paper, and recycled materials to represent different emotions. After building their puppets, they use a Sphero Indi robot as a 'Feelings Messenger', coding it with color tiles to travel between puppet stages and deliver emotion cards. Children perform mini puppet shows, expressing how their Mood Monsters feel and react in different situations, while the Indi robot helps connect the stories?blending creative making, technology, and emotional expression in a playful, memorable way.

ci: The products people use go through a process of change.
lo: Where food comes from; How food can be changed for different purposes; An appreciation of food

s.d: Students embark on a 'food origins adventure' by taking the Insta360 camera on a virtual field trip around the school garden, kitchen, or local community spaces where food is grown, prepared, or shared. Working in small groups, they capture immersive 360-degree photos and short videos at each stage?planting seeds, harvesting herbs, or mixing ingredients. Back in class, students explore these scenes on tablets, spotting clues about how food changes from garden to plate. Each group selects their favourite moment and narrates a short story about what is happening in the scene, imagining the journey from seed to snack. The final artefact is a class 'food journey gallery'?a collection of interactive 360-degree scenes with student voiceovers, ready for families to explore on open day. This activity transforms everyday spaces into a living food story, helping children see the hidden steps behind every meal.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students bring food to life using Animate from Audio in Adobe Express (https://new.express.adobe.com/home/tools/animate-from-audio), turning a fruit, vegetable, or favourite snack into a talking character. Each child draws or photographs their chosen food, then records a short message as if they are the food itself?sharing how they were grown, changed, or enjoyed. The teacher guides the process, uploading the artwork and syncing the voice recording so the character lip-syncs in real time. Students can add expressive backgrounds, stickers, or props to show where their food comes from or how it is transformed. The final product is a playful, animated food explainer, ready to be screened at a class 'food film festival'. This activity helps students sequence food changes and express appreciation for the journey every meal takes.

Students become food process filmmakers by creating stop-motion animations that show how a favourite food changes from start to finish. Using Stop Motion Studio, they sequence scenes with playdough, paper cut-outs, or real ingredients?such as a tomato turning into pasta sauce or wheat becoming bread. Each frame captures a step in the transformation, with students narrating or adding speech bubbles to explain what is happening. The app's onion-skinning and frame-by-frame editing features let children experiment with timing and movement, making their food stories come alive. The finished artefact is a short, creative stop-motion video that can be shared with families or screened at a class 'food film night'. This hands-on activity helps children visualise and retell the hidden processes behind everyday foods.

Students become local food detectives by using the Field Guide to Victoria app to investigate which plants and animals in their area can become food. They browse the app's rich database to find examples like apples, honey, or native herbs, then match these to foods they eat at home or school. Each student chooses one local food source and creates a simple poster or digital collage showing its journey?from growing in the wild or on a farm, to being harvested and prepared. The app's detailed photos and facts help students notice the diversity of food sources around them, sparking curiosity about where meals really begin. The final product is a class display of 'local food journeys', connecting personal eating habits to the natural world. This activity grounds food appreciation in real, local examples children can see and touch.

Students become food story curators by using PicCollage to create vibrant visual timelines of how a favourite food changes from start to finish. They gather photos, drawings, and stickers to illustrate each stage?such as planting seeds, growing, harvesting, cooking, and eating. Using PicCollage's drag-and-drop layout, children sequence the images and add speech bubbles or labels to explain what is happening at each step. Students can include family recipes or cultural traditions related to their chosen food, making each collage unique. The final artefact is a colourful timeline poster, printed for the classroom or shared digitally with families. This activity helps children see the many steps and people involved in bringing food to the table, deepening their appreciation for everyday meals.

Students design and build a vibrant raceway that traces the adventure of food from farm to table! Using cardboard, craft paper, felt, recycled boxes, and toy vehicles or marbles, children create 3D models of farms, trucks, markets, and kitchens along a winding track. They then use Sphero Indi cars (or similar age-appropriate programmable vehicles) decorated as 'food items' to travel the raceway, stopping at each stage to discuss how food changes and moves through systems. This hands-on journey connects personal meal experiences to bigger food networks, making food origins and transformations come alive through building, storytelling, and play.

ci: The properties of materials influence how objects move and their use.
lo: Properties of materials; How objects move; How we use materials

s.d: Let your Preps become material detectives as they program Bee-Bots to travel across different textured mats?smooth, bumpy, soft, or hard?investigating how each surface changes the robot's movement. This hands-on adventure brings the line of inquiry 'how objects move' to life, letting students feel and see the science in action. Invite the art teacher to help students design and paint their own obstacle mats, transforming the classroom into a collaborative makerspace. Each child creates a short video tour narrating their Bee-Bot's journey and discoveries, ready to share with families at home. Bee-Bots' sequence-and-repeat function lets students experiment with more complex movement patterns, encouraging problem-solving and prediction. Kids walk away with a sense of wonder and the confidence to explore how the world works?one Bee-Bot mission at a time.

Prep students become young scientists by creating interactive digital books showcasing how different materials affect the way objects move. Exploring the line of inquiry on properties of materials, they investigate objects that roll, slide, bounce, or float, then capture their discoveries in words, drawings, and photos. Each child adopts the role of a museum curator, narrating their book as if introducing real artefacts to visitors from another school. The finished eBook features student-recorded audio, labelled diagrams, and simple experiments documented step-by-step, ready to be shared at the Prep learning expo and emailed home. Book Creator's voice recording and drawing-over-photo features allow even non-writers to author rich, multimodal pages that bring their observations to life. This empowers every child to see themselves as both a creative maker and a scientific storyteller, confident to explain how the world works beyond the classroom.

Invite students to become movement scientists by recording slow-motion videos of objects rolling, sliding, or bouncing on different surfaces using Seesaw's built-in camera. This brings the line of inquiry 'how objects move' into focus, as children compare which materials make things go fast, slow, or stop. Connect with literacy by having students narrate their videos, describing what they see in their own words and building rich vocabulary. The class creates a digital exhibition, with each video paired with a voice-over and a prediction for 'what would happen if?' scenarios, shared with families online. Seesaw's drawing tools let students annotate their videos with arrows and labels, highlighting key observations. Kids finish the project as confident communicators, excited to ask questions and explain their thinking.

Preps become inventors as they use Sketchbook to draw fantastical machines that use unusual materials?imagine a boat made of sponges or a flying car with paper wings. This creative challenge dives into 'how we use materials', encouraging students to think beyond the everyday and dream up wild new possibilities. Invite the music teacher to help students match sound effects to their inventions, adding a sensory twist to their designs. The final product is a digital gallery of annotated invention sketches, each paired with a short audio clip, ready to display on the classroom screen for a family open night. Sketchbook's layering feature lets students experiment with combining different textures and colours, making their ideas pop. Children leave with creative confidence and a sense of possibility, ready to see materials in a whole new way.

Let students become puppet show hosts, using Puppet Pals to create mini-plays where characters face challenges?like building a bridge from spaghetti or racing on a jelly ramp. This activity brings the 'properties of materials' to centre stage, as students act out what happens when materials are strong, bendy, slippery, or sticky. Invite a local engineer (even via video) to send in a question for the puppets to solve, making the learning feel real and important. The final artefact is a collection of puppet show videos, each one telling a story about choosing the right material for the job, ready to share at assembly or with families. Puppet Pals' custom background feature lets students upload photos of their own classroom experiments, blending real and imagined worlds. Kids come away feeling like problem-solvers and storytellers, with the confidence to test new ideas.

Students design and build their own mini racetracks using cardboard, tubes, recycled containers, and a variety of craft materials, then test different objects (like marbles, toy cars, or balls) made from materials such as wood, plastic, and metal to see how they move. Using simple stop-motion video apps on iPads, students capture their races and observe how different surfaces and materials affect speed and movement. They experiment with adding ramps, barriers, or textured sections, then improve their designs to make the fastest or slowest track. This project encourages hands-on exploration of materials, properties, and motion, linking science concepts with creativity and digital storytelling.

ci: An inquiry into rights and responsibilities in the struggle to share finite resources with other people and with other living things.
lo: Lines of inquiry to be confirmed once planner is uploaded

s.d: Children build a 'Family Traditions Sound Board' using Makey Makey and real objects from home?each object triggers a special family story or song when touched. This hands-on activity brings the idea of sharing finite resources to life by letting students explore how family traditions and celebrations connect us and shape our responsibilities. Invite families to send in a small item or photo representing a tradition, and students become museum curators, explaining the meaning behind each object to visiting buddies or parents. The final artefact is a tactile, interactive display where touching each item plays a unique pre-recorded message or song about that family's culture. Using Makey Makey's ability to turn everyday conductive materials into interactive buttons, students experience technology as a bridge between home and school. They leave with a sense of pride in their background and a new appreciation for the rich diversity in their classroom.

Students use Tablet Magnifiers to investigate everyday resources?such as water droplets, grains of rice, or recycled materials?used in the classroom or at home. They capture magnified images that reveal hidden textures, shapes, or impurities, sparking discussion about why resources are finite and how we can use them responsibly. Students then create a visual resource diary, pairing each close-up photo with a reflection on how that resource is used and what might happen if it runs out. This activity encourages critical thinking about sustainability and personal responsibility. The final product is a digital or printed diary of magnified resources with student reflections.

Students use Apple Clips to film short video pledges where they clearly state one responsibility they will take on to care for and share finite resources, such as saving water, recycling, or helping classmates. They enhance their videos by adding live titles to highlight key words and use animated stickers to emphasise their message creatively. Students also apply visual effects like filters or overlays to illustrate how their actions positively impact people, animals, or the environment. These individual videos are compiled into a class 'Responsibility Wall'?a digital gallery that sparks conversations about sharing resources and respecting others. Throughout the process, students practise speaking confidently and listen to peers' ideas, deepening their understanding of rights and responsibilities. This activity empowers students to express their role in caring for the planet and their community through engaging multimedia storytelling.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students animate a character based on a special family member or ancestor using Adobe Express's 'Animate from Audio' feature. This creative twist brings the central idea to life by letting children give voice to their family's values and stories in a playful, digital way. To deepen the experience, students host a 'Living Family Museum' where their animated characters introduce themselves and share a tradition or lesson learned. The final artefact is a collection of lively, talking portraits that can be shared with families or featured at assembly. The 'Animate from Audio' tool lets even the youngest learners turn their own voices into expressive, moving characters?no reading required. Kids walk away with digital storytelling skills and a fresh understanding of how technology can make family history come alive.

Prep students design a 'Family Celebration Pathway' for Sphero Indi cars, using coloured tiles to represent different family traditions, values, or members. This tactile activity ties directly to exploring connections and diversity within families, as each pathway becomes a unique journey through a child's heritage. Students then swap pathways with a classmate and navigate each other's family stories, sparking conversations about similarities and differences. The finished artefact is a set of colourful, coded routes, each accompanied by a simple legend explaining what every colour means in the context of that family. Sphero Indi's programmable tiles allow for sequencing and branching, letting students build in choice points or 'celebration stops' along the way. Children leave with a sense of pride in their family and a new appreciation for the journeys of others.

Students design and craft a banner that represents a special family tradition or celebration using felt, recycled fabric, colored paper, and string. They embed simple LED sticker lights (with coin batteries and adult guidance) to highlight important symbols or words, learning basic circuits as they decorate. The banners can include drawings, collaged photos, or small objects that tell their family's story. This hands-on project combines crafting and basic electronics, helping students share their unique backgrounds while literally shining a light on the diversity within their class community.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Family histories shape who we are and what we value
lo: What makes a family; The people in your family; Your family history; What is important to your family

s.d: Children become time-travelling storytellers by animating scenes from their own family histories, bringing grandparents, siblings, and cultural traditions to life. This activity dives into the line of inquiry 'your family history', letting each child stage and record their own family's story as a playable puppet show. Invite families to send in old photos or special objects, so students can transform ordinary details into starring roles on the digital stage. The end result is a lively, voice-acted animated puppet show clip that can be shared at a 'family film festival' with classmates and parents. Using Puppet Pals' custom photo import, children can place real family faces onto the puppets ? a feature that always gets giggles and wonder. Every child walks away seeing their own family story as worth telling, with new pride in their roots.

Students build a vibrant digital collage titled 'What Makes My Family Unique?', curating images, stickers, and handwritten words that represent their family's important traditions and values. This directly connects to the line of inquiry 'what is important to your family', giving students space to celebrate everything from favourite foods to special celebrations. Students swap collages in small groups and try to guess the stories behind each photo or symbol, sparking conversations about diversity and common ground. The finished collages are displayed on a digital class wall for families to explore at home via QR code, creating a mini-exhibition of belonging. PicCollage's cut-out tool lets children trace around family photos or drawings to create playful, sticker-style versions of their loved ones and special objects.
