Students leave with a new appreciation for what makes every family different and the confidence to share what matters most to them.

Children transform a family photo or drawing into a talking character using ChatterPix Kids, giving voice to a loved one or family pet. Each student records a short greeting, story, or favourite family saying, animating the mouth to match their words for a playful, personal touch. This activity supports the line of inquiry 'the people in your family', helping children see each family member as a storyteller with something special to share. For added fun, students can swap devices and listen to each other's talking portraits, noticing similarities and differences in family traditions or languages. The finished talking images are compiled into a class video montage, ready to be shared at a family celebration event. ChatterPix Kids' simple drawing and sticker tools let even the youngest learners personalise their creations, making every family member feel like a star.

Students become family portrait artists, using Brushes Redux to illustrate a 'family circle' that celebrates all types of families ? whether they live together or far apart. This activity explores the line of inquiry 'what makes a family', encouraging children to include everyone they consider family (pets, cousins, neighbours, or chosen family too). Invite a local artist or community elder to share how portraits tell stories across cultures, inspiring students to think beyond traditional family trees. The final digital paintings are printed and displayed in a 'Celebrating Our Circles' gallery at school, with each artist's recorded voice message explaining who's in their circle and why. Brushes Redux's layering feature lets even young children experiment with building up their artwork bit by bit, adding details and backgrounds to make each portrait pop. Every child leaves with the confidence to see their family structure represented proudly and creatively.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students become voice actors for their own family ancestors (real or imagined) by creating an animated portrait that tells a one-minute story from their family history. This hands-on activity is rooted in the line of inquiry 'your family history', giving children the thrill of 'becoming' a great-grandparent, aunty, or family hero for a day. Children can trade voices with a classmate, bringing each other's ancestors to life and discovering new perspectives. Their finished artefact is a talking-head animation that can be safely shared with families or included in a class time-capsule video. The 'Animate from Audio' feature in Adobe Express lets children sync their own voices to a character's mouth, making even the shyest storyteller beam with pride. Students walk away with a sense of connection ? not just to their own family, but to the diverse stories in their community.

s.t: Time Capsule Treasure Boxes & Talking Tiles
s.d: Students design and build their own 'time capsule treasure box' using cardboard, recycled containers, colored paper, and craft materials, decorating it with symbols and drawings representing their family's unique history, traditions, and values. Each child adds small crafted items (like a mini flag, family pet drawing, or a handmade tradition token) inside the box. Using simple recording buttons (such as Talking Tiles or Talking Photo Frames), students record a short message or story about one special family memory or value and attach it to their box. This hybrid project lets students physically build, decorate, and curate a box of family treasures while integrating technology for sharing personal stories, sparking conversations about diversity and belonging in 'Where We Are in Place and Time'.

ci: Schools are organised to help students learn and work together
lo: The organisation of the Junior School; Routines that allow developing independence; How to make the classroom and playground healthy and safe

s.d: Children become 'school explorers' by programming Bee-Bots to travel around a giant floor map of the Junior School, visiting key places like the library, nurse's office, and playground. This hands-on adventure brings to life how schools are organised to help everyone learn and work together. Each team takes on the role of tour guides, imagining what a new student would need to know to feel welcome and safe in their new environment. The final product is a filmed Bee-Bot 'welcome tour' that can be shared with next year's Preps and new families. Using Bee-Bot's sequence-and-repeat function, students learn to plan efficient routes and debug their journeys. By the end, every child feels like a confident navigator and a caring host, ready to help others belong.

Students use the insta360 camera to create a virtual classroom and playground tour, highlighting routines, safe spaces and areas for collaboration. Working in small groups, they record 360-degree videos that show how the Junior School is organised, including key locations like the reading corner, art area, and outdoor play zones. The immersive footage allows students to demonstrate how routines?such as lining up, handwashing or sharing materials?help everyone work together. After filming, students add simple voice-over explanations about how these routines support independence and safety. The finished tours are shared with new students or visiting families, helping them understand how the school community functions. Teachers assess students on their ability to identify and explain routines and organisational features using their video tours.

Children bring their self-portraits to life by recording their voices with ChatterPix Kids, turning a drawing or photo of themselves into a talking introduction. This playful activity builds confidence in communication and supports routines that help students develop independence. Each child becomes the 'classroom greeter', sharing their name, something they love, and one way they help keep the classroom healthy and safe. The final talking portraits are stitched together into a class video to welcome visitors and new students. By using ChatterPix Kids' mouth animation and sound effects, students add a spark of personality and humour. They walk away knowing their voice matters and feeling excited to speak up in their new community.

Students become junior reporters and create a digital 'Healthy and Safe School' guidebook for new Preps, filled with photos, captions, and their own recorded advice. This project spotlights the line of inquiry into 'how to make the classroom and playground healthy and safe' by inviting children to notice, explain, and model daily routines and safety actions. With the class acting as experts for next year's cohort, each child chooses a favourite classroom or playground routine?like handwashing, using quiet voices, or looking after play equipment?and demonstrates it for their peers. The final artefact is a vibrant, multimedia eBook combining each child's narrated photo page, illustrations, and simple safety tips, published as a digital welcome pack to be shared with future Preps and their families. Book Creator's built-in audio recording and drawing tools let students layer voice, doodles, and photos onto each interactive page, turning everyday moments into a lively, shareable resource. By seeing themselves as capable contributors, students gain pride in their independence and feel empowered to shape a welcoming, caring school community.

Students use Apple Clips to film short 'How-To' videos that demonstrate classroom routines or playground safety tips. They act out steps for tasks like lining up, washing hands, or using equipment safely, using animated text and stickers to highlight key actions. Students narrate their videos to explain why these routines help everyone learn and play together. The finished clips are compiled into a class 'Routine Library' that new students can watch to learn about school life. This activity builds independence and reinforces the importance of organisation and safety in the school community.

Students design and craft a 3D puppet or figure representing themselves using cardboard tubes, fabric scraps, yarn, and recycled craft bits to showcase features and clothes that reflect their family and culture. Each puppet gets a simple 'home' or scene made from a shoebox or cardboard base, decorated with symbols, drawings, or photos about their family traditions and values. Using a Bee-Bot, students program a short journey between different families' scenes, stopping at each to share a recorded message or story about what makes their family unique (recorded with a talking button or iPad). This collaborative parade celebrates identity and diversity while integrating storytelling, building, and introductory robotics.

ci: People use imagination and materials to express stories, ideas and culture through performance.
lo: Different materials to make puppets; Types and uses of puppets by different cultures; Features and purposes of puppet performances

s.d: Students become storytellers by designing an interactive digital puppet theatre book that brings their own puppet characters and performances to life. Exploring the line of inquiry on 'features and purposes of puppet performances', students craft pages that introduce different styles of puppetry and narrate their show step by step. Each group adopts the role of cultural ambassadors, embedding greetings, music, or traditions from a chosen culture to deepen empathy and worldliness. The final artefact is a clickable eBook, bursting with hand-drawn illustrations, recorded puppet voices, and embedded video skits, ready to be shared with families or younger year levels. Using Book Creator's comic templates and the option to embed video or audio directly on each page, students create a multimedia showcase that feels like a real puppet theatre programme. This journey gives students a sense of creative pride and the power to use digital storytelling to celebrate culture and imagination in their community.

Students compose original soundtracks and sound effects for their puppet performances, discovering how music and audio bring out emotion and meaning. By exploring the features and purposes of puppet performances, they see how sound shapes a story's mood and helps audiences understand the characters. To make it even more real, students are tasked with creating a signature 'puppet melody' that could be used in all Year 1 puppet shows?turning them into the sound designers for the whole year level. The final product is a collection of custom audio tracks, complete with voiceover, music, and sound effects, delivered as part of the puppet show experience for families. Using GarageBand's Live Loops, students experiment with layering, tempo, and simple audio effects to match the story's feeling. They'll leave with creative confidence and a new way to express stories, knowing that even the youngest students can be composers.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students use the Animate from Audio feature in Adobe Express (https://new.express.adobe.com/home/tools/animate-from-audio) to bring their puppet characters to life as animated storytellers. Each student records a short narration or message from their puppet's perspective, such as introducing themselves or sharing a favourite cultural folktale. The teacher guides students in selecting a character style and syncing their voice, so the digital puppet lip-syncs to their unique story. The finished artefact is a short animated video, perfect for sharing in class or as part of a digital puppet parade. This process lets students experiment with voice, expression, and digital storytelling, deepening their understanding of how puppets communicate ideas and emotions. Students gain confidence as performers and see how technology can amplify their creative voices.

Students animate their own puppet faces using ChatterPix Kids, voicing a message from the puppet's perspective about its cultural origins or the story it tells. This activity lets them explore the types and uses of puppets in different cultures, giving voice to what a puppet might 'say' if it could talk back. As a fresh angle, students swap puppets and record each other's characters, learning to represent stories not their own and thinking about perspective. The final artefact is a collection of 10-second talking puppet videos, each with a cultural message, which can be strung together for a digital puppet parade at assembly. ChatterPix Kids' background music and sticker features allow students to enhance their puppets' personalities and settings in playful ways. Students leave with empathy for different cultures and the joy of expressing another's story as if it were their own.

Students map out puppet designs and stage layouts collaboratively on Freeform, drawing, sticking, and linking ideas as a creative team. This brings alive the unit's focus on imagination and materials, showing how planning and sharing ideas lead to richer puppet performances. Groups are invited to pitch their show to a Year 2 class, just like a theatre company presenting to a real audience, asking for feedback to fine-tune their ideas. Their finished artefact is a digital design board, complete with sketches, textures, and stage plans, which can be printed and displayed in the art room or shared digitally with families. Freeform's infinite canvas and linking tools let students connect character sketches with material samples and scene ideas?giving them a taste of real theatrical design. They leave the unit knowing their ideas matter, and that great performances start with creative teamwork.

s.t: Shadow Stories: Puppet Theater in a Box
s.d: Students design and build their own shadow puppets using cardboard, paper, fabric scraps, and popsicle sticks, then create a mini puppet theater from a recycled box. Using a simple flashlight or a programmable Bee-Bot with a torch attachment, they experiment with casting shadows and bringing their characters to life. Students work in groups to invent and perform original stories, exploring how movement, shapes, and light can express ideas and emotions. This hands-on project fuses storytelling, cultural exploration, and STEM principles, letting students express themselves creatively while learning about the art of puppetry.

ci: Communities work together by creating systems to help people live and learn.
lo: The roles people play in a community; Systems and routines that help us stay organised; How communities work together to meet needs

s.d: Students become city planners by designing and programming BeeBots to travel through a model town representing different community roles ? from fire station to library to market. This hands-on adventure dives deep into how systems and routines help communities stay organised, as each BeeBot journey represents a vital daily routine. Imagine the excitement as students swap roles to become the 'mayor,' making decisions about traffic, detours, and even emergencies that test their systems. The final class map is a vibrant, obstacle-filled town with labelled pathways and buildings, ready to be showcased to families or Year 2s. The real magic comes from BeeBot's sequence-and-repeat function, letting students create efficient routines and even 'fix' traffic jams by debugging their code. By mastering this, students see themselves as problem-solvers who can make a community run smoother ? and they walk away ready to spot and improve real-life routines around them.

Students step into the shoes of community helpers and create digital ID badges using PicCollage, adding their own photo, symbols of their role, and a list of their daily tasks. This creative project explores the many roles people play in a community, making the invisible work of helpers feel important and real. Each child is challenged to design not just for themselves, but to make a badge for a classroom visitor or a friend, helping them see the world from another's point of view. The finished badges are printed and hung on a 'community wall' or shared as a digital gallery for families to guess the role ? sparking lively conversations about contribution. By using PicCollage's freeform cut-out and sticker layering features, students can make each badge colourful and unique, reflecting the diversity of their community. They leave with a sense of pride in the roles around them ? and the confidence to step into new ones.

Students give a voice to everyday objects from their school ? like a lunchbox, a clock, or the classroom bin ? using ChatterPix Kids, making each item explain the system or routine it belongs to. Tying directly into the idea of systems that help us stay organised, this playful activity invites students to think about the hidden helpers in their world. Students swap objects with a buddy and record two perspectives on the same routine: one from the object and one from a person who uses it. The final clips become a hilarious but insightful video wall or class podcast, ready to delight another class or the school assembly. ChatterPix Kids' draw-to-animate mouth and voice-change filters bring each object to life in a way that sticks with students. After this, students spot systems everywhere ? and realise even small routines matter in making a community tick.

Students use Apple Clips to create video profiles of different community roles, such as teachers, doctors, or shopkeepers. They act out or interview someone in that role, using live titles and stickers to identify key responsibilities and routines. Students narrate how each role helps the community function smoothly and why teamwork is important. The finished video profiles are compiled into a digital 'Community Heroes Gallery', sparking discussion about the systems and people that support daily life. This activity builds understanding of community structure and the value of collaboration.

Students become junior coders by creating animated stories in ScratchJr that show what happens when a community system breaks down ? like a lost library book, a late bus, or a missing lunch monitor. This challenge links perfectly to the line of inquiry about how systems and routines help us stay organised, as students tinker to find out what really happens when the pieces don't fit together. Working in pairs, they invent a solution and code it into their story, sharing a 'fix-it ending' that could inspire others. The finished animations are shared with Prep buddies or uploaded for families to watch, sparking conversations about teamwork and responsibility. ScratchJr's advanced use of message blocks (to trigger events across characters) lets students build more complex, realistic interactions than simple movement alone. They come away proud not just of their coding, but of their ability to problem-solve and help a community bounce back.

s.t: My Busy Town: Interactive Jobs & Journeys Map
s.d: Students will co-create a large, colorful 3D map of a community using cardboard, felt, recycled boxes, and paper rolls to represent buildings, roads, and parks. Each child crafts a 'community worker' character (like a teacher, baker, or crossing guard) and designs a simple vehicle or tool for their role using craft materials. Using Sphero Indi cars, students program simple routes for their community worker to travel between key locations, demonstrating how different jobs and routines connect and help the town run smoothly. This project immerses students in the systems and roles that organise a community, blending creative building with beginner robotics in a playful, hands-on way.

ci: Movement is dependent on different forces.
lo: Ways objects move; The influence different materials have on movement; How designs can be adapted and improved

s.d: Students become movement detectives, programming Sphero Indi cars to zip across different surfaces and ramps, exploring how push, pull, and friction change their speed and direction. This hands-on experiment dives straight into how materials and surfaces influence movement, making the invisible world of forces visible. Students take on the role of engineers, designing obstacle courses to challenge a rival class and then swapping to see whose design is trickiest to conquer. Their final showcase is a short video race report, narrated like sports commentators, capturing the most surprising moments and clever design tweaks. By using Indi's colour tile programming and speed sensors, students can compare how the same car behaves on carpet, cardboard, and smooth tables. They finish with real evidence that their design choices matter?and the confidence to test, tweak, and try again.

Young inventors use Makey Makey to build their own 'movement machines'?simple contraptions that trigger sounds or lights when objects are pushed, pulled, or rolled. This playful project brings the line of inquiry about adapting and improving designs to life, as students tinker with materials and connections. Students become inventors for a day, creating a device for a classmate with a unique challenge (like a one-handed launcher or a 'race starter' for a friend with limited mobility). The class hosts a mini Maker Expo, inviting families to try out each invention and vote for the most creative adaptation. Exploring Makey Makey's conductivity testing feature, students discover which everyday materials (foil, playdough, fruit) best complete their circuits and why. They walk away seeing themselves as real-world problem solvers, ready to invent for others?not just themselves.

Students become science reporters, using the iPad's Slow Motion Physical Analysis tool to film objects rolling, sliding, and bouncing down ramps of different angles and materials. This investigation spotlights the way objects move and how forces like gravity and friction shape their journey. Students create 'Movement Mysteries'?short clips with a puzzling start and a dramatic reveal, challenging older buddies to guess what force or material made the difference. The finished product is a gallery of slow-motion clips, each paired with a student-recorded voiceover explaining their scientific thinking. The slow-motion feature lets students capture details the naked eye would miss, such as the exact moment a ball changes direction or slows down. They leave with sharper observation skills and a new appreciation for the hidden science in everyday play.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students bring the forces of movement to life by animating a character?like a bouncing ball or a sliding penguin?using Adobe Express's Animate from Audio feature (https://new.express.adobe.com/home/tools/animate-from-audio). This creative storytelling task lets students experiment with different materials and surfaces in their stories, showing how pushes, pulls, and friction affect movement. Acting as science storytellers, students craft a digital tale to teach next year's Preps why some things zoom and others crawl. The final artefact is a lively animated video, complete with student-recorded narration and expressive movements that highlight key science concepts. Animate from Audio transforms their voices into character motion, making every story unique and full of personality. Students finish the project proud to be both scientists and storytellers, ready to explain tricky concepts in fun, memorable ways.

Students become inventors and illustrators, using Brushes Redux to design and digitally sketch their own moving toy?showing how its parts work together to roll, spin, or bounce. This creative task links directly to adapting and improving designs, as students revise their blueprints based on what worked (or didn't) in hands-on trials. Students swap sketches with a partner and try to 'build' each other's design with classroom materials, then give feedback on what was clear or confusing. The final artefact is a digital portfolio page, combining step-by-step sketches, notes, and a reflection on what made the best designs successful. Brushes Redux's layering feature lets students show the inside workings of their toys and experiment with different materials and movement paths. They walk away with a designer's eye?able to imagine, test, and communicate how things move in the real world.

Students design and build their own mini racetrack ramps using cardboard, tubes, popsticks, and recycled materials, experimenting with angles, heights, and different surface textures. They craft unique race vehicles from bottle caps, straws, and clay, then use Sphero Indi robots to test and compare how both their handmade cars and the robot move down the tracks. iPads are used to record slow-motion videos of the races, helping students observe the effects of push, pull, and friction. Through playful competition and iteration, students apply the Design Cycle to improve their tracks and vehicles, discovering how forces and materials affect movement in the real world.

ci: Invertebrates are essential to living things and the environment.
lo: The characteristics of invertebrates; The interdependence of invertebrates and their environment; Life cycles of invertebrates

s.d: Students become real-world 'invertebrate detectives', using the Field Guide to Victoria app to scan the playground and discover the secret lives of bugs right under their noses. This hands-on investigation brings the line of inquiry about the characteristics of invertebrates to life, as students hunt, identify, and photograph local species. Instead of just learning, they act as citizen scientists, gathering data that could help a local environmental group or even the council. Their final artefact is a digital 'Bug Gallery'?a collection of annotated photos and fun facts about each invertebrate they find, ready to share with families and the school community. The app's advanced filter and compare features let students spot subtle differences between lookalike species, sparking lively debates about what makes each bug unique. Students finish the project seeing themselves as real scientists and advocates for the tiny creatures that keep our environment buzzing.

Students use Apple Clips to create video documentaries about invertebrates they find in the schoolyard or local environment. They film close-ups of insects, worms, or spiders, using stickers and animated text to label features and describe life cycles. Students narrate how each invertebrate interacts with its environment and why it is important for the ecosystem. The finished documentaries are shared in a class 'Invertebrate Gallery', encouraging curiosity and respect for small creatures. This activity helps students connect observation skills with scientific communication in a fun, accessible way.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students use the Animate from Audio feature in Animating a Character with Adobe Express (https://new.express.adobe.com/home/tools/animate-from-audio) to bring invertebrate experts or bug characters to life. Each student records their voice as a butterfly, ant, or spider, explaining their unique features or how they help the environment. The tool automatically lip-syncs the character to the student's narration, creating a lively, animated explainer. Students can add backgrounds or props that match their chosen invertebrate's habitat, making the story more engaging. The final product is a short, animated video that can be shared with the class or posted on the school website. This activity builds confidence in oral storytelling and helps students communicate scientific ideas in a playful, memorable way.

Students become eco-storytellers, crafting visual stories about how invertebrates and their environments depend on each other using PicCollage. This activity spotlights the interdependence between bugs and their habitats, making the invisible connections visible. Taking inspiration from environmental campaigns, students create persuasive posters or storyboards aimed at convincing adults to protect local invertebrate habitats. The finished collages are printed and displayed in school corridors or shared digitally with the broader community. PicCollage's cut-out and layering tools let students blend their own photos, drawings, and text with creative backgrounds, making each story pop. Students leave empowered to use their voices?and visuals?for real-world change.

Students become young entomologists by designing an interactive eBook that guides readers through the wild world of invertebrates and their amazing life cycles. Exploring the interdependence of invertebrates and their environment, each child curates fact pages, animated diagrams, and photo galleries that reveal how creatures like beetles, worms, and spiders help sustain healthy ecosystems. As a unique perspective, students adopt the persona of a chosen invertebrate and write diary entries chronicling a day in its life, highlighting challenges and triumphs from the invertebrate's viewpoint. The final artefact is a vibrant, multimedia eBook, complete with audio narration and clickable hotspots, ready to be shared with Prep buddies and families through a QR code at the school entrance. Book Creator's built-in comic templates and drawing tools empower even the youngest authors to blend science, art, and storytelling in rich, interactive ways. By publishing as real experts, students discover their voice as advocates for the small but mighty creatures that keep our planet in balance.

Students will design and build imaginative 'Bug Hotels' using recycled boxes, cardboard tubes, paper rolls, natural materials (leaves, twigs, bark), and craft supplies. Using iPads, they will photograph their creations and record short voice tours explaining which invertebrates might live in their hotel and how the habitat supports them. This project combines hands-on construction with digital storytelling, deepening students' understanding of invertebrate needs and how humans can share the planet by providing safe spaces for tiny creatures. The activity encourages empathy, creativity, and real-world connections to environmental stewardship.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: An understanding of history helps us to see how the past shapes the future.
lo: Ways in which children's lives have changed over time; Reasons for changes to children's lives over time

s.d: Students transform the classroom into a living timeline by programming Sphero Indi cars to travel along coloured paths representing different eras of childhood. Each group designs a segment of the timeline, decorating it with artefacts, toys, or images from a specific decade?like marbles for the 1950s or tablets for today. Using Indi's colour tiles, students code the car to stop at each era and play a sound or light pattern that matches the time period. As the Indi travels, students narrate short stories about what life was like for children in each era, highlighting changes in technology, school, and play. The journey ends with a 'future' station, where students imagine and code what might come next. This interactive, movement-based activity makes abstract historical change tangible and memorable.

Students reimagine an old-school playground using Brushes Redux, designing vibrant digital murals that blend artefacts and play equipment from different decades. This directly explores how play and technology have changed children's lives over time. They get to interview grandparents or family friends and turn those stories into digital art, mixing real experiences with their own creative vision. The finished murals are displayed in a virtual gallery for families to explore via QR codes around the school. Brushes Redux's layering tool lets students mix hand-drawn backgrounds with photographic textures?adding depth and surprise to each creation. By seeing their family stories come alive as art, students feel like history-makers themselves.

Students become junior reporters and film short 'breaking history' news segments revealing a major change in children's lives, such as the arrival of television, changing school technology or new ways to play. They plan a headline, perform in period-inspired costumes and capture close-up footage of relevant toys or artefacts with iMovie's built-in camera. Groups arrange clips on the timeline, trim unwanted footage and add titles identifying past, present and future. Voice-over narration explains what changed, why it may have changed and what remained familiar for children. Students add transitions and copyright-safe music from iMovie's built-in soundtrack library to produce a polished one-minute news report. The completed reports form a class newsreel that helps families compare childhood across generations.

Students curate a digital bookshelf on Epic, hand-picking old and new stories that highlight what it meant to be a child in different times and places. This deep dive into historical perspectives helps them wrestle with why some changes?like who gets to go to school?matter so much. For extra spark, students recommend titles with a 'Read This If...' tagline (e.g. 'Read this if you want to know what kids did before TV!'), sharing their picks with pen-pal classrooms at another school. Their curated collections become a living resource for the year level, revisited and updated as students uncover new connections between stories and artefacts. Epic's collection-building feature allows them to tag books by theme, era, or even big ideas like 'fairness' or 'invention'. By choosing and championing books for real readers, students find their voice as critics and historians alike.

Children step into the shoes of kids from different eras using Puppet Pals, scripting and recording puppet shows about school, chores, or favourite games from long ago. This playful storytelling brings to life the line of inquiry about how children's routines?and rights!?have shifted over time. Students swap scripts with a buddy and perform each other's stories, seeing history through another's eyes and learning empathy as well as facts. Each show is exported as a short animated episode, premiered for parents and younger students at a 'History Comes Alive' puppet festival. By using Puppet Pals' custom character builder, students recreate themselves and real-life artefacts as digital puppets, making the past feel personal. They finish the project not just as storytellers, but as time travellers with a knack for bringing history into the present.

Students design and build a mini 'museum exhibit' showcasing toys from the past, present, and their imagined future using shoeboxes, cardboard, fabric scraps, and recycled materials. They create models of old toys (like spinning tops or rag dolls), modern toys, and invent a futuristic toy, then use Bee-Bots or Sphero Indi to 'guide' visitors along a timeline path between exhibits. Students integrate simple craft with programmable robots, exploring how play and technology have changed over time. This hands-on museum helps them connect their own experiences to history, sparking reflection on change and continuity in children's lives.

ci: Emotions, values, and relationships guide how we connect and collaborate
lo: The function of different parts of the brain; Situations that cause pleasant and unpleasant feelings; Actions that support wellbeing

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Invite students to become 'Feelings Friends' by recording their voices describing a time they felt a big emotion?like excitement, worry, or frustration?using the Animate from Audio feature in Animating a Character with Adobe Express (https://new.express.adobe.com/home/tools/animate-from-audio). Each child selects a playful character or animal avatar, then narrates how they recognised their feeling and what helped them manage it. The tool automatically lip-syncs their voice to the character, creating a lively, relatable explainer. Students can add backgrounds or props that match their story, such as a playground for joy or a quiet reading nook for calm. Their finished artefact is a short animated video, perfect for sharing with Prep buddies or at a class wellbeing assembly. This activity helps children practise emotional vocabulary and see themselves as experts in understanding feelings.

Students use Apple Clips to create video journals that explore how different situations make them feel and how they can support their wellbeing. They record themselves describing a time they felt happy, worried, or proud, using stickers and animated text to represent emotions and actions. Students narrate strategies they use to manage feelings or connect with others, making the videos both personal and practical. The finished journals are compiled into a class 'Feelings Library', which can be revisited during wellbeing discussions. This activity builds emotional vocabulary and self-awareness in a supportive, creative way.

Invite students to compose their own 'Emotion Soundtracks' in GarageBand, matching music to feelings like joy, anger, or worry. Tackling the line of inquiry about actions that support wellbeing, children explore how different sounds can help lift moods or calm nerves. They'll take on the role of 'Wellbeing DJs', curating playlists for classroom mindfulness breaks and even polling teachers about which tracks help the most. The final product is a set of short, original tracks?ready to play during transitions, at home, or in a school wellbeing newsletter. GarageBand's Smart Instruments let even Year 1s layer drums, pianos, and strings, crafting emotional soundscapes far beyond simple beats. Every student leaves knowing music is a tool they can use to guide their feelings, anytime and anywhere.

Students become storytellers by coding interactive stories in ScratchJr where characters face friendship hiccups?and show strategies for making things right. This brings the central idea to life, as children design situations where values and relationships shape what happens next. Each student can choose to make their character a helper, a peacemaker, or even a bystander, then code what happens if they try a new kindness strategy. Their artefact is a tappable story on the iPad, ready to be played for a Pre-Prep buddy or posted to the school website as a 'Kindness Adventure'. ScratchJr's background and speech bubble features let children personalise settings and dialogue, making their empathy lessons come alive. They finish with the superpower of using their ideas?and code?to help others work out problems and feel better.

Empower children to become 'Emotion Reporters' by using iMovie to conduct and edit interviews with classmates about what helps them feel safe and happy at school. Students film each other sharing strategies for handling tricky moments, then use iMovie's simple editing tools to trim clips, add titles, and insert cheerful background music. The finished artefact is a polished video montage, ready to be screened at a parent wellbeing night or shared on the class blog. This process encourages students to listen actively, ask thoughtful questions, and celebrate the diversity of ways their peers manage emotions. By seeing themselves as both interviewers and storytellers, children build confidence and empathy. The final video becomes a class resource for ongoing wellbeing conversations.

s.t: Mood Monsters: Build Your Own Feelings Friend!
s.d: Students design and craft their very own 'Mood Monster' using recycled boxes, fabric scraps, pipe cleaners, buttons, and colored paper. Each Mood Monster will have features that represent different emotions?like changeable mouths, movable eyebrows, or attachable 'emotion hats'?to help students express how they're feeling. Using a simple digital camera or iPad, students will photograph their Mood Monster showing various emotions, then create a short narrated slideshow or digital story about their Mood Monster's feelings and how they manage them. This project brings emotional literacy to life, blending imaginative making with technology to help students explore and share who they are.

ci: Storytellers use different methods to convey meaning.
lo: Mediums and techniques artists use; Connections between story and illustrations; How ideas and information are communicated

s.d: Students become cosmic storytellers by using Sky Map to explore and narrate the patterns they see in the Melbourne night sky. This hands-on sky-watching adventure taps straight into how storytellers use different methods to convey meaning, letting students discover how ancient cultures connected constellations with myths and legends. Imagine students taking on the role of astronomer-guides for their families, sharing the stories behind Orion or the Southern Cross in a stargazing showcase night. Their final artefact is a digital sky tour, where each student records an audio guide explaining the story and science behind their favourite constellation. Sky Map's augmented reality overlay lets students match real-time stars with their mythological counterparts, turning the sky above Wesley College into a living storybook. Students leave with a sense of wonder and the confidence to see themselves as both scientists and storytellers.

Students bring celestial objects to life by giving the moon, sun, or planets a voice with ChatterPix Kids. This playful approach dives into how ideas and information are communicated, showing that even scientific facts can be told through character and personality. Students become space reporters, asking their chosen sky object to explain its role in day and night, seasons, or moon phases as if being interviewed for a news segment. The finished product is a series of short, funny video messages where the moon might explain why it changes shape or the sun might boast about making shadows. Using ChatterPix Kids' voice recording and animated mouth features, students add sound effects and expressions to make their characters memorable. They gain creative confidence and realise that science stories can be as entertaining as any fairy tale.

Students step into the shoes of illustrators and directors by crafting animated puppet shows that explain sky patterns and Earth's place in the solar system with Puppet Pals. This taps into the line of inquiry about connections between story and illustrations, as students experiment with backgrounds, characters, and movement to make abstract science concepts visible. To shake things up, students can retell a cultural sky story from a perspective different from their own?perhaps narrating a Dreamtime legend or a myth from another continent. The final artefact is a digital puppet play, complete with voiceovers and custom backdrops, ready to be shared with another class or at a family showcase. Puppet Pals' custom character creation feature lets students design their own sun, moon, or planet puppets using photos or drawings, adding a unique artistic flair. Students walk away with new storytelling skills and the ability to express scientific ideas in imaginative ways.

Students curate visual storyboards using PicCollage to map out how artists use different mediums to represent the sky, from Aboriginal dot paintings to NASA photographs. This directly explores the mediums and techniques artists use, inviting students to compare and contrast how meaning is conveyed through colour, shape, and style. Students act as art critics, choosing their favourite sky-inspired artworks and writing mini-reviews to share with a school-wide digital gallery. Their final artefact is a vibrant collage poster, annotated with their own captions and insights, ready to be displayed in the hallway or emailed home. PicCollage's web image search and layering tools empower students to blend hand-drawn sketches, real photos, and text in ways that go far beyond basic cut-and-paste. Students discover that their artistic voice matters and that science and art can work together to tell powerful stories.

Students compose and record an original soundscape that tells the story of night and day using GarageBand, layering sounds to evoke the changing sky. This immersive music-making explores how ideas and information are communicated through artistic mediums beyond words or pictures. Students become sonic storytellers, curating an audio exhibition for the school foyer where families and peers can experience the moods and patterns of the sky with closed eyes. The final artefact?a digital audio track?can be published as a mini-album or podcast episode, inviting listeners on a journey from sunrise to starry night. By experimenting with GarageBand's virtual instruments, loops, and live audio recording, students blend real-world sky observations with invented sounds to create a truly original narrative. Through this, they discover their power to convey meaning and wonder in ways that transcend the page, nurturing creative confidence and expressive agency.

Students design and build their own interactive shadow theaters using large cardboard boxes, colored cellophane, paper cut-outs, and craft sticks to create scenes of the sky?day, night, moon phases, and seasons. Using a simple torch or a Sphero Indi robot with a mounted LED (driven along tracks to mimic the sun or moon's movement), they animate their stories, exploring how light and shadow change with Earth's rotation and lunar cycles. Students work through the Design Cycle to plan, prototype, test, and refine their theaters, expressing their understanding of sky patterns through both engineering and storytelling. This project merges physical making with technology, empowering students to express their place in the universe through light, movement, and creative performance.

ci: A sequence of processes enables a system to function.
lo: The systems in our lives; The purpose of various systems; How systems are made of many interdependent parts

s.d: Students will become system designers by creating obstacle courses for BeeBots that represent real-world sequences, like how mail gets delivered or how lunch moves from the kitchen to the classroom. This hands-on exploration brings alive the idea that 'a sequence of processes enables a system to function,' showing how each step is essential for everything to work smoothly. Invite older students or local postal workers to review the BeeBot routes and offer feedback on what would happen if a step is skipped or repeated. Each team will film their BeeBot travelling through their designed process and add voiceover explanations of what could go wrong at each step. The sequence-and-repeat button on BeeBots lets students design more complex, looping routes that truly mirror real-world systems with repeated actions. Kids walk away seeing everyday routines as cleverly organised chains ? and gain the confidence to spot and fix broken steps.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Children will animate household or classroom objects ? like a lunchbox, tap, or recycling bin ? to narrate their own system stories, bringing the invisible steps to life. This playful approach lands the unit's big idea that systems in our lives are made up of many interdependent parts, each with its own voice and role. By having their characters explain what happens when one part 'goes on strike,' students get to see processes from a new perspective and debate which parts are truly essential. Their final artefact is a lively digital animation, complete with expressive voices and personalities, ready for sharing with families at an assembly or on a class website. The 'Animate from Audio' feature in Adobe Express takes student-recorded voices and automatically brings their object characters to life, syncing movement to speech for maximum impact. Students leave with creative confidence and a sharper eye for the hidden teamwork in every system around them.

Students will compose their own 'system soundtracks' in GarageBand, layering sound effects and musical themes to represent each step in familiar processes like making toast or getting ready for school. This activity explores how systems are made of many interdependent steps, with each sound symbolising a part of the whole. Invite a local radio producer or school music teacher to vote on which soundtrack best tells a clear process story without any visuals at all. Kids publish their final audio tracks as a 'Guess the System' challenge for other classes ? can listeners identify the process just by hearing the sequence? GarageBand's 'Live Loops' feature lets students easily experiment with repeating patterns, showing how some system steps loop back or repeat for things to run smoothly. They finish the unit thinking in sequences and patterns, ready to spot and analyse systems everywhere they go.

Students use Teachable Machine to create a model that recognises and classifies images of different everyday systems?such as clocks, traffic lights, or classroom routines?by uploading photos or drawings. They train the model to identify each system, then test it with new examples to see how well it can distinguish between them. This activity deepens understanding of how systems are made of interdependent parts and how they function in daily life. The process mirrors how smart home devices and industrial automation systems use AI to recognise and respond to different system states. Students share their classifier and reflect on how technology can help us manage and improve the systems around us.

Students become system storytellers, authoring digital books that follow one process through every tiny detail ? like how breakfast gets from farm to table or how lost property is returned at school. This activity makes the purpose of various systems clear, letting kids choose different voices (the farmer, the egg, the hungry student) for each step. Students swap books with a buddy and try to spot any missing or mixed-up steps, then give friendly 'editor' feedback to strengthen each other's work. The final artefact is a multimedia book, packed with photos, captions, and even recorded sounds, ready to be shared at a family showcase or added to the school library for next year's learners. Book Creator's comic templates help even young writers sequence, visualise, and annotate each part of their chosen system like a pro. They build storytelling skills and the know-how to untangle even the trickiest everyday processes.

Students work in teams to design and build a large, whimsical Rube Goldberg-style machine that represents a typical school day system?like getting ready in the morning or moving from class to class. Using cardboard ramps, dominoes, marbles, recycled tubes, string, and simple levers, they create a chain reaction where each step symbolises a part of the daily routine. Students document each system step using iPads to take photos or record short videos, sequencing the process digitally and physically. This hands-on project helps them see how each part of a system connects, and what happens when one step is missing or out of order.

ci: Changes to materials affect how we use and reuse them in daily life.
lo: Understanding material properties; Reuse and recycling through physical change; Sustainably managing materials

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students become animated science explainers by using the Animate from Audio feature in Animating a Character with Adobe Express (https://new.express.adobe.com/home/tools/animate-from-audio). Working in pairs, they record their voices describing how a chosen material?such as rubber, aluminium foil, or fabric?can be bent, stretched, or crushed and then reused. The teacher helps students select or draw a character that represents a 'Material Detective', which lip-syncs to their narration. Each student group creates a short animated clip where their character demonstrates the physical change using expressive gestures and props. These clips are compiled into a class video gallery, showcasing a variety of materials and transformations. The process encourages students to use precise vocabulary and visual storytelling to make the science of materials engaging for a young audience.

Students engineer simple musical instruments from reused materials?like cardboard, foil, and bottle caps?then use Makey Makey to turn them into playable digital sound machines. This creative challenge connects directly to the inquiry into how we can reuse and recycle materials through physical change. By inviting a local musician or music teacher to 'judge' their inventions in a friendly class showcase, students see their work valued by an expert beyond school. The final artefact is a working instrument that plays digital notes or rhythms when touched, with each student performing a short piece to demonstrate. Makey Makey's ability to map different materials to keyboard or drum sounds means students can experiment with surprising combinations and even code their own sound effects. They leave empowered to see everyday waste as a source of invention and joy.

Students will use Delightex to design interactive storyboards that trace the journey of a recycled material as it undergoes physical changes?bending, stretching, tearing, or crushing?before becoming something new. This immersive digital storytelling directly explores the line of inquiry on how materials are reused and recycled through physical change. Students take on the role of materials engineers, narrating from the perspective of a humble bottle cap or cardboard box as it transforms and finds a second life in the community. Their final artefact is a clickable, animated storyboard?complete with student-recorded voiceovers and branching choices?that families and peers can experience online. Delightex's branching scenario builder enables students to create alternate endings and decision points, highlighting how sustainable choices can change a material's destiny. By stepping into the shoes of everyday materials, students become creative advocates for responsible resource use and circular thinking.

Students become investigative journalists, creating mini-documentaries with iMovie that follow the 'life story' of a single material?from its original use, through physical changes, to its final recycled form. This project brings the central idea to life, showing how changes to materials affect their journey and value in daily life. Students interview family members or community experts about how they reuse or recycle at home, weaving these real voices into their films. The final artefact is a short, engaging video with split-screen interviews, time-lapse footage of material transformations, and student narration, ready to be shared at a school assembly or on the class blog. IMovie's split-screen and picture-in-picture features let students show before-and-after scenes side by side, making the story of change vivid and memorable. They gain the power to tell real stories that spark action and empathy in their community.

Students use Brushes Redux to create digital artworks that reimagine everyday waste?like plastic bottles or paper scraps?as beautiful, useful new objects. This taps into the inquiry about reuse and recycling through physical change, inviting students to see discarded materials through an artist's eyes. Students curate a virtual 'Recycled Art Gallery' for the school website, where families and peers can vote for the most creative transformations. The finished artefact is a vibrant digital painting, complete with layers and textures, accompanied by a short artist's statement about the material's journey. Brushes Redux's advanced layering and blending tools empower students to experiment with transparency and overlapping effects, mimicking the look of real recycled materials. They walk away with creative confidence and a fresh perspective on turning waste into wonder.

Students design and build their own mini musical playgrounds using recycled materials like cardboard tubes, tin cans, fabric scraps, plastic lids, and rubber bands. Using Makey Makey kits and iPads, they turn their creations into interactive sound sculptures?tapping, bending, or stretching different parts triggers digital sounds or music. Through hands-on exploration, students investigate how physical changes to materials alter their properties and sounds, linking science, art, and technology. This project encourages creative reuse, teamwork, and reflection on how materials can be transformed for new, joyful purposes.

ci: Patterns in the sky help us understand our place in the universe.
lo: Earth's place in the solar system; Observable patterns in the sky; Tools and methods we use to observe the sky

s.d: Students design immersive 360? virtual scenes of the night sky, placing constellations and planets in their correct positions to model real astronomical patterns. This activity brings observable sky patterns to life by letting students construct and navigate their own virtual heavens. Students become virtual planetarium guides, recording audio tours that explain the significance of different sky patterns to an imagined audience of younger students or community visitors. The final artefact is a walk-through virtual sky, complete with hotspots and voiceovers, which can be shared as an interactive link with families or displayed at a school science night. Delightex's hotspot feature enables students to embed facts, questions, and cultural stories at each star or planet, transforming a simple model into a rich, exploratory experience. This process sparks curiosity and pride, empowering students to be both creators and educators in their community.

Students become cosmic storytellers by coding interactive animations that show the journey of Earth through the solar system. This hands-on coding experience deepens understanding of Earth's place among the planets and the observable patterns in the sky. Students take on the role of astronomers from different cultures, weaving in stories or myths that explain night and day or the changing moon. Each student codes a short, shareable animation?complete with moving planets, spinning Earth, and dialogue bubbles?that can be screened for families or a buddy class. The advanced 'trigger on tap' and 'repeat forever' blocks allow for looping planetary orbits and interactive exploration, far beyond basic linear stories. Students leave with a sense of agency as digital creators, seeing themselves as scientists and storytellers who can explain our universe in creative new ways.

Students become night-sky detectives, using the Sky Map app to track the positions of planets, stars, and the Moon over multiple evenings. This immersive sky-gazing adventure directly explores observable patterns in the sky, helping students link what they see above to Earth's place in the solar system. For a new perspective, students each pick a cultural star story?Aboriginal Australian, Greek, or Chinese?and compare how different societies interpret the same constellations they find using Sky Map. The final product is a class stargazer's field guide, featuring annotated screenshots from Sky Map, student-written myth retellings, and sky-watching tips for families. By using Sky Map's real-time augmented reality overlay and time-travel feature, students can see past and future sky patterns?revealing how the night sky changes with seasons and location. This experience builds a sense of cosmic curiosity, connecting students and their families to ancient traditions of sky-watching and sparking a lifelong wonder about our universe.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students bring solar system concepts to life by creating animated explainers using the Animate from Audio feature in Adobe Express (https://new.express.adobe.com/home/tools/animate-from-audio). Working in small groups, students record their voices as they narrate the journey of a planet, the cycle of day and night, or the phases of the Moon. The tool automatically lip-syncs their narration to a chosen character?such as an astronaut, the Sun, or a talking planet?making the explanation engaging and memorable. Each group produces a short animated video where their character describes a real sky pattern or answers a common question about space. These videos can be shared with younger classes or families, turning students into confident science communicators. The process encourages clear explanation, creative storytelling, and a playful approach to science communication.

Students author interactive digital books that explore Earth's place in the solar system, observable sky patterns, and the tools used to study space. Each student or pair creates a multimedia page for a class anthology, featuring their own diagrams of the solar system, annotated photos of the Moon or Sun, and short audio reflections about what surprised them during sky observations. Book Creator's features allow students to embed videos, record voice notes, and add clickable hotspots for fun facts or cultural stories about constellations. The final product is a collaborative e-book that can be read on tablets or projected for a class exhibition. This digital book not only showcases scientific understanding but also celebrates diverse perspectives on the night sky. Students develop pride as published authors, sharing their discoveries with peers and families.

Students will work in small teams to design and build a large, circular 'solar system racetrack' using cardboard, paper plates, bottle caps, and craft materials to represent the Sun and planets. Each group will craft a push-powered planet vehicle (using straws, balloons, or wind-up mechanisms) and program a simple Sphero Indi robot to follow their planet's orbital path around the Sun. Along the way, students decorate their orbits with facts and patterns about day/night and moon phases, connecting physical movement to celestial cycles. The project fuses engineering, art, and basic robotics to help students visualize and experience how planets move in our solar system.

ci: Water is a limited resource that is essential to life.
lo: Unequal access to water; Communities affected by water access; Transferral of water from source to use; Responsibility as global citizens

s.d: Students design and test water delivery routes using Sphero Indi robots, simulating how water travels from its source to homes and schools. This activity brings to life the transfer of water from source to use, making the invisible journey visible and hands-on. Students work as town planners, facing real-world obstacles like hills, pollution, or broken pipes that they must solve creatively. Their finished courses are set up as a 'Water Relay Challenge' for visiting classes to try, sparking curiosity and teamwork. Using Sphero Indi's colour tile coding and programmable speed settings, students can experiment with efficiency and problem-solving. They leave with a systems-thinking mindset and a practical sense of how technology can help solve water access challenges.

Students explore the school garden or nearby pond using Seek by iNaturalist to identify water-dependent plants, insects, and birds. They photograph and record each species, using the app's identification feature to learn their names and habitats. In small groups, students note which living things rely on water and discuss how changes in water availability might affect them. They then design an infographic or poster that visually maps these connections between water, living things, and healthy ecosystems. Through this, students consider how unequal access to water impacts both wildlife and human communities. Finally, the class displays their infographics to raise awareness about the importance of caring for water resources as responsible global citizens.

Students become water detectives, curating a digital library collection in Epic that spotlights stories and facts about communities facing water challenges. Exploring the line of inquiry about how communities are affected by water access, they hunt for books, videos, and audiobooks that bring real voices and places into the classroom. Each student interviews a family member or neighbour about their own water experiences, then finds a matching story in Epic to compare. The final collection is published as a class 'Water Wisdom' shelf, which can be recommended to other year levels or featured in the school newsletter. Epic's built-in quizzes and read-to-me function allow students to personalise their recommendations for different readers. Students walk away with research skills and a deeper appreciation for the diversity of water stories around the world.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students use Animate from Audio in Adobe Express (https://new.express.adobe.com/home/tools/animate-from-audio) to create animated water droplet characters who narrate their journey through the water cycle. Working in pairs, students record their voices as the droplet travels from a cloud to a river, through pipes, and finally to a tap or garden. The tool automatically lip-syncs the character to their narration, making the science story engaging and memorable. Each pair chooses backgrounds and props to illustrate evaporation, condensation, and collection. Their finished animations are screened for the class, sparking discussion about where water comes from and why it is precious. This creative storytelling approach helps students internalise scientific concepts and see water as an active part of their world.

Students become inventors of the future, using Book Creator to design and publish digital comic books about creative ways to save water at home and school. This project taps into the responsibility as global citizens, inviting students to imagine themselves as sustainability heroes. Each comic book is crafted to inspire real action, with students including tips, challenges, and even 'water-saving fails' to make it relatable. The comics can be shared with families or featured in a school-wide Water Action Day, turning every student into an advocate. Book Creator's comic templates and audio narration tools allow students to bring their stories to life with speech bubbles, sound effects, and their own voices. By publishing for a real audience, students gain confidence in their ideas and see themselves as changemakers.

Students will work in teams to design and build mini villages using recycled cardboard, fabric scraps, sponges, and foil, then engineer clever water-collection and distribution systems for their community. They'll use droppers or spray bottles to simulate rain, testing how well their creations capture, store, and share water between 'houses' and 'gardens'. Incorporating simple circuits with LED 'water alert' lights (using coin batteries and conductive tape), students explore how technology and teamwork can help manage water fairly. This hands-on project immerses children in the challenges of water access, encouraging empathy, problem-solving, and creative solutions for a sustainable planet.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Exploring the past helps us to understand the present.
lo: Evidence and its significance in a place; Connections between the past and present within a place; Personal history shapes the present

s.d: Students become time travellers by capturing immersive 360-degree photos of Wesley College's oldest sites, artefacts and hidden corners. This firsthand evidence collection brings the line of inquiry about the significance of evidence in a place to life, right in students' hands. Invite a local historian or an alumni grandparent to join a virtual walk, adding their own memories and stories as students guide them through the captured scenes. The final gallery is a virtual tour full of clickable hotspots, where every child's voice and photo is woven into a living history for families and the wider school community to explore. Using the insta360's 'deep zoom' feature lets viewers see tiny details missed by the naked eye, sparking fresh questions about what has changed over time. Students realise they are both the explorers and keepers of their college's living story, confident to ask questions and share discoveries.

Young historians become school podcasters, interviewing elders, teachers and classmates about personal memories of Wesley College. This hands-on investigation connects directly to the line of inquiry around how personal history shapes the present. Students take on the role of 'memory detectives', weaving together facts and feelings as they draw out surprising details and reflections from their guests. Their finished podcast series becomes a time capsule, shared on the school website and at assembly, letting everyone hear multiple generations' voices. The podcast equipment's noise-reduction microphones help even the quietest students capture crisp audio, making every story clear and powerful. By the end, students know their questions matter?and that every voice can change how we understand the present.

Students create digital then-and-now collages, placing historic photos of Wesley College side by side with their own snapshots from the same locations today. This activity directly explores how connections between the past and present within a place shape what we see and value. Students become story curators, selecting images that highlight surprising changes?maybe a tree that's doubled in size, or a sports field that used to be a garden. Their finished PicCollage galleries are displayed in the library, inviting parents and visitors to guess which photo is old and which is new. Using PicCollage's 'cutout' tool, students layer themselves into historic scenes, playfully inserting themselves into moments from decades ago. Children walk away feeling part of something bigger than themselves, able to spot change and continuity wherever they go.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students bring Wesley College artefacts to life by recording their voices as if they are the objects themselves, using the Animate from Audio feature in Adobe Express (https://new.express.adobe.com/home/tools/animate-from-audio). Each child selects a significant item?such as an old school bell, a sports trophy, or a library book?and scripts a short story or memory from the artefact's perspective. The teacher guides students as they record their narration, and the tool automatically lip-syncs a chosen character to their voice. These animated artefact storytellers are compiled into a class showcase, where families and peers can listen to the 'memories' hidden in everyday objects. This activity deepens students' understanding of how evidence and stories from the past shape our sense of place. Children finish with a playful, memorable product that makes history feel personal and alive.

Students code their own mini-animations showing a day in the life of a child at Wesley College, comparing the present with an imagined day in the past. This creative project explores how personal history and daily routines link the past to who we are today. Students step into the shoes of children from another era, debating what games, transports, and classroom rules might have been different or surprisingly similar. Their completed ScratchJr stories can be presented to Prep students or uploaded to a class showcase for families. The 'voice recording' and 'background switching' features of ScratchJr let students narrate their stories and flip between past and present scenes within a single project. By blending storytelling and coding, students discover they can shape and share stories that connect generations.

Students design and build miniature 'time capsule' boxes using recycled materials, decorating them with symbols and artefacts representing important moments from Wesley College's history and their own lives. They then create a collaborative treasure trail map of the campus, marking where each capsule could be 'hidden', and use Sphero Indi cars to navigate a large, hand-crafted floor map, stopping at each time capsule location to share stories. This project blends physical crafting, storytelling, and basic coding, encouraging students to connect past and present through hands-on exploration and teamwork. It brings the unit to life by making history tangible, personal, and interactive.

ci: Humans have a responsibility in their relationships to value the rights of others
lo: The difference between needs and wants; Everybody has rights and responsibilities; What is a respectful relationship

s.d: Students will bring 'rights' to life by photographing classroom objects and making them 'speak' about what a respectful relationship means in Year 2. This fresh take on the line of inquiry about everybody's rights and responsibilities helps kids see the classroom from the perspective of the resources they use every day. Imagine hearing the class teddy explain why it loves being looked after or the recycling bin asking for fair treatment. Each student records a short voiceover, then uses stickers and digital drawing to give their object a unique personality, creating a talking gallery for families to enjoy on Seesaw. The secret sauce is ChatterPix's custom stickers and drawing tools?students can turn even the most ordinary object into a star with a message. Suddenly, valuing others' rights feels real and personal, and students see themselves as guardians of fairness in their own space.

Students direct their own mini-plays showing tricky friendship moments where needs and wants clash, using Puppet Pals to animate characters and voice every side. This directly explores what makes a respectful relationship, letting students test out ways to solve real playground dilemmas before they happen. Students swap roles and voice the opposite side?walking in someone else's shoes to build empathy. The finished puppet show videos are premiered at a 'Peace & Play' film festival for Year 1s and Prep, opening up a whole-school conversation about fairness. Puppet Pals' advanced feature lets students layer custom backgrounds and props, so every scene feels like their world. Kids leave with sharper conflict skills and the confidence to speak up kindly when things go wrong.

Students will become 'rights detectives' by curating a digital bookshelf of stories from Epic that highlight kindness, inclusion, and standing up for others. This links beautifully to the central idea about valuing the rights of others in our relationships, sparking discussion about whose voices are heard and whose are left out. Students review books from different perspectives (character, bystander, or even the 'villain') and write mini book-reviews for a Year 2 'Rights Reading List'. Their collection and reviews are showcased to families through a QR poster in the library, inviting everyone to join the respectful relationship conversation. Epic's collection and search features help students hunt for diverse stories and even create theme folders for others to explore. By the end, students see themselves as young changemakers?sharing stories that inspire real-world kindness.

Each student creates a digital self-portrait surrounded by symbols of their needs, wants, and responsibilities, using Brushes Redux to layer, blend, and experiment fearlessly. This creative task builds self-awareness and invites reflection on the difference between needs and wants, a key line of inquiry. Students then swap iPads and annotate a peer's portrait, recognising each other's unique identities and rights, which turns the artwork into a conversation. The completed gallery is displayed at a lunchtime 'Walk of Respect', turning the corridor into a celebration of diversity for the whole school. Brushes Redux's layering and transparency features let students add hidden meanings and reveal details only visible on close inspection, sparking great discussion. Kids walk away feeling proud of who they are and more curious about what matters most to others.

Students record 'Day in the Life' audio diaries imagining themselves as someone with different needs?a new student, a younger sibling, or a classroom helper?using Seesaw's voice recording and emoji feedback tools. This grounds the unit's exploration of empathy and fairness, as students practice recognising and valuing the rights of others through role play. Students invite a family member to listen and add a voice comment, bridging home and school perspectives. The final class collection is published as a digital empathy wall, with voice clips and emoji reactions visible to the school community. Seesaw's voice comment and teacher-moderated publishing features make this a safe space for sharing honest thoughts and celebrating courage. Students leave feeling heard, valued, and ready to treat others with real understanding.

Students design and build their own 'Identity Island'?a 3D pop-up park that represents who they are and what makes a respectful community. Using cardboard bases, recycled materials, fabric scraps, markers, and craft supplies, each child creates miniature features (like bridges of kindness, sharing swings, or fairness fountains) that symbolize rights, responsibilities, and values important to them. Then, using Bee-Bots, students program simple routes for their bots to 'visit' each island, sharing stories about their choices as the Bee-Bot explores. This project celebrates individuality and respectful relationships through hands-on making and storytelling, reinforcing empathy and inclusion.

ci: Creativity allows people to express their understanding of the world.
lo: The ways people use technology to express creativity; How texts and images work together; How technology influences our creativity

s.d: Students become visual poets, designing striking posters that blend words and images to express how creativity shapes their view of the world. This taps straight into the line of inquiry about how texts and images work together to communicate ideas. Each student chooses a personal experience or perspective and transforms it into a visual message that could inspire others?imagine a mini-exhibition in the school foyer. The final artefact is a high-impact digital poster, ready to be printed or displayed on classroom screens and shared with families. Canva's Magic Write feature lets students experiment with AI-generated poetic phrases, remixing them with their own voice and style. By the end, students see themselves as creative communicators who can make their ideas stand out in a crowded world.

In this creative adventure, students produce stop-motion animations that bring their own imaginative stories to life, using everyday objects and crafted figures. This hands-on project explores how technology influences our creativity, encouraging students to turn static scenes into dynamic tales. Students take on the role of film directors, collaborating in small teams and even inviting a Year 1 class as their premiere audience for feedback. The finished piece is a short stop-motion film, complete with sound effects and music, ready for a red-carpet screening at a family movie night. Stop Motion Studio's onion skinning feature lets students perfect their frame-by-frame movements, adding polish and professional flair. Students walk away with storytelling confidence and a director's eye for detail.

Students curate a living digital gallery, collecting and commenting on examples of creative expression from around the world?street art, digital comics, memes, and more. This activity dives into the diversity of voice and perspectives, showing how technology connects us to creative ideas from every culture. Each student becomes a curator, adding their own discoveries and sparking conversations by asking questions or challenging classmates to see things differently.
