Each team becomes a biomimicry design studio pitching what humans could learn from their creature when solving a real problem such as rubbish collection, seed dispersal, rescue gripping or low-energy movement. The final artefact is a working adaptation test rig that performs a challenge on demand while students explain the survival advantage it models to another Year 5 class. Lego Spike Prime's motor blocks, force sensor and data display allow students to measure grip strength, timing or success rate instead of relying on opinion. Students begin to see living things as brilliant engineers, and themselves as designers who can borrow respectfully from nature.

Students publish an interactive 'Decision Atlas of Light, Life and Land' where each page begins with a real-world dilemma: which material should cover a habitat, which adaptation matters most, or where erosion might change a place next. The book braids the central idea together by showing how interactions between living things, materials and light help people make better decisions about the world. They write as museum curators preparing a family science night exhibit, balancing scientific accuracy with the challenge of making a younger visitor stop, wonder and ask a better question. The final artefact is a multimedia ebook with labelled diagrams, student narration, comparison panels and a final 'decision checkpoint' families can answer at home. Book Creator's comic templates, audio hotspots and read-to-me publishing features let students layer voice, image and explanation without leaving the tool. Students gain the confidence to become science communicators who do more than report facts ? they help an audience decide wisely.

s.t: Camouflage Coastlines: Build, Erode & Light-Test Survival Creatures
s.d: Students use the Design Cycle to invent a fictional shoreline creature, then prototype its body adaptations with clay, cardboard, fabric scraps, foil, cellophane, popsticks, pipe cleaners, recycled packaging and hot glue. They build a mini coastal habitat in a tray with sand, gravel, rocks and water channels, then simulate weathering and erosion using spray bottles, droppers and gentle water flow to see how the habitat changes. Using LED torches and a simple Arduino or light-sensor meter, teams test how well their creature's colours, textures and reflective features help it hide, signal or survive under different light conditions. After collecting evidence, students redesign both creature and habitat to explain how living things, materials, erosion and light interact to help us make decisions about the world.

ci: Communities interact with the environment in different ways.
lo: The need for conservation; Community values inform management of the natural environment; Ways environmental stewardship can drive change

s.d: Students dive into the Minecraft: Ocean Heroes world (https://education.minecraft.net/en-us/lessons/ocean-heroes) to become digital conservationists, rescuing coral reefs, mangroves, and kelp forests. This adventure brings the line of inquiry about the need for conservation to life, letting students see the impact of their actions on delicate ecosystems. As virtual marine biologists, students must negotiate with other players to balance resource use and habitat protection?mirroring real-world community decisions. Their final artefact is a narrated virtual tour of their restored underwater habitat, recorded and shared with the school community to inspire real ocean stewardship. They will use Minecraft's in-game camera and book-and-quill tools to document before-and-after changes, adding expert-level annotations and action plans. Students emerge with a sense of agency, knowing they can make a difference for our planet's most vulnerable environments.

Students use the Field Guide to Victoria app to investigate local species and habitats, turning their neighbourhood into a living laboratory. This hands-on exploration links directly to understanding how community values shape management of the natural environment. Acting as citizen scientists, they collaborate with First Nations experts or local rangers to record sightings and learn traditional knowledge about species protection. Each student creates a digital field guide entry?complete with photos, mapped locations, and voice notes?to be published for families and local conservation groups. The app's advanced species search and geo-tagging features allow students to pinpoint rare finds and track changes over time. Students finish with a deep appreciation for Victoria's biodiversity and the confidence to advocate for its protection.

Students curate a collaborative Padlet wall using the map view to plot global and local conservation efforts, visually connecting their findings to real places. This activity shines a light on how environmental stewardship can drive change, as students compare actions taken by different communities around the world. They step into the role of global correspondents, researching and posting updates as if reporting live from the field. The final Padlet is an interactive map, rich with student-written news flashes, photos, and video interviews, shared at assembly or with partner schools. Padlet's map view and comment threads let students debate which conservation strategies are most effective and why. They leave empowered to see themselves as part of a global movement for positive change.

Students produce stop-motion animation shorts that tell the story of a threatened ecosystem and how a community bands together to save it. This creative project explores the line of inquiry about the need for conservation through storytelling and visual arts. Students can flip the script by animating from the perspective of an animal or plant, highlighting how human choices ripple through an ecosystem. The final artefact is a polished stop-motion film, complete with voiceover and sound effects, screened for families and uploaded to the school website. Stop Motion Studio's onion-skinning and time-lapse features help students create smooth, professional-quality scenes with clever transitions. They gain the skills to use media for advocacy and the courage to speak up for the voiceless in our environment.

Students become data detectives, using Microsoft Excel to analyse waste and energy usage patterns in their school and community. This investigation supports the line of inquiry into how community values inform environmental management, as students uncover trends and propose targeted solutions. They can take on the role of sustainability consultants, presenting their findings to the school council or local government. The final artefact is an interactive dashboard?complete with charts, conditional formatting, and scenario modelling?shared at a sustainability expo. Excel's 'What-If Analysis' and pivot tables let students predict the impact of different conservation strategies and visualise real change. Students walk away with confidence in using data as a tool for action and evidence-based decision-making.

Students will design and construct interactive model habitats for endangered local species using recycled materials, cardboard, fabric scraps, clay, and natural found objects. They will embed simple sensors (e.g., with Makey Makey or micro:bit) to create dynamic features?like warning lights for pollution or sound alarms for habitat disturbance?that activate when parts of the habitat are touched or disturbed. The project encourages students to research the needs of their chosen species, incorporate First Nations land management insights, and demonstrate conservation challenges and solutions through their builds. This hands-on, tech-enhanced maker challenge brings environmental stewardship to life, inviting creative problem-solving while fostering empathy for the planet's vulnerable inhabitants.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: The discovery of resources has impacted the growth and development of nations.
lo: Significance of resource discovery in development of societies; Impact of migration on cultural, social and economic growth; Exploration and settlement effects on Indigenous and colonial populations

s.d: Students enter a teacher-created Wise Discussion Chatbot using the Character Interview scenario to question 'Mei Lin', a fictional Chinese migrant travelling to the Victorian goldfields in 1854. They ask, 'Why did you leave home for Australia?' and 'How did laws and attitudes affect your choices?' The chatbot's curriculum connection prompts students to test Mei Lin's account against evidence about migration, resources and colonial society. Students identify causes, consequences and possible bias before drafting follow-up questions. They produce a perspective summary separating historical evidence from plausible fictional detail. A class comparison reveals how resource discovery shaped experiences differently for migrants, Indigenous peoples and settlers.

Students map the journeys of migrants and prospectors during the Australian Gold Rush using National Geographic MapMaker, tracing routes from countries of origin to the goldfields. This hands-on mapping brings to life the line of inquiry about how migration has driven cultural, social, and economic growth in Australia. To deepen perspective, students research and overlay the traditional lands of Indigenous nations, sparking discussion about whose stories are told and whose are often left off the map. The final product is a layered, annotated digital map that visually narrates the intertwined paths of Indigenous communities and newcomers. By using MapMaker's custom annotation and layering features, students can add historical images, text boxes, and even draw boundaries to make their maps rich and complex. They leave with a sharper sense of place?and a new appreciation for the many journeys that have shaped Australia.

Invite students to step into the shoes of an Indigenous person, a colonial settler, or a newly arrived migrant and craft a digital diary in Book Creator, capturing daily life during a pivotal resource discovery moment. This narrative approach brings empathy and personal voice to the exploration of how settlement and resource extraction affected both Indigenous and colonial populations. Students swap diaries with a peer and add a 'response entry' from the perspective of a different group, encouraging them to wrestle with multiple viewpoints. The end result is a multimedia eBook, complete with voice recordings, period images, and interactive timelines, ready to be shared with families at an open night. Book Creator's comic panel templates and audio hotspots let students blend visuals, text, and sound in creative ways that go beyond static writing. Students finish with a deeper empathy for others' stories and the confidence to express complex histories in engaging, multimodal formats.

Students compose original soundscapes in GarageBand to capture the atmosphere of the goldfields, bustling ports, or quiet Indigenous lands before and after settlement. This creative challenge links directly to the inquiry into the effects of exploration and settlement on different populations. Invite a local historian or community elder to listen and provide feedback, connecting classroom creativity with real-world expertise. The final artefact is a short audio piece or podcast segment, layered with narration, environmental sounds, and music, published for the school community as an audio gallery. GarageBand's Live Loops and voiceover features empower students to blend music, sound effects, and spoken word in ways that make history come alive. They walk away with fresh skills in digital storytelling?and a new way to express the emotional side of Australia's past.

Students use Delightex to design interactive storyboards that follow the ripple effects of resource discovery across different groups and eras in Australia. This activity directly unpacks how the significance of resource discovery led to rapid change and sometimes conflict, sparking questions about fairness and progress. To challenge assumptions, students must include at least one 'what if?' branch?imagining how events might have unfolded if resources had been shared differently or migration patterns had changed. Their finished artefact is an interactive storyboard with branching paths, images, and embedded text, which can be explored by other classes or parents online. Delightex's branching scenario builder lets students create non-linear stories that encourage active exploration and critical thinking. In the process, students develop creative confidence and the ability to see history as a web of choices, not just a straight line.

s.t: Goldfields Quest: Design Your Migration Adventure Map
s.d: Students will design and construct an immersive, 3D board game that traces the journeys of diverse groups during the Australian Gold Rush. Using cardboard, clay, fabric, recycled materials, and craft supplies, they'll build landscapes (bush, goldfields, towns), create custom game pieces representing migrants and Indigenous peoples, and engineer interactive elements like bridges or 'chance' wheels. Incorporating a programmable Sphero Indi or similar robot as the 'traveller,' students will code it to navigate the map, encountering historical challenges and decisions based on real events and perspectives. This hands-on project fuses design thinking, storytelling, and empathy, helping students understand how movement, resources, and choices shaped Australia's past.

ci: Managing change requires acceptance, knowledge and strategies.
lo: Establishing, managing and maintaining relationships; Managing behaviours in digital situations; Managing changes associated with puberty

s.d: Students become podcast hosts, recording a 'Change Stories' series where they interview each other about experiences of managing big changes?like moving schools, making new friends, or navigating puberty. This activity dives deep into the central idea that managing change takes acceptance, knowledge and strategies, as students reflect on real-life moments of courage and growth. Invite a school counsellor or an older student as a special guest for a live Q&A, letting students ask their most pressing questions about change and relationships. Each group produces a polished podcast episode, complete with intro music, sound effects, and thoughtful conversation, which can be shared with the whole year level or even families. Using the podcast mixer and multi-track recording features, students layer voices, music, and questions for a professional sound that goes far beyond basic voice memos. They walk away with the confidence to tell their stories and the empathy to listen deeply to others?skills that last well beyond primary school.

Students step into the shoes of digital citizens by building interactive scenarios in Delightex, where they must make choices about online behaviour, friendships, and digital dilemmas. This directly explores the line of inquiry around managing behaviours in digital situations, letting students safely experiment with tricky choices before they face them in real life. For an extra layer, students swap scenarios with another class and vote on the best strategies for handling online drama or misunderstandings, sparking lively debate and perspective-taking. The finished artefact is a branching, clickable story where every decision leads to a different outcome?perfect for sharing at a digital safety assembly or with younger students. Delightex's conditional logic and 'decision point' features let students design real consequences and multiple endings, making their stories far more dynamic than a static slideshow. They leave empowered to navigate the online world with savvy and kindness, ready to be leaders in their digital communities.

Students create digital self-portraits in Sketchbook, visually expressing how their identity is shaped by relationships, change, and personal growth. This ties into the unit's focus on establishing and maintaining relationships, encouraging students to reflect on who supports them through change and how they see themselves evolving. Students swap portraits anonymously and write 'identity stories' for each other, guessing the feelings and strengths behind the art?then reveal and discuss together. The final gallery is a vibrant digital exhibition, displayed on classroom screens or shared with families, celebrating the diversity and resilience in Year 5. Advanced layering and blending tools in Sketchbook allow students to add symbolic elements, textures, and even hidden messages to their portraits. They come away with a stronger sense of self and a deeper appreciation for the many ways we all grow and change.

Students become wellbeing researchers, designing anonymous surveys in Microsoft Forms to uncover how their peers feel about change, friendships, and growing up. This activity sharpens their understanding of how strategies and knowledge help manage change, as they collect real data from their own community. After gathering responses, students analyse the results and present surprising trends?like what makes classmates feel supported, or which strategies actually help when things get tough?to the year level or even the school council. Each group creates a dynamic report with graphs and key findings, offering practical tips for making Wesley College an even kinder, more supportive place. By using branching questions and response validation, students can personalise the survey experience and ensure honest, thoughtful answers. They walk away as changemakers, knowing their voices?and the voices of their peers?can shape a more empathetic and inclusive community.

Students direct and edit mini-documentaries in iMovie, capturing 'A Day in the Life' of someone experiencing change?whether it's starting puberty, moving to a new country, or navigating a friendship challenge. This hands-on project explores the unit's themes of empathy and respectful communication, as students step into another person's shoes and tell their story visually. For a fresh angle, students can collaborate with Visual Art to include digital portraiture or animation sequences, blending art and film to deepen the narrative. The final product is a short, polished film ready for a year-level film festival or a virtual screening for families and the wider school. IMovie's split-screen and picture-in-picture features let students layer interviews, voiceovers, and creative visuals for a truly professional finish. They gain storytelling skills and a powerful sense that everyone's story matters?and that change, while sometimes hard, connects us all.

s.t: Emotion Motion Robots: Build Your Feelings Friend
s.d: Students design and construct a physical 'Feelings Friend' robot that visually expresses different emotions and personal traits using craft materials like cardboard, LEDs, motors, fabric, and recycled items. Working through the Design Cycle, they prototype faces, accessories, and moving features that symbolize aspects of their identity and wellbeing (e.g., a spinning heart for kindness, light-up eyes for curiosity). Using micro:bit or Hummingbird kits, students program their robots to display emotion animations or simple movements in response to buttons or sensors. This hands-on project links self-reflection with digital citizenship by inviting students to share and celebrate diversity, empathy, and self-management in a creative, memorable way.

ci: The media engages its audience and invites a response
lo: How media targets audiences; Techniques used to engage and persuade; Critical evaluation of media messages

s.d: Let students become real media critics by producing a podcast episode that dissects how advertising influences our choices as consumers. This hands-on investigation dives into the line of inquiry about the techniques media uses to engage and persuade audiences, with students analysing catchy jingles, slogans, and emotional hooks. Invite a local journalist or radio host (virtually or in person) to share insights, so students see how the pros shape messages and responses. Each group publishes a polished podcast episode?complete with intro music, interviews, and their own critical takes?ready for the school community and families to stream. Using podcast equipment's multi-track mixing and audio editing features, students layer sound effects and music to make their message pop. They walk away with the confidence to question and decode every ad they see, not just take it at face value.

Students take on the role of ethical ad designers, creating a campaign for a sustainable product that challenges typical consumerism. This activity spotlights how media targets audiences by asking students to flip the script?can you persuade classmates to care about fairness and the planet rather than just 'buy, buy, buy'? Students must research the environmental and social impact of their chosen product and pitch their campaign to a panel of real parents or community members. The final artefact is a vibrant, animated web page or poster, complete with compelling visuals and a call to action, ready for display at a school expo or online showcase. Adobe Express's Animate from Audio and Magic Design features let students bring their campaign to life with moving graphics and auto-generated layouts that grab attention. Students finish with creative muscle and a toolkit for using media to inspire positive change, not just more consumption.

Flip the classroom by having students design and host a Kahoot quiz that tests their peers' ability to spot persuasive media tricks and hidden biases in real-world ads. This directly supports the line of inquiry around critically evaluating media messages, as students must craft questions that reveal how easily audiences can be swayed. For extra spark, invite teachers or another year level to play the quiz, turning students into quizmasters and media literacy champions for the wider school. The finished Kahoot is a live, competitive quiz event?complete with leaderboard, discussion breaks, and instant feedback?that can be replayed at assemblies or family nights. Students harness Kahoot's advanced question types, like image-based questions and multi-select, to make their quiz both tricky and engaging. They leave with sharper eyes for media manipulation and the thrill of leading learning for others.

Unleash students' creativity by having them map the journey of a product from creation to consumer using Freeform's infinite canvas. This activity digs into the environmental and ethical impacts of products, encouraging students to visualise every step?resources, labour, transport, packaging, and advertising spin. To broaden perspectives, students must include voices from different points in the supply chain, imagining what a factory worker, marketer, or eco-activist might say. Their final artefact is a sprawling, interactive mind map filled with sketches, sticky notes, voice memos, and web links, ready for a gallery walk or digital sharing with families. Freeform's collaborative real-time editing lets groups build and annotate together, layering in multimedia evidence and commentary. Students finish with a systems-thinking mindset and a knack for seeing the hidden stories behind everyday purchases.

Turn students into real-world researchers by designing and running a survey with Microsoft Forms to uncover what influences their peers' buying decisions. This activity directly explores how media targets audiences and the power of peer and social influences. Students compare their findings with national data or invite a local business owner to discuss how they use similar research. The final artefact is a set of interactive charts and data stories, built with Forms' branching logic and automatic analytics, ready to share at a student-led media literacy forum. Students use advanced features like response validation and custom themes to make their survey both professional and engaging. They come away with hands-on experience in data-driven decision-making and the confidence to question the forces shaping their own choices.

s.t: Brand New Me: The Ethical Sneaker Hackathon
s.d: Students team up to design and prototype their own 'ethical sneakers' using recycled materials (cardboard, fabric scraps, plastic bottles) and basic electronics (LEDs, simple circuits) to integrate interactive features like light-up logos or pressure sensors. Using tablets and the Makey Makey kit, they program a digital 'ad campaign' that activates when their sneaker is stepped on or touched, linking the physical prototype to a creative digital message about fair trade, sustainability, or consumer choices. Throughout, students apply the Design Cycle to research real sneaker brands, brainstorm features that reflect responsible consumerism, and iteratively build and test their hybrid creations. The project culminates in a 'Sneaker Expo' where teams showcase both their wearable prototypes and their persuasive tech-powered campaigns, reflecting on how products and advertising express values and influence choices.

ci: An inquiry into the interconnectedness of human-made systems and communities; the structure and function of organisations.
lo: Lines of inquiry to be confirmed once planner is uploaded

s.d: Students become investigative journalists, curating a digital wall of real-world advertising campaigns that have shaped consumer choices and even swayed public opinion. This activity brings to life the central idea of how human-made systems?like advertising and media?interconnect with communities and influence sustainable futures. To deepen the challenge, students must include and contrast campaigns from different cultures or decades, sparking debate about fairness and manipulation. Their final Padlet is a vibrant, multimedia timeline, featuring embedded video ads, scanned print posters, and voice-over critiques. Using Padlet's map view, they plot where each campaign originated, revealing global patterns in consumer influence. Students finish with a sharp eye for hidden bias and a toolkit for questioning what they see in the world around them.

Students step into the role of ethical consumer advocates, producing a podcast episode that exposes the environmental and social impact of everyday products. This directly explores how organisations and systems shape the world's sustainable future?a key unit focus. Inviting a local business owner or sustainability expert for a recorded interview gives students a real audience and expert voice. The final artefact is a polished podcast, complete with intro music, sound effects, and student-led discussions ready for the school community to stream. They use Canva's podcasting tools (https://www.canva.com) to edit, layer interviews, and add professional touches. Students walk away with confidence in speaking up, knowing their voices can drive change.

Students become creative directors, designing eye-catching ethical advertising campaigns for products that support fair trade or environmental sustainability. This task challenges them to flip the script on traditional advertising?aligning with the inquiry into how influences shape consumer choices. Students must create two contrasting adverts: one using persuasive techniques for a 'fast fashion' product, and one for a sustainable alternative, then invite peers to vote on which is more convincing and why. Their final artefact is a set of professional-quality posters, shared digitally with families and displayed in a virtual gallery. Canva's Magic Write feature helps students craft punchy, original slogans and copy that stand out. They leave empowered to use media for good, not just persuasion.

Students become global supply chain detectives, mapping the journey of a common product?like a chocolate bar or sneaker?from raw materials to the shop shelf. This activity brings the structure and function of organisations to life, showing how interconnected our choices are with distant communities and environments. Students are challenged to annotate their maps with ethical dilemmas at each stage: Where are workers treated fairly? Where is the biggest environmental impact? Their final product is an interactive, annotated map tracing supply routes, ethical hotspots, and decision points, published for the school community to explore. Using MapMaker's custom annotation and layer tools, students add photos, links, and pop-up facts for a rich, interactive experience. They finish with a global perspective on how every purchase connects them to people and places far beyond their own.

Students become data analysts, using Microsoft Excel to investigate how advertising and peer influence affect spending habits among their peers. They design and distribute a survey about recent purchases, brand preferences, and the impact of social media ads, then collect and organise the responses in Excel. Students use built-in charting tools to visualise trends?such as which advertising techniques are most persuasive or which products are most influenced by peer recommendations. Their final artefact is a data dashboard featuring graphs, pivot tables, and a short written analysis that highlights key findings and ethical considerations. This process sharpens their critical thinking and statistical literacy, revealing how data can uncover hidden patterns in consumer behaviour. Students present their dashboards to the class, sparking discussion about how informed choices can lead to more sustainable consumption.

s.t: Future Market Makers: The Ethical Pop-Up Shop Challenge
s.d: Students design and build miniature pop-up shop stalls from recycled cardboard, fabric scraps, and craft supplies, representing businesses that prioritise ethical and sustainable consumer choices. Using micro:bit or Makey Makey kits, they integrate interactive digital elements?like simple LED displays or touch sensors?to showcase advertising strategies, product info, and eco-impact stats. Teams prototype their stall layout, signage, and product packaging, then pitch their business model to classmates, reflecting on how organisation, ethical decisions, and advertising shape consumer behaviour. The hands-on project empowers students to creatively visualise and test real-world sustainable commerce in a collaborative, memorable Makerspace experience.

ci: Scientists undertake experimentation to confirm, contest and create new theories.
lo: The scientific method; How experiments lead to new understandings; The relationship between planets and the Sun; Energy transfer and transformation in circuits

s.d: Students become scientists inside Minecraft by designing and running experiments in the 'The Scientific Method' lesson world (https://education.minecraft.net/en-us/lessons/the-scientific-method). As they test hypotheses and collect data, students experience first-hand how experimentation can confirm, challenge, or spark new scientific theories. They work in teams to solve open-ended challenges, debating different approaches and learning that sometimes the most unexpected results lead to the biggest breakthroughs. Their final artefact is a digital science journal?screenshots, experiment logs, and reflections?shared with the year level as a virtual science fair. They use Minecraft's in-game camera and Book & Quill to capture and annotate their discoveries, making their process visible and interactive. Students leave with a scientist's mindset: curious, collaborative, and ready to question the world around them.

Students use Sky Map to track and identify planets and constellations, turning their iPads into a window to the solar system. This brings the line of inquiry about the relationship between planets and the Sun to life, as students see planetary motion in real time. They take on the role of 'astronomy guides,' creating narrated video tours for Year 3 students who are just starting to explore space. Each student produces a short, screen-recorded stargazing guide, complete with their own voiceover and highlighted celestial objects. The app's augmented reality overlay helps students compare what they see in the sky to what is mapped in the app, deepening their understanding of planetary positions and orbits. By teaching others, students gain confidence in explaining complex ideas and realise that science is something they can share, not just study.

Students engineer and code Lego Spike Prime robots to model energy transfer and transformation in simple circuits. This hands-on investigation connects directly with the unit's exploration of how energy moves and changes form within systems. Working in teams, students design a 'chain reaction' machine that powers a sequence of events?like lighting an LED, spinning a motor, or triggering a buzzer?mirroring real-world energy flows. Their finished machines are showcased in a live demo day for parents and the school community, with each team explaining the science behind their design. Students dive into the Spike Prime's data logging feature to track voltage and current, using real-time graphs to support their explanations. They walk away with the ability to turn abstract energy concepts into something they can see, measure, and improve.

Students train an image-classification model in Teachable Machine to investigate how packaging influences sustainable consumer choices. They photograph or collect examples of products with features such as recycling symbols, excessive wrapping, green colour palettes and vague environmental claims, then sort them into carefully defined classes. Using Teachable Machine's image project, webcam capture and live confidence scores, teams test whether the model can distinguish strong sustainability evidence from visual greenwashing. Misclassifications prompt students to revise their categories, balance the training samples and question the assumptions embedded in their dataset. Each team produces a tested classifier and a written set of evidence-based packaging criteria for responsible shoppers. A class demonstration compares how reliably the models judge unfamiliar products and exposes why both people and machines need trustworthy evidence.

Students design and conduct surveys to investigate consumer behaviour, collecting data on choices that affect sustainability and the environment. They input their survey results into Microsoft Excel and use pivot tables to organise and summarise the data effectively. By applying conditional formatting, students highlight trends and patterns in consumer decisions, such as preferences for eco-friendly products or energy use habits. They compare their class data with national statistics to explore how individual choices relate to broader societal behaviours. Students then create a dynamic infographic dashboard featuring colourful charts, key insights, and evidence-based recommendations. This dashboard becomes a visual tool to communicate how consumer behaviour influences sustainability, empowering students to see themselves as informed changemakers.

s.t: Smart Swap Stop: The Sustainable Vending Machine Challenge
s.d: Students team up to design and build a working prototype of an eco-friendly vending machine using recycled cardboard, plastic bottles, motors, LEDs, and micro:bit controllers. Each group invents a machine that 'dispenses' sustainable choices?like reusable or upcycled items?triggered by coded micro:bit sensors or buttons. Students must prototype mechanical components (doors, levers, conveyor belts) and program digital feedback (lights, messages) to simulate real-world consumer decisions and environmental impacts. This project brings together engineering, coding, and creative problem-solving, letting students explore how technology can influence responsible consumerism and promote a sustainable future.

ci: The influences on our consumer choices reveal the interdependence between human and natural systems and call for responsible action toward just and sustainable futures.
lo: Influences on consumer choices (function); How consumer decisions impact living things and their habitats (causation); Alternative models of consumerism that honour a fair and sustainable future (perspective)

s.d: Students will step into the world of Minecraft: Sustainable Food Production (https://education.minecraft.net/en-us/lessons/sustainable-food-production) to explore the full journey of products from farm to table and beyond. This immersive simulation brings to life the interdependence between human consumer choices and natural systems, showing firsthand how every purchase has ripple effects on land, water, and habitats. Acting as investigative journalists, students will interview virtual farmers, waste managers, and shopkeepers, then report on how their own daily choices connect to global food systems. Their final artefact is a digital expos??complete with screenshots and in-game diary entries?published as a virtual exhibition for the school community. The in-game camera and book-and-quill features let students capture evidence and craft narratives that combine visual storytelling with persuasive writing. Students leave with the confidence to question the hidden stories behind what they buy, ready to advocate for food choices that nurture both people and planet.

Students will create interactive digital books that unpack the secret language of advertising and how it shapes what we buy. This activity dives into the unit's inquiry into the influences on consumer choices, challenging students to become both critics and creators of persuasive messages. Each student takes on the role of an advertising detective, deconstructing real-world ads before designing their own ethical campaign for a sustainable product. Their finished book is filled with annotated ad examples, original jingles, and embedded video reflections, ready to be shared at a family reading night or online showcase. Book Creator's built-in comic templates and multimedia embedding let students layer text, voice, and video for a truly multimodal artefact. By the end, students see themselves as savvy media navigators?able to spot manipulation and champion messages for good.

Students will become energy detectives using Micro:bit: Energy Awareness (https://microbit.org/teach/lessons/?selected=energy-awareness) to track and analyse real energy use at school and home. This hands-on investigation ties directly to the inquiry into how consumer decisions impact living things and their habitats, making the invisible visible through data. Students collaborate as sustainability consultants, gathering sensor data to uncover hidden energy drains and propose actionable changes. Their final product is a data-driven campaign?infographics and recommendations?shared with the school leadership team to spark real improvements. The Micro:bit's data-logging feature empowers students to collect, graph, and interpret authentic usage patterns, going far beyond guesswork. Students walk away as empowered changemakers, knowing they can use technology to drive responsible action for a just and sustainable future.

Students will design eye-catching infographics that reveal the true cost of everyday products?from raw materials to environmental impact?using Canva. This creative challenge dives into the perspective line of inquiry, asking students to compare traditional consumerism with alternative, fairer models. Each student becomes a visual storyteller, weighing up the journey of a product and imagining how things could be different if everyone made more conscious choices. The finished infographics are printed as posters for a 'Sustainable Choices' gallery walk, sparking conversation throughout the school. Canva's Magic Write and data visualisation tools let students blend persuasive copy with real statistics and custom illustrations. Students leave with the creative confidence to make complex issues clear, inspiring others to rethink what responsible shopping can look like.

Students will use National Geographic MapMaker to create interactive maps tracing the global journey of a single product?such as a chocolate bar or a T-shirt?from source to store. This mapping project brings the causation line of inquiry to life, showing how consumer decisions ripple across continents, affecting people, habitats, and economies. Students adopt the perspective of investigative geographers, uncovering surprising connections between their choices and faraway places. Their final artefact is a digital map with annotated routes, pop-up facts, and embedded photos, ready to be presented to families at an open night or published on the school website. The platform's layering and annotation features empower students to visualise complex supply chains and environmental footprints in a way that static maps never could. Students finish with a global mindset and the ability to see the world in every purchase they make.

s.t: Ad-Busters Arcade: The Sustainable Choice Showdown
s.d: Students design and build interactive arcade-style games using recycled materials (cardboard, bottle caps, rubber bands, LEDs, switches) that challenge players to spot greenwashing, make ethical consumer choices, or navigate the consequences of fast fashion and food waste. Incorporating Makey Makey kits or micro:bit controllers, teams wire up their games so choices trigger real-time feedback?lights, buzzers, or scoreboards?teaching critical thinking about advertising and sustainability. Each game includes persuasive elements and hidden ads crafted by students, connecting to their research on how media influences purchasing decisions. The arcade culminates in a class expo where peers and staff play, reflect, and vote for the most impactful, creative, and thought-provoking builds.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Human needs drive the development of nations.
lo: How human needs drive national development; Role of migration in nation building; Impacts of development on Indigenous and colonial populations

s.d: Students step into the shoes of migrants during the Australian Gold Rush using the 'Australian Gold Rush' Minecraft lesson (https://education.minecraft.net/en-us/lessons/australian-gold-rush2), experiencing firsthand how human needs sparked the feverish development of a nation. This immersive role-play brings the line of inquiry 'how human needs drive national development' to life, letting students navigate tough choices around survival, prosperity, and community. As they journey from ship to goldfields, students debate whose voices are missing from the story?Indigenous, Chinese, women, or children?and how those perspectives might change the history books. Their final artefact is a digital diary, created with the in-game book and quill, filled with snapshots and reflections from each stage of the journey. Students use the teleportation feature to visit key locations and the in-game camera to document their discoveries, making their learning visible and interactive. By the end, students don't just read about history?they live it, gaining empathy and a deeper sense of how individual needs and dreams shape a nation's story.

Students design and build an interactive 3D Merge Cube museum exhibit showcasing the impacts of migration and colonisation on Australia's Indigenous and colonial populations. This hands-on experience tackles the line of inquiry about the impacts of development, letting students curate artefacts, stories, and voices that matter. Each student becomes a museum curator, deciding how to represent both Indigenous resilience and colonial change in a way that challenges visitors to think differently. The final exhibit is a digital, hold-in-your-hand Merge Cube that can be explored by classmates, families, or even at a school open night. Using the Merge EDU Object Viewer, students embed audio narrations, 3D models, and layered AR labels to bring their stories to life?far beyond flat posters or slides. Students walk away understanding that how we present history shapes whose voices are heard and remembered.

Students create animated explainer videos in Adobe Express to unpack how migration waves have shaped Australian citizenship and identity over time. This creative process directly explores the line of inquiry about the role of migration in nation building, encouraging students to connect historical events to present-day multicultural Australia. Instead of just reporting facts, students take on the role of documentary filmmakers, weaving personal and community migration stories into their narratives. Their final product is a polished, shareable video that can be screened at assembly or sent home to families. Students use the Animate from Audio feature to turn their voiceovers into expressive, moving characters?making their stories engaging and relatable. By mastering digital storytelling, students learn how to communicate complex ideas and bring history to life for real audiences.

Students author interactive eBooks in Book Creator, weaving together personal migration narratives, historical research, and reflections on how needs shape societies. This activity draws directly from the central idea that human needs drive the development of nations, encouraging students to blend their own family stories with broader historical patterns. Students become both historians and storytellers, interviewing relatives or community members to add authentic voices and perspectives. The finished eBook features clickable audio interviews, embedded video clips, and student-created illustrations, ready to be published online or printed for the school library. By using Book Creator's comic templates and multimedia embedding, students craft layered, engaging stories that invite readers to explore multiple viewpoints. This project builds creative confidence and helps students see themselves as part of Australia's ongoing story.

Students produce stop-motion films dramatizing key turning points in Australia's migration and colonisation story, using Stop Motion Studio to animate scenes from both Indigenous and colonial perspectives. This activity dives deep into the impacts of development on different populations, challenging students to represent voices often left out of the mainstream narrative. Students become directors and historians, tasked with retelling events like the First Fleet landing or the Gold Rush from multiple, sometimes conflicting, viewpoints. Their final film is a short, shareable stop-motion animation, complete with voiceovers, sound effects, and hand-crafted sets. By using Stop Motion Studio's onion skinning and frame-by-frame editing features, students create seamless, professional-looking animations that captivate viewers. This experience empowers students to use creative media to question, reimagine, and share history in ways that spark real conversations.

Students design and build interactive 'time capsules' that tell layered migration stories using both physical craftsmanship and simple electronics. Using recycled boxes, craft materials, and conductive tape or basic circuitry kits (e.g., Makey Makey or Chibitronics), students create dioramas or sculptural capsules representing a chosen era or migration journey in Australia. Each capsule features touch-activated elements?like opening a door or pressing a symbol?to trigger audio snippets, LED highlights, or digital slideshows on a connected tablet, revealing personal, Indigenous, and national migration narratives. This immersive project invites students to weave together place, time, and identity through hands-on making, storytelling, and basic coding, culminating in a class 'museum' of interactive capsules.

ci: An inquiry into the nature of the self; beliefs and values; personal, physical, mental, social and spiritual health; human relationships.
lo: Lines of inquiry to be confirmed once planner is uploaded

s.d: Students use Padlet to create a collaborative digital wall where they post thoughtful questions and responses about beliefs, values, and personal identity. They design open-ended prompts that encourage peers to share stories about what shapes their sense of self, mental wellbeing, and relationships. Using Padlet's multimedia features, students embed images, short videos, and links to support their reflections and deepen the conversation. They organise posts into thematic columns, such as 'Values I Live By' or 'What Influences My Choices,' fostering a rich, interactive dialogue. This activity helps students explore diverse perspectives on personal and social health while practising respectful communication and critical thinking. The final Padlet wall becomes a shared resource that can be revisited and expanded by future classes or families.

Students will create an animated explanatory video where they break down how the brain processes stress and positive emotions, combining diagrams, voiceover, and moving images. This hands-on project ties directly into understanding the physiology and function of the brain and how it links to wellbeing and learning. Students take on the role of 'brain tour guides,' designing their videos for parents tuning in at the Year 6 Wellbeing Night, showing off their expertise in a format families can actually learn from. The finished artefact is an interactive video with clickable hotspots and animated pathways, published to a shared gallery for community viewing. Explain Everything's infinite canvas and layering tools let students zoom in on microscopic details, animate neural pathways, and even add their own quiz questions inside the video. Students grow into confident science communicators, ready to explain tough concepts outside school walls.

Students will design and launch a school-wide survey to uncover how different beliefs, values, and personal habits shape wellbeing at Wesley College. This directly supports the inquiry into how management of wellbeing impacts learning and our sense of self. Working as real-world researchers, they'll include questions that challenge assumptions and invite honest stories?maybe even uncovering unexpected patterns across year levels or friendship groups. The artefact is a dynamic, visually engaging report built from real community data, ready to be presented at assembly or shared with the student council. By using Microsoft Forms' branching logic and instant analytics, they'll customise follow-up questions and see trends unfold in real time. Students walk away with genuine research skills and the confidence to use data to inspire change.

Students will compose and record original soundscapes that evoke different mental states?calm, focus, stress, or joy?using loops, live instruments, and voice effects. This links music and emotion, highlighting the influence of mindset and experience on wellbeing, and lets students experiment with strategies for self-regulation. Their soundtracks become the audio backdrop for Year 3 drama performances about friendship and identity, deepening connections across the school. The final product is a collection of digital tracks, remixed and published as a Year 6 'Wellbeing Album' for the community to stream, use, and discuss. GarageBand's automation curves and smart controls give students real control over dynamics, tempo, and mood, letting them express subtle shifts in feeling. Students finish with creative confidence and a toolkit for using sound to support their own?and others'?wellbeing.

Students will curate a digital library of stories, graphic novels, and articles that represent a wide spectrum of identities, neurodiversities, and wellbeing challenges, becoming literary detectives for their peers. This connects directly to the unit's exploration of identity within collectives and how experiences shape our sense of self. Taking on the role of librarians for a month, they'll recommend texts to younger students and even write their own reviews, sparking school-wide conversations about inclusion and empathy. The finished artefact is a themed, annotated reading list hosted on Epic, complete with video endorsements and custom reading challenges for the whole year level. By using Epic's collection-building and integrated video review features, students create rich, multimedia recommendations that reach beyond just words. They leave as champions for diverse voices?and trusted reading guides to the whole learning community.

s.t: Brainwaves Balance Board: Build Your Mindful Maze
s.d: Students will design and construct a tabletop 'balance board' maze that symbolises the journey of self-regulation and wellbeing. Using cardboard, marbles, recycled materials, and art supplies, each group creates a unique maze representing different brain regions, emotions, and mindset challenges. With a Makey Makey kit and Scratch, students embed interactive digital checkpoints?such as sound effects or animations triggered as the marble passes milestones?blending physical engineering with coding. This creative build challenges students to reflect on their own identities, experiences, and strategies for maintaining balance in learning and life.

ci: People recognise important events through celebrations and traditions.
lo: The traditions of our families and communities; How and why people celebrate; The similarities and differences between celebrations

s.d: Children will bring celebrations to life by programming BeeBots to travel along giant floor maps representing different cultural festivals, from Lunar New Year parades to Diwali lantern trails. This hands-on journey taps into the line of inquiry about the traditions of our families and communities, letting students experience movement and sequence as part of celebration. Students will work in pairs to design their own celebration route, then swap maps with another group and try to decode the story or tradition being represented. The final artefact is a colourful, annotated festival map with a BeeBot journey that families can follow during a class showcase. By using BeeBots' sequence-and-repeat function, students can choreograph multi-step dances or processions, just like real festivals. They finish with a sense of pride in sharing their own traditions and the confidence to understand those of others.

Students will turn their family celebration drawings into talking portraits using ChatterPix Kids, giving voice to traditions in their own words. This activity dives into how and why people celebrate, inviting children to articulate the meaning behind special foods, clothes, or rituals. To make it extra special, students will record greetings or stories in a language spoken at home, then play these for the class to highlight the diversity of voices. The end result is a gallery of animated, talking celebration portraits that can be shared with families on a class iPad or at an assembly. The magic comes from ChatterPix Kids' ability to animate any drawing with a moving mouth, making even the shyest students eager to share their story. Children walk away knowing their voice matters and that every tradition has a story worth telling.

Children will create vibrant digital collages of celebrations from around the world using PicCollage, blending photos, stickers, and their own artwork. This activity explores the similarities and differences between celebrations, sparking conversations about what makes each tradition unique or shared. Each student will take on the role of a 'celebration detective', searching for clues in images to spot common threads like food, music, or symbols across cultures. Their finished product is a colourful, annotated collage that can be printed for a classroom gallery or emailed home as a digital postcard. PicCollage's 'cutout' tool lets students snip out their own faces or hand-drawn elements to insert themselves into the festivities, making each collage truly personal. They gain the joy of seeing themselves as part of a global community of celebration.

Students will use Freeform to collaboratively build mind maps of celebration symbols, connecting fireworks, candles, drums, and more to the cultures that use them. This taps directly into the inquiry about the traditions of families and communities, helping students visually organise how different elements come together in celebration. Pairs will interview a classmate about a family tradition and then add a new branch to the map, growing the web of connections as the class learns together. The final artefact is a living, evolving digital mind map that can be projected and explored as a group, or printed as a giant poster. Freeform's sticky-note and drawing tools let even the youngest students add their own doodles and ideas, making the map a true community creation. Children finish with a sense of belonging and the ability to see connections between their own lives and those of their friends.

Children will become celebration explorers by using Seesaw to discover local plants, animals, and places that feature in Australian celebrations, from wattle for Wattle Day to magpies in Aboriginal gatherings. This links to the line of inquiry about the traditions of our communities, showing how the natural world shapes the way we celebrate. Each student will act as a 'nature reporter', finding a plant or animal that is special to their family or community's celebration, and sharing a fun fact with the class. Their work becomes a class 'Celebration Nature Guide', a booklet or digital slideshow pairing each celebration with its local natural symbols. The app's advanced search and photo ID features help even young children match real-life finds with celebration stories. Students leave with new eyes for the world around them, realising that every celebration is rooted in the place they call home.

Students design and craft their own unique musical shakers inspired by a family or cultural celebration, using recycled containers, rice, beads, and colourful decorations like fabric, stickers, and metallic paper. After decorating, students use a simple recording tool on iPads (such as the camera or voice memos app) to capture the sound of their shaker and share a short story about its meaning. The class then assembles all the shakers and recordings into a 'Celebration Soundscape', building a multisensory display that celebrates the diversity of traditions in their community. This project helps students express themselves through both hands-on making and digital storytelling, connecting sound, art, and culture.

ci: We all have roles and responsibilities in the community
lo: Roles people play; Responsibilities in the community; How working together helps everyone

s.d: Let students become 'community helpers' by designing and wiring their own interactive 'Job Board' using Makey Makey and everyday objects like playdough, cardboard, and foil. This hands-on activity dives into the idea of roles people play, as each job on the board triggers a sound or message explaining its responsibilities. Invite a real staff member from the school (like the librarian or groundskeeper) to record a voice message for their role, so students can hear authentic voices when their job is selected. The final artefact is a large, colourful board with touchpoints that play different sounds or messages about school jobs, ready to be shared at assembly or in the foyer for families to try. Students will use Makey Makey's ability to turn any conductive material into a computer key, making their board truly interactive and tactile. Kids leave with a sense of pride in their own job as 'school explainers' and a new appreciation for how everyone helps the community run smoothly.

Prep students become digital storytellers by coding a mini-animation about a day in the life of a school helper using ScratchJr. This activity brings to life the line of inquiry about responsibilities in the community, letting students choose and act out roles like crossing guard, teacher, or nurse. They can swap roles and imagine what it would be like to walk in someone else's shoes for a day, sparking empathy and big conversations about fairness. The finished piece is a short, colourful animation with characters moving and talking, which can be shown on the big screen during a class 'Community Heroes' film festival. ScratchJr's record-voice and tap-to-animate features let even non-readers personalise their stories with their own voices and simple code blocks. Students finish with a burst of confidence, knowing they can use technology to tell real stories about the people who help them every day.

Students dive into a curated collection of picture books and simple nonfiction texts on Epic, exploring stories of different helpers in schools and communities around the world. This directly supports the line of inquiry into the many roles people play, broadening students' views beyond their own classroom. After reading, students become 'book detectives', hunting for unusual or unexpected jobs and sharing their discoveries with a buddy class in Year 1. Their 'Community Helper Book Hunt' is turned into a digital bookshelf, which can be shared with families through the school newsletter. Epic's read-to-me function and built-in quizzes help students engage independently, even if they're not yet fluent readers. Each child walks away inspired, realising there are countless ways to contribute and that every job matters.

Students create a 'Community Roles Movie' using Apple Clips, where each child stars as a different helper in the Wesley College school community. Exploring the idea of 'how working together helps everyone,' they act out scenes showing teamwork?like setting up snack time, caring for the library, or keeping the playground safe. Children experience role reversal by swapping jobs and narrating from the perspective of their chosen role, building empathy and understanding for classmates' contributions. The final artefact is a vibrant, subtitle-rich movie montage, ready to share at assembly or with families on the class blog. Apple Clips' live titles feature lets even emergent writers add real-time captions, supporting early literacy and accessible storytelling. Through playful filmmaking, students see themselves as valued contributors, proud of their part in a community where every role matters.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students work with their teacher to bring school helpers to life using the Animate from Audio feature in Animating a Character with Adobe Express (https://new.express.adobe.com/home/tools/animate-from-audio). Each child records their voice describing a classroom job?such as 'I am the Line Leader. I help everyone walk safely in the hallway.'?and selects a character to match. The teacher operates the tool, and the app automatically lip-syncs the character to the student's voice, creating a playful animated explainer. These short clips are combined into a 'Meet Our Helpers' video that can be shown at assembly or shared with families. This activity helps students practise speaking and listening while celebrating the many ways people contribute to a caring school community. Children see their ideas come to life and feel proud to introduce the important jobs that keep their classroom running smoothly.

Students design and build their own 'Command Centre' using recycled boxes, cardboard tubes, paper plates, and colourful craft materials to represent different classroom jobs and routines (like Line Leader, Librarian, or Gardener). Each role gets its own interactive station with moving parts (spinners, flaps, sliders) that students engineer themselves. Using an Osmo iPad base with the 'Monster' app, students animate their Command Centre: drawing or photographing their built stations, then bringing them to life with digital characters who 'perform' the jobs. This hands-on project helps students understand how roles and routines help organise their classroom community, blending creative making with playful technology.

ci: An inquiry into the natural world and its laws; the interaction between the natural world and human societies.
lo: Lines of inquiry to be confirmed once planner is uploaded

s.d: Invite Prep students to become real-world nature detectives by exploring the school grounds and local parks with Seek by iNaturalist. Children use the app's live camera identification feature to scan plants, insects, and fungi, watching as the app suggests names and fun facts in real time. Each child selects their favourite discovery?such as a dandelion, ladybird, or mossy patch?and captures a photo with the app. Back in class, students share their finds and compare which living things need sunlight, water, or shelter. The teacher helps the class create a colourful wall chart mapping out all the species identified, sparking discussions about caring for local habitats. This hands-on adventure transforms everyday walks into scientific expeditions, building curiosity and a sense of stewardship for the living world.

Children become environment detectives, crafting an interactive digital book of living and non-living things they find around St Kilda campus. This activity immerses them in the world of plants, animals, and objects by inviting them to observe how human societies and nature interact in familiar playgrounds, gardens, and classrooms. Each student adopts the role of a curious scientist, snapping their own discovery photos and recording playful audio clues to challenge classmates and families to guess what each object is and why it matters. The finished eBook brims with student photos, voiceovers, and clickable question bubbles?ready to publish to the class library or share at assembly. Book Creator's 'Read to Me' accessibility feature lets children listen back to their own narrations, supporting emerging readers and celebrating every voice. Young learners walk away seeing themselves as real-world explorers whose questions and creativity help others care for the living world.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Transform Prep students into animated science explainers using the Animate from Audio feature in Animating a Character with Adobe Express (https://new.express.adobe.com/home/tools/animate-from-audio). After investigating how the sun and weather affect plants and animals, each child records a short explanation?such as how a sunflower follows the sun or why worms hide when it rains. The teacher helps students select a friendly animal or plant character, then uploads the audio so the character lip-syncs their words. The final artefact is a talking digital character video, ready for a classroom 'Weather Wonders' showcase or to be sent home to families. This process makes invisible science ideas visible and memorable, as students see their own voices bring learning to life. Children finish with a sense of pride, knowing they can teach others about the natural world in a creative, playful way.

Prep students animate their hand-drawn living and non-living things by giving them voices with ChatterPix Kids, turning their nature discoveries into playful storytellers. This activity directly explores how human societies interact with the natural world, as students explain what makes something living or non-living in their own words. After visiting the school garden or playground, students can choose an object or creature and imagine its perspective, speaking as a bee, a tree, a rock, or a bottle cap left behind. The final artefact is a talking photo?each student's illustrated character brought to life with a recording?ready to be shared in a class assembly or with families through a digital gallery. ChatterPix Kids' unique mouth animation feature lets children match their voice recordings to the moving mouth on their drawing, making the learning experience both magical and memorable. This empowers even the youngest learners to see themselves as creative communicators and environmental stewards, using technology to amplify their ideas about caring for our world.

Kick off your Prep scientists' journey by sending them on a living things treasure hunt using the Seesaw app, searching for plants and animals in the school garden and local parks. This hands-on adventure is a perfect way to spark curiosity about the natural world and its laws, as students notice, name and wonder about the living things all around them. Invite a local gardener or parent with a green thumb to join the walk and share their own plant stories, helping children see how humans interact with and care for the environment. Each child will create a mini 'field guide' page with their own photo and observation, ready to be shared as a class book for the library or a digital slideshow for families. The app's built-in 'species location' feature lets students see which animals and plants are unique to their area, making each find feel special. Students finish the hunt with the confidence to spot, name and care for living things wherever they go.

Students design and construct their own mini 'Bug Hotels' using recycled boxes, cardboard tubes, sticks, leaves, and natural materials to create cozy habitats for imaginary or real mini-beasts. After building, they use a simple tablet camera app (e.g., iPad Camera) to document their creations, narrating what creatures might live there and why each habitat feature is important. Students reflect on what living things need to survive and how humans can help care for tiny creatures in the environment. This project blends hands-on building, digital storytelling, and inquiry into how the world works for insects and animals.

ci: Human actions change the environment.
lo: How people interact with different environments; The effect people have on the environment; Ways in which people can take action and care for the environment

s.d: Prep students become nature documentarians by using the Insta360 camera to capture immersive, 360-degree videos of their school garden or a local park. Working in small groups, they film from the perspective of a tiny animal?like a bug crawling through grass or a bird flying above trees?highlighting how different environments provide shelter, food, and challenges. After filming, students view their footage on tablets, noticing details they might miss with regular photos, such as hidden rubbish or animal tracks. Teachers guide a discussion about how these environments change when people help or harm them, using the footage as a springboard. The final product is a virtual 'environment walk' that families and other classes can explore, sparking conversations about caring for local habitats. This activity transforms students into storytellers who see the world through new eyes and inspires them to notice and protect the places around them.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Prep students work with their teacher to create talking animal avatars using the Animate from Audio feature in Adobe Express (https://new.express.adobe.com/home/tools/animate-from-audio). Each child chooses an animal from a desert, ocean, or forest and records a short message?such as a turtle asking for clean water or a koala describing its favourite tree. The teacher helps students select a character and uploads their voice, letting the avatar lip-sync their words. These animated clips are combined into a class video, forming a chorus of animals sharing their hopes and worries about their environments. The finished video is screened at assembly or shared with families, sparking empathy and action. Students see themselves as advocates for nature, using digital storytelling to give a voice to creatures who cannot speak for themselves.

Children use Stop Motion Studio to create playful stop-motion stories showing how people can help or harm different environments. Working in pairs, they build simple sets from blocks, fabric, and natural materials to represent a forest, ocean, or desert. Using toy animals and people, they animate short scenes?such as a forest being cleaned up, rubbish washing into the sea, or animals finding new homes after a fire. Students capture each frame, then add voice narration or sound effects to bring their stories to life. The finished stop-motion films are screened in a class 'film festival', inviting discussion about the choices people make and their impact on the planet. This hands-on activity turns environmental responsibility into a creative adventure, helping students see themselves as storytellers and changemakers.

Prep students use the Field Guide to Victoria app to discover real plants and animals that live in local environments like parks, beaches, or bushland. In small groups, they browse photos and listen to animal sounds, then choose a favourite species to investigate. Each group creates a simple fact sheet or drawing about their chosen plant or animal, noting what it needs to survive and how people can help or harm it. Teachers prompt students to notice patterns, such as which animals need clean water or which plants grow near playgrounds. The class assembles a giant wall mural showing all their discoveries, with each species linked to a positive action kids can take. This activity builds curiosity and a sense of connection to the living world right outside their door.

Students use PicCollage to design vibrant digital posters that show ways people can care for the planet at school and home. They snap photos of classmates recycling, watering plants, or picking up litter, then combine these with stickers, drawings, and action words. Each child creates a poster featuring their own 'eco-hero moment', adding speech bubbles to explain their action?such as 'I turn off the tap to save water!' or 'We plant seeds for the bees.' The posters are printed and displayed around the school, turning everyday actions into inspiring examples for others. By using PicCollage's cutout and background features, students experiment with layouts and visual storytelling. This activity helps them see that small choices add up to big changes when everyone gets involved.

Students will design and build miniature environments (desert, ocean, or forest) using recycled boxes, fabric scraps, paper, and natural materials. They'll craft native animals from modeling clay and create simple obstacles or shelters within each habitat. Using Sphero Indi cars, students will program simple color-coded paths for their 'animal' to explore, demonstrating how different habitats provide for living things and how human changes (like adding or removing elements) impact the journey. This playful, hands-on project helps students see their actions' effects on the planet while combining imaginative making with beginner robotics.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: An inquiry into orientation in place and time; personal histories; the relationship between and the interconnectedness of individuals and civilisations.
lo: Lines of inquiry to be confirmed once planner is uploaded

s.d: Students become cultural storytellers by crafting and performing digital puppet shows that celebrate a tradition or festival from their own family or community. This activity brings alive the Prep theme of how we express our personal histories and connect with others through traditions. To spark curiosity, students can swap their puppet shows with a buddy class and discover a celebration they've never heard of, then record a question to ask the original creator. The final artefact is a short animated video featuring hand-drawn characters, props, and a voiceover retelling a real celebration story, shareable with families and across year levels. By using Puppet Pals' custom photo import feature, students can turn family photos or scanned drawings into their own unique puppets ? making the experience even more personal. Children walk away proud that their story matters, and gain the confidence to share and respect different traditions.

Students compose a soundscape that captures the mood and energy of a celebration, drawing from music, rhythm, and sounds they've experienced at home or in their community. This taps into the central idea by exploring how emotions and memories are connected to musical traditions and celebrations. Invite a local musician (in person or via video call) to share a favourite cultural instrument or festival song, inspiring students to experiment with new sounds in their creations. Each student produces a 30-second audio track using GarageBand, layering live claps, voice, and simple digital instruments ? these can be shared with families during an end-of-unit celebration assembly. The hidden gem is GarageBand's Live Loops, which let students visually build patterns and mix sounds like a real DJ, even without prior music skills. By expressing themselves through music, each child gains creative bravery and a deeper sense of how sound brings people together.

Students will author a digital picture book that tells the story of a family or community celebration, weaving together their own memories and imaginative details. This project delves into the central idea by spotlighting personal histories and the ways in which traditions connect individuals across time and place. To bring in a new perspective, students become junior cultural ambassadors, creating their stories to read aloud to a buddy class or to share at assembly as a window into the diversity within their community. Each finished book features voice narration, student-drawn illustrations, and even short audio clips of celebratory music or greetings in different languages. Using Book Creator's built-in audio and video recording tools, students can embed spoken word and sound, giving their books a multisensory, multicultural richness that goes far beyond static pages. By publishing their books to a real audience, students learn that their stories and traditions are valued, building pride in their identity and empathy for others.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Prep students become animated storytellers by using Animate from Audio in Adobe Express (https://new.express.adobe.com/home/tools/animate-from-audio) to bring a celebration story to life. The teacher guides the class as each child records their voice describing a special object, food, or costume from a family tradition, then selects a character or animal to lip-sync their words. Students watch as their chosen character 'speaks' their story, adding a magical twist to sharing personal experiences. These animated clips can be combined into a class video gallery or looped on a screen during a celebration assembly. Animate from Audio's instant lip-syncing makes even shy students excited to narrate, as their words are brought to life by a friendly digital avatar. This activity helps children see that every voice and tradition is worth celebrating, and sparks curiosity about the objects and rituals that matter to their classmates.

Students paint a digital mural inspired by the colours, patterns, and scenes from their family's celebrations, combining art with stories about how these images make them feel. This creative journey helps them reflect on community connections and the emotions linked to shared traditions. Children team up in small groups to create 'celebration blends'?merging details from two different cultural events into a single mural panel, sparking questions about what makes each celebration unique and what brings them together. The finished work is a vibrant digital gallery that can be projected at assembly, printed as a collaborative poster, or sent home as a digital postcard. Brushes Redux's layering tool lets students overlay patterns, photos, and hand-drawn sketches, so their artwork feels rich and deeply personal. By making art that celebrates both difference and connection, students gain pride in their own identity and empathy for others.
