Prep students become festival planners, using Sphero Indi cars and colour tiles to design a 'Celebration Journey Course' that models the steps of a real tradition ? from preparation through to the big event. Working in groups, they empathise by listening to a classmate's celebration story, then define and map out the stages as physical stops on their carpet pathway using props like mini paper gates, flags, or family photos. Ideating together, they test different sequences, debugging when Indi doesn't follow the path as planned, and prototype with various colour-tile combinations to represent important moments (like a red tile for fireworks or a blue for water rituals). At the end, students run a live 'Celebration Parade' where the Indi cars travel the route while classmates narrate the journey, inviting parents or older students to watch. This project fuses hands-on design, spatial thinking, and empathy, giving children the power to turn lived experiences into collaborative, joyful action.

ci: To be healthy, people's basic needs must be met.
lo: How our brain is growing and changing; How our emotions, behaviours and actions promote relationships; How we care for our bodies

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Children become their own healthy-living superheroes by animating a character that shares one essential tip for caring for our bodies. This playful activity brings the line of inquiry about how our actions support wellbeing to life, letting each child see themselves as an expert. Imagine the pride when students see their animated character teaching next year's Preps a trick for eating well, moving joyfully, or calming big feelings. Each child creates a short, lively animation with their own voice and a hand-drawn or digital character, ready to be shown at assembly or on the class screen. The 'Animate from Audio' feature lets even the shyest Prep bring their ideas to life with talking, blinking, moving characters?no reading required. Every child walks away feeling like their voice matters and that they can help others be healthy too.

Students invent and wire up a 'Feelings Soundboard' using Makey Makey and everyday objects to explore how emotions, behaviours and actions shape healthy relationships. By connecting bananas, playdough, or foil shapes to different emotions, children discover how our brains and feelings are always sending signals. Invite a Year 1 buddy class to try out the soundboard and guess which feeling each sound represents, sparking real conversations about empathy and friendship. The final artefact is a tactile, interactive station where pressing each object plays a recorded sound or word?giggles, soothing music, or a cheerful 'hello'. Using Makey Makey's ability to turn almost anything into a keyboard, students learn to see technology as something they can shape with their own hands. They leave with a sense of agency and a toolkit for expressing feelings in creative, playful ways.

Students use Apple Clips to create 'Healthy Habits' video guides that show how to care for their bodies and minds. They act out routines?such as brushing teeth, exercising, or practising mindfulness?and use stickers and animated text to highlight each step. Students narrate why these habits are important for staying healthy and feeling good. The finished videos are compiled into a class 'Wellbeing Wall', which can be revisited during health discussions. This activity encourages students to take responsibility for their wellbeing and share practical tips with peers.

Prep students become 'Healthy Living Detectives' by using Epic to hunt for stories and videos from around the world about how people meet their basic needs. This sparks curiosity about the central idea that everyone needs food, water, safety, and love to grow and thrive. Each child chooses a favourite story and retells it in their own words to a small group, practising communication and active listening. The class creates a digital bookshelf of 'Healthy Heroes'?stories that celebrate different ways people look after themselves and each other. Epic's 'Read-to-Me' feature means every child can access rich texts, even before they can read independently. Children finish this project seeing themselves as story-sharers and experts in what it means to be healthy, no matter where you live.

Children become artists and scientists as they use Brushes Redux to draw a 'Growing Brain Garden', showing how their brain changes and blossoms when they learn new things or practise healthy habits. This connects directly to the line of inquiry about how our brain grows and changes, making invisible processes visible and joyful. Invite students to swap iPads and add a 'helpful thought' or 'kind action' to a classmate's garden, so each drawing becomes a patchwork of shared ideas. The final gallery is a digital mural displayed on the classroom screen or printed as a poster for the school corridor. Brushes Redux's layering feature lets students build up their garden in stages?roots, shoots, flowers, and fruits?mirroring the way healthy habits grow over time. Kids leave with a vivid sense that their choices can help their brains and friendships flourish.

s.t: My Celebration Self: Wearable Story Hats
s.d: Students design and craft vibrant, wearable hats that tell the story of their unique identity, family, and favourite celebration. Using cardboard headbands, coloured paper, fabric scraps, recycled materials, and decorative bits, each child builds a hat featuring symbols, drawings, and 3D elements representing their traditions, foods, and special moments. With iPads, students use a simple AR (augmented reality) app to record a short video introducing their hat and its meaning, then add a QR code tag to their creation for friends to scan and watch. This hands-on project celebrates diversity, creativity, and community, making identity visible and shareable in a joyful, playful way.

ci: People express their emotions through the way they communicate.
lo: Different ways to communicate emotions; How art, music and movement express feelings; Understanding others' expressions through body language and facial cues

s.d: Students become emotion detectives by creating animated puppet shows that explore how people express feelings through words, tone, and gestures. This activity brings the line of inquiry 'different ways to communicate emotions' to life, as students experiment with voices, facial expressions, and movement to show happiness, sadness, or excitement. After watching a video call from a real actor or drama teacher, students try out professional tips for showing emotions without saying a word. Their final show is shared with Prep students, who guess each character's feeling?turning Year 1s into expert communicators and role models. Using Puppet Pals' custom character builder, students design their own expressive avatars and sets, making each story unique and personal. They finish with the confidence to read and show feelings in creative ways, both on stage and in real life.

Young artists paint digital self-portraits that reveal their emotions using colour, shape, and line, inspired by Frida Kahlo. This connects directly to the line of inquiry 'how art expresses feelings', letting students experiment with visual language to represent joy, anger, or calm. Each child swaps portraits with a classmate and interprets what emotion the artist tried to show, sparking conversations about empathy and seeing through another's eyes. The finished gallery is displayed for families, with QR codes linking to the artist's voice explanation of their choices. Students use Brushes Redux's layering feature to try bold backgrounds and overlay facial expressions, just like professional illustrators. By the end, they see themselves as artists who can express complex feelings without saying a word.

Students compose short pieces of music that capture the mood of different emotions?like a bouncy tune for happiness or a slow, soft melody for sadness. This activity brings the line of inquiry 'how music expresses feelings' into action, as students discover how sound choices can tell a story. After listening to soundtracks from favourite movies, students discuss how music changes the way they feel about a scene, then try to create their own 'emotion soundtracks'. Their finished tracks are played as background music for story time in Prep, letting younger students guess the feeling each song is meant to show. GarageBand's Live Loops feature gives even beginners the power to mix instruments and rhythms for instant results. Students leave with the confidence to use music as a language for feelings, not just words.

Students become empathy explorers by recording short video reflections about a time they felt a strong emotion and how they showed it. This links to the line of inquiry 'understanding others' expressions through body language and facial cues', as students watch each other's videos and guess the emotion being described. Students invite a family member to record their own reflection, sparking intergenerational conversations about feelings. The final video collection is shared at a class 'Feelings Film Festival' for families, celebrating honest expression and connection. Seesaw's drawing-on-video tool lets students annotate their own faces with arrows and emojis to highlight key expressions. By participating, students practise recognising emotions in themselves and others, building empathy for every interaction.

Students collaborate to create a giant digital mind map of emotion words, symbols, and body language cues, using Freeform's open canvas. This directly supports building vocabulary for feelings and exploring the many ways people communicate emotions. Each group is challenged to include words in different languages spoken at home, making the map a celebration of Wesley's diverse community. The finished mind map is printed as a poster for the school foyer, inviting families and visitors to add their own ideas with sticky notes. Freeform's ability to add sketches, photos, and sticky notes on an infinite canvas helps students connect ideas visually and creatively. Students walk away knowing they are part of a community where every feeling and voice matters.

Students design and build creative 'wearable machines' that show different emotions using moving parts and colour-changing features. Using cardboard, felt, ribbons, recycled bits, paper plates, and simple mechanisms (like spinning emotion dials, pop-up eyebrows, or flapping wings powered by split pins and string), they craft hats, masks, or badges that physically change to express feelings. Students then use a simple coding robot (like Sphero Indi) to 'activate' their wearable by driving it onto colour-coded tiles that trigger the wearer to show a specific emotion. This hands-on project lets students explore how we express ourselves through movement, colour, and design, blending art, technology, and self-awareness in a joyful, memorable way.

ci: Systems are involved in preparing products for consumers.
lo: Where products come from; The systems products go through; How people choose their products

s.d: Students engineer a dynamic delivery route by designing obstacle courses for Sphero Indi robots to simulate the journey of a product?such as milk or apples?from farm to consumer. Using coloured tiles and physical props, they map out each stage: farm, factory, packaging, transport, and shop, adding challenges like 'traffic jams' or 'detours' to mimic real-world logistics. Students programme Indi to follow the correct sequence, testing and refining their routes to ensure the product arrives safely. They document each stage with photos and captions, explaining how changes in the system affect the journey. The final artefact is a narrated photo story or video walkthrough of their Indi's adventure, highlighting key vocabulary and decision points. This activity immerses students in systems thinking, sequencing, and creative problem-solving as they bring the product's journey to life.

Students turn everyday products?like a banana, loaf of bread, or t-shirt?into talking characters using ChatterPix Kids, giving each item a unique voice to narrate its journey from origin to consumer. They draw a mouth on a photo of the product, record a short story about its travels through farm, factory, transport, and shop, and use stickers to add hats, trucks, or scenery for each stage. Some students might make their product boast about being 'locally grown,' while others create a 'day in the life' from the perspective of a product facing tricky choices, such as packaging or transport delays. The finished artefact is a collection of lively, informative mini-videos ready to share with families or display at assembly. Kids experiment with expressive voices and creative storytelling, making the invisible systems behind everyday items visible and memorable. This activity builds sequencing, vocabulary, and empathy for the journey products take.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students use the Animate from Audio feature in Adobe Express (https://new.express.adobe.com/home/tools/animate-from-audio) to create an animated explainer about how a product?like a loaf of bread or a pair of jeans?travels from farm to shop. Each child records their voice narrating the stages, then selects a character such as a friendly farmer, delivery truck, or shopkeeper to lip-sync their story. The tool automatically animates the character's mouth to match the narration, making the process engaging and accessible for young learners. Students can add expressive gestures and backgrounds to highlight key moments, like harvesting, packaging, or arriving at the store. The final artefact is a short, animated video that can be shared with families or used as a class resource to explain how systems work. This activity helps students sequence events, use new vocabulary, and see themselves as storytellers who can explain complex ideas in a fun, visual way.

Students become investigative reporters by using Epic to explore digital books and videos about the origins and journeys of food, clothing, and everyday products. They search for the most surprising or unusual product stories?like how pineapples travel or the secret life of socks?using Epic's read-to-me and search features to access rich content, even as emergent readers. After gathering facts, students prepare interview questions for a guest expert (such as a chef, farmer, or shop owner via video), inspired by their Epic discoveries. Their final artefact is a digital 'Ask the Expert' Q&A booklet, filled with their best questions and answers from real-world insiders. This process encourages curiosity, critical thinking, and the ability to connect information from multiple sources. Students finish the activity feeling like real researchers, empowered to ask questions and challenge what they find on the supermarket shelf.

Students author interactive digital books in Book Creator that trace the journey of a chosen product?such as chocolate, bread, or a cotton t-shirt?from its origin to their home. Each page represents a stage in the system: farm, factory, transport, shop, and consumer, with students adding photos, drawings, voice recordings, and labels to explain what happens at each step. They use Book Creator's multimedia features to embed short videos or sound clips, making the process vivid and accessible. For example, a student might record themselves explaining how wheat is harvested or draw a map showing the product's route. The final artefact is a multimedia book that can be shared with families or displayed on classroom devices. This activity builds sequencing, vocabulary, and digital storytelling skills while making complex systems tangible for young learners.

s.t: From Farm to Table: Supply Chain Train Adventure
s.d: Students design and build a giant tabletop 'train track' system using cardboard, tubes, recycled boxes, and craft materials to represent the journey of a product (like bread or a t-shirt) from its origin to the consumer. Along the track, they create and decorate stations for each stage?farm, factory, transport, shop, and home?using found materials, drawings, and labels. A Sphero Indi or push-along train serves as the 'product,' traveling through each stop as students narrate and sequence its journey. This playful project helps students physically map out and understand how products move through organised systems, connecting vocabulary and concepts to a hands-on, collaborative creation.

ci: Weather affects our lives in different ways.
lo: Types of weather conditions; How weather impacts our lives (clothing, activities, food, feelings); Why weather changes (seasons, patterns)

s.d: Students become weather storytellers by creating stop-motion animations that bring different weather events to life?such as a rainstorm filling a garden, clouds drifting across the sky, or the sun melting a snowman. Using Stop Motion Studio, they photograph small props, drawings, and classroom objects, then sequence the images to show weather changing over time. Students narrate their animations with simple voiceovers, explaining how people, animals, or plants respond to each type of weather. The finished films are screened in a 'Weather Film Festival' for families and other classes, sparking conversations about adaptation and change. Stop Motion Studio's onion-skinning and frame-by-frame editing features help students experiment with movement and storytelling. They leave with a sense of pride in their creative process and a deeper understanding of how weather shapes our world.

Students code their own animated story in ScratchJr, where a character chooses outfits and activities based on the daily weather forecast. This playful project brings the line of inquiry about how weather impacts our lives?clothing, activities, food, and feelings?into the world of storytelling and choice. Students imagine themselves as meteorologists on TV, creating weather reports that help their character (and viewers!) decide what to wear or eat. The finished animations are compiled into a class 'Weather News Hour' and shared with a Year 2 buddy class, sparking cross-year conversations. Using ScratchJr's 'trigger on tap' and 'repeat' blocks, students experiment with cause-and-effect, letting their stories change as the weather does. They finish with a sense of agency, knowing their choices matter and that technology can help us adapt to the world around us.

Students become weather detectives by using the Field Guide to Victoria app to investigate how local plants and animals respond to changing weather. They search for species that are active in different conditions?like magpies hunting after rain or wattle trees blooming in spring?and collect digital 'field notes' with photos and short captions. Each student creates a mini-guidebook page about a favourite plant or animal, describing how it adapts to sunny, rainy, or windy days. The class assembles these pages into a digital 'Weather and Wildlife' guide, which is shared with the school library. The app's rich images and local species database help students connect weather patterns to real-life changes in their own neighbourhood. They finish with a sense of connection to place and a new appreciation for how living things adapt to the world around them.

Students create vibrant weather mood boards in PicCollage, collecting photos, emojis, and weather icons to show how different weather makes them feel and what they might do or eat on those days. This connects to the line of inquiry about how weather influences our feelings, activities, and food choices. Students take on the role of 'weather wellness coaches', designing posters to help classmates choose activities or snacks for sunny, rainy, or chilly days. The finished mood boards are printed and displayed in the school foyer, inviting families to vote for their favourite 'weather day'. PicCollage's 'cutout' and 'doodle' tools let students personalise their boards with hand-drawn touches and creative cropping, making each one unique. They discover that weather isn't just something that happens outside?it's something we feel, adapt to, and celebrate together.

Students become sound designers, using GarageBand to compose short weather-inspired soundscapes?thunderstorms, gentle rain, gusty winds, or sunny mornings?by layering digital instruments and real-world recordings. This creative process deepens understanding of how weather can be experienced through our senses, tying into the exploration of weather patterns and their impact. Students are challenged to create a 'guess the weather' listening game for their peers, swapping roles as musicians and meteorologists. The final product is a class audio playlist, shared with families via QR codes, turning the corridor into a weather symphony. GarageBand's 'Live Loops' feature lets even young students experiment with repeating patterns and dynamic changes, capturing the rhythm of real weather. They finish with a new way to express emotion and story, realising that weather can be felt as much as seen.

s.t: Weather Wonder Wheels: Rolling Forecast Dioramas
s.d: Students design and build a rolling diorama that shows different weather scenes using large recycled cardboard tubes as the base. They craft interchangeable weather panels (sunny, rainy, windy, snowy) with collage materials, cotton balls, fabric scraps, and tissue paper, attaching them around the tube. Using simple axles and wheels, students create a handle to rotate their diorama and reveal changing weather. With the help of an iPad, they record short videos narrating their diorama's story, explaining how people and places adapt to each weather type?blending creative making, storytelling, and weather science.

ci: Living things have structures that allow them to survive in different environments.
lo: The physical structure of plants and bees; How features support survival in different environments; Human impact on living things

s.d: Students become real-world nature detectives as they use the Field Guide to Victoria app to hunt for local bees and plant species in the school grounds. This hands-on adventure ties directly to understanding how the physical structures of plants and bees help them survive in their Melbourne environment. Students work in teams, just like park rangers, gathering evidence and debating whether each species they find is a survival superstar or needs our help to thrive. Their fieldwork isn't just for class?it's turned into an illustrated nature guide for Prep buddies and families, packed with student photos, location notes, and fascinating facts. The app's advanced search and filter features empower even young learners to make connections between what they see and ecological adaptations. By the end, students see themselves as true protectors of local living things, ready to make a difference.

Let students reimagine the buzz of a bee as they engineer interactive pollination models using Makey Makey kits and everyday classroom materials. By tinkering with circuits, they discover how a bee's body is perfectly designed to collect and move pollen between flowers?a hands-on take on the unit's focus on structure and survival. Students swap roles with scientists and inventors, brainstorming ways humans could mimic bee adaptations to solve real pollination problems. The result is a working prototype: pressing a flower triggers a sound or light, showing the moment of pollination in action, and each group films a demo to share at assembly. By custom-mapping Makey Makey controls to trigger unique sounds or stories, students create multisensory models that surprise and delight. They leave with a fresh respect for both nature's design and their own problem-solving powers.

Students use Seek by iNaturalist to investigate the physical structures of plants and insects, such as flowers, leaves, or bees, in the school garden or local area. They photograph and identify different species, focusing on features like leaf shape, flower colour, or bee body parts. Students then create a labelled diagram or poster highlighting how these features help the living things survive in their environments. This activity deepens understanding of how structure supports survival and links directly to the study of adaptation. Teachers can prompt students to compare features across species and discuss how humans can help protect these living things. The diagrams or posters can be shared in a class gallery or science corner.

Students dive into the Epic library to become 'fact-finding journalists' on a mission to uncover the most mind-blowing plant and bee survival stories from around the world. This research quest links directly to how features help living things survive in wildly different environments. Each student adopts the persona of a 'news reporter' and creates a breaking news script about an amazing adaptation?like a bee that braves icy mountains or a plant that drinks fog. Their final report is recorded as an audio newsflash and played for other classes and families, complete with fun sound effects. Epic's Read-To-Me and audiobook features mean every student, no matter their reading level, gets access to rich, high-interest science storytelling. Students walk away as confident researchers and storytellers, ready to turn every new question into a headline.

Students turn into tiny bee or plant ambassadors by using ChatterPix Kids to give a voice to their favourite pollinator or leafy friend. This playful project brings the idea of human impact on living things to life, encouraging students to imagine what their subject would say if it could speak out for its own survival. Imagine a sunflower pleading for less litter in its garden, or a bee buzzing about why flowers need space to grow! Each student creates a short video where their plant or bee shares its survival struggles and wishes for a brighter future, which is then broadcast at lunchtime to inspire the school community. They'll use ChatterPix's sticker and text overlay tools to add facts, questions, or calls to action to their digital characters. Students finish up with the brave voice and empathy to speak up for nature, not just listen to it.

Students will design and build a large, 3D collaborative garden using recycled boxes, paper tubes, and craft materials to create flowers, plants, and a variety of habitats. They'll craft simple bee robots using Sphero Indi cars decorated as bees, then code the Indis to 'pollinate' their handmade flowers by following colour-coded paths they design with tape and paper. As they test and refine their gardens, students observe how bees interact with plants and discuss ways to make their garden more bee-friendly. This hands-on quest helps them understand the vital relationship between plants, pollinators, and the shared responsibility of caring for our planet.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Stories and artefacts help us to understand connections between the past, present and future.
lo:
How we learn about the past
Why people preserve stories and artefacts
How stories and artefacts can be shared into the future

s.d: Students become time-travelling storytellers by recording a video diary from the perspective of a family artefact?imagining its journey across generations. They explore how stories and objects connect the past, present, and future by embodying the artefact's voice and experiences. To ignite empathy and historical imagination, students will share their artefact's 'memories' as if the object could speak, then interview classmates' artefacts for a classroom 'museum conversations' showcase. The final product is a vibrant, captioned video montage that blends narration, stickers, and effects to bring the artefact's story to life for a real audience of families and peers. Apple Clips' Live Titles feature empowers even emerging writers to narrate their ideas fluently, automatically turning speech into animated captions. Students experience the power of perspective-taking and realise their own stories have value and the ability to shape how the future remembers the present.

Young inventors turn everyday objects into interactive 'memory triggers' by creating simple circuits that play a family member's recorded story when touched. This hands-on exploration deepens understanding of why people preserve stories and artefacts?by making invisible memories audible and tangible. Students invite grandparents or parents to record short messages about a special object, transforming classroom artefacts into living stories through real-time circuits. The completed artefacts become part of a walk-up heritage gallery at assembly where families and other students can activate voices from the past with just a gentle touch. Makey Makey's ability to convert anything conductive into a playable trigger allows students to build physical-digital connections that make history literally touchable. Children discover that the stories and objects they preserve today are tomorrow's bridges to belonging and memory.

Budding directors animate intergenerational family tales by creating puppet shows that jump between 'long ago', 'now', and 'what might come next'. This playful narrative format helps students investigate how people learn about the past and imagine the future by blending real family anecdotes with creative twists. Audience feedback comes from a surprising source: Year 6 'history buddies' who review the puppet shows and give advice on making the stories even more powerful. Each student produces a short digital puppet play starring characters from their own family, complete with voice acting and scene changes. The advanced custom backgrounds feature lets students import photos of real family artefacts or places to set the scene authentically. Through performing these stories, students embrace their role as keepers and re-inventors of family and community heritage.

Young detectives become digital archaeologists by using tablet magnifiers to conduct close-up investigations of classroom artefacts and family treasures. This concrete visual analysis supports the inquiry into how we learn about the past, as students discover clues hidden in textures, materials, and tiny details. Students present their discoveries as 'micro-mystery' challenges?sharing extreme close-ups and inviting classmates to guess the object and its story before revealing the full photo and its history. Their final artefacts are a set of zoomed-in, annotated photos with voice notes, displayed in a rotating digital gallery for families and peers. The freeze-frame image capture and annotation features enable students to highlight, label, and narrate details that would otherwise go unnoticed. By seeing the extraordinary in the ordinary, children gain a sense of wonder and agency as budding historical investigators.

Children author collaborative digital books that weave together their family stories, special artefacts, and predictions for the future of storytelling. This living anthology directly addresses how stories and artefacts can be shared into the future, giving each student a permanent voice in the class history. The books are designed as gifts for next year's cohort, who will inherit and add to the anthology, creating a tradition of story preservation across year levels. Each student's contribution includes photos, audio clips, and drawings, resulting in a multimedia eBook accessible to families and future Year 1s. Book Creator's comic templates and voice recording features enable even reluctant writers to showcase their ideas in diverse ways. Students come to see themselves as both historians and future-shapers?entrusted with carrying stories forward.

Students will design and build a 'time capsule robot' using recycled boxes, craft materials, and simple circuits (LEDs, battery packs) to light up a special compartment. Each child crafts their robot to represent their family now, then fills the capsule with a small artefact or drawing about their family's past, present, or hopes for the future. Using Sphero Indi or Bee-Bot, students program their robot to 'travel' along a timeline mat, stopping at different eras to share their artefacts and stories with classmates. This project brings together storytelling, hands-on making, and basic robotics to help students explore family history and imagine how traditions and technology might change over time.

ci: We learn about ourselves through the games we play.
lo: How to identify and manage emotions; How players' choices affect relationships; Our responsibilities when playing games

s.d: Students become feelings detectives by recording short selfie videos explaining how a favourite playground game makes them feel and why. This dives straight into the big ideas of identifying and naming emotions through the games we play. Flipping the script, students send their videos to a Year 6 buddy, who tries to guess the game based on the emotion clues alone?sparking empathy and perspective-taking across ages. The final artefact is a digital feelings gallery, where families are invited to match emotions to games at home. Seesaw's drawing and annotation tools let students doodle emojis and highlights over their own videos, capturing the rollercoaster of fun, frustration, or pride. Kids leave with a richer vocabulary for feelings and the confidence to express what play means to them.

Students design and code their own digital board game in ScratchJr, where different player choices trigger animated outcomes?friendly, fair, or not-so-fair. This hands-on task brings to life how players' decisions impact relationships and teamwork. Students swap their games with another class, challenging their peers to spot moments of fairness or conflict, and reflect on how it feels to win, lose, or fix a problem together. The finished artefact is an interactive digital board game, with branching paths and character reactions, that other classes can play on iPads. By using ScratchJr's speech bubble and background-change features, students pack their games with different moods, surprising twists, and visible consequences for each choice. Kids walk away as game makers who understand that every move can shape friendships.

Students produce a mini documentary where they interview classmates about their go-to classroom games and how these games build fairness, respect, and responsibility. This taps deeply into the unit's exploration of our roles and choices when playing with others. Students act as junior news reporters, including 'breaking news' segments when a new rule is introduced and reactions ripple through the group. The final artefact is a polished newsreel with voiceovers, interviews, and live-action game footage, ready for a school assembly screening. IMovie's split-screen mode allows students to compare 'before and after' moments?how a game feels with and without certain rules?side by side, sparking richer discussion. Students gain confidence as storytellers and spot the small changes that make games feel fair for everyone.

Students use Sphero Indi cars to create a real-life feelings obstacle course, where each coloured tile represents a different emotion experienced during games?excitement, frustration, pride, or disappointment. This activity makes the abstract idea of identifying and managing emotions concrete and active. To add an extra layer, students partner up and design 'challenge moments' in the course, swapping roles as drivers and course designers to feel both sides of teamwork and decision-making. The artefact is a video walk-through of each unique course, with student voiceovers explaining the emotional journey and the strategies for tackling tricky spots. Sphero Indi's sensor-based colour reading brings the invisible world of feelings to life, letting students see how choices shift the emotional path. Kids leave with empathy for others and strategies for navigating ups and downs?on and off the playground.

Students become empathy superheroes by snapping photos of real classroom games in action, then building comic-style storyboards in PicCollage to show how kind and unkind choices affect everyone in the game. This directly explores our responsibilities and the impact of choices in play. Instead of telling, students imagine they are advice columnists, adding speech bubbles with tips or 'what could you do next?' prompts for tricky moments. The finished artefact is a digital comic strip collection, shared with Prep classes as a visual guide to playing fairly and handling feelings. PicCollage's sticker and cutout features let students remix their own faces and friends into superhero or coach roles, making the learning personal and memorable. Students emerge as creative problem-solvers, ready to support others and lead by example.

s.t: Friendship Forts: Build & Code Your Team Hideout
s.d: Students work in small teams to design and construct colourful cardboard 'forts' or cozy hideouts using large boxes, fabric scraps, paper, and markers. Each team personalises their fort to reflect their unique group identity, decorating with symbols, drawings, and words that represent fairness, respect, and teamwork. Using Sphero Indi cars, students collaboratively create a simple coded pathway leading friends to their fort, reinforcing the importance of clear rules and cooperation. This project celebrates classroom community and gives students a tangible, playful space to discuss and role-play positive social behaviours.

ci: Artefacts provide a window into the beliefs and values of cultures.
lo: Beliefs and values contribute to a culture; The importance of rituals and traditions; How artefacts capture history and cultural expression

s.d: Invite students to bring a treasured artefact from home and transform it into a talking storyteller using ChatterPix Kids. This brings the unit's central idea?artefacts as windows into beliefs and values?alive by letting objects share their own cultural stories. Students will imagine their artefact's journey across time, giving it a voice to explain its ritual, tradition, or meaning in a way that celebrates both similarities and differences. The final result is a gallery of artefact portraits, each with a unique, student-created narration that can be shared with families and the school community. ChatterPix's drawing and sticker features let students add cultural symbols or dress to their artefact, making each story even more expressive. Students walk away seeing themselves as creative curators, able to honour and share cultural identity with a playful twist.

Students become cultural detectives, assembling a digital museum book in Book Creator that showcases artefacts, recipes, dances, and stories from their own and classmates' backgrounds. This taps into the line of inquiry about how rituals and traditions shape communities, as students collect and curate real examples from home and around the world. To deepen the experience, students can interview a family member or community elder, then include a transcript or audio snippet in their page. The finished eBook is a vibrant, multimedia museum that can be published to the class website or shared at a cultural celebration night. Using Book Creator's comic templates, students can turn interviews and artefact histories into engaging, visual narratives. This project gives every child the chance to see their family story valued and learn how to preserve culture in creative ways.

Students animate a cultural celebration?like Lunar New Year, Diwali, or a family tradition?using ScratchJr to bring the sights and sounds of rituals to life. This activity explores how beliefs and values are expressed through music, dance, and food, making the abstract tangible through code. By swapping projects with a buddy from another cultural background, students get to see their own traditions through someone else's eyes and ask new questions. The end product is a short, interactive animation that can be played on class iPads or looped on a display during assembly. ScratchJr's background and character editing tools let students customise scenes with meaningful artefacts and symbols. Kids leave with not just coding skills, but a sense of pride in their heritage and a curiosity about the world beyond their own.

Students use the insta360 camera to create immersive digital exhibitions of cultural artefacts and rituals. Working in small groups, they film 360-degree scenes that showcase artefacts, traditional clothing, or re-enactments of rituals from their own or researched cultures. The camera's panoramic view allows students to capture the setting, participants and key details, helping viewers feel present at the event. After filming, students record short narrations explaining the beliefs, values and history represented by each artefact or ritual. The finished 360-degree exhibitions are shared with the class, who explore them on iPads and discuss similarities and differences between cultures. Teachers assess students on their ability to interpret and communicate the significance of cultural artefacts using immersive media.

Students dive into Epic's diverse digital library to research artefacts and traditions from cultures they don't know much about, becoming junior anthropologists for the week. This links to the line of inquiry about how beliefs and values contribute to culture, encouraging respectful curiosity and empathy. Students can recommend a favourite story or artefact to another class, acting as 'reading ambassadors' and sparking cross-classroom conversations. Their final product is a short video or audio book review, spotlighting a story or artefact that surprised them, which can be shared with the school library or on the class blog. Epic's read-to-me function lets students access books above their reading level, opening up a world of global stories. By the end, students feel empowered to explore beyond their own experience and share discoveries with others.

Students will design and build miniature parade floats that represent a cultural celebration or tradition from their own background or one they've researched. Using recycled boxes, fabric scraps, coloured paper, and craft materials, they'll craft 3D floats and then integrate simple LED circuits (battery packs, LEDs, copper tape) to illuminate their creations. Students will document their design choices and the story behind their float using iPads to record a short video explanation, which is displayed alongside their float. This project encourages creative expression, hands-on making, and respectful sharing of diverse cultures through both physical building and basic tech integration.

ci: Technology can influence the way ecosystems can survive.
lo: An ecosystem has animals, plants and microorganisms; Technology can cause ecosystems to adapt and evolve; Technology can help or hinder ecosystems

s.d: Students become young ecologists, using the Field Guide to Victoria app to investigate real animals and plants living right here in our local ecosystems. As they explore how ecosystems are made up of animals, plants and microorganisms, students discover which species are thriving and which are struggling in our area. They take on the role of 'ecosystem detectives', gathering evidence to present to a panel of local community members or parents on the health of their chosen ecosystem. The final artefact is a digital field report with annotated photos, species facts, and students' own observations, ready to be shared with families or even local park rangers. By diving into the app's interactive identification keys and audio calls, students practise advanced observation and recording skills beyond basic browsing. They finish with a sense of real-world impact, knowing they can spot and speak up for local wildlife.

Students program BeeBots to navigate a giant floor map representing a living ecosystem, with paths winding past plants, animals, and human-made technology. This hands-on coding adventure brings to life the idea that technology can help or hinder ecosystems, as students set up 'challenges' where BeeBots must avoid pollution zones or deliver seeds to help regrow a forest. Students act as ecosystem engineers, redesigning the map after each round to make it more sustainable or to introduce new threats. The end product is a time-lapse video of their evolving ecosystem, with BeeBots' journeys showing how small changes ripple through the whole system?perfect for sharing at assembly or in a class blog. Students use BeeBots' sequence-and-repeat function to create efficient routes, learning to debug and optimise their code. They walk away as confident problem-solvers who see technology as a tool for positive change in the world around them.

Students use Seek by iNaturalist to survey the school grounds or a nearby green space, capturing photos of plants, insects, and small animals they find. They identify each species using the app's image recognition and learn key facts, including whether the species are native or introduced. Students record their observations in a digital log, noting habitat details and any signs of adaptation. Using their data, they construct a detailed ecosystem web that illustrates connections between the living things they discovered. This hands-on investigation highlights how technology can monitor biodiversity and support ecosystem health. Teachers guide a discussion on how different technologies might help or challenge ecosystems' survival and evolution.

Students author their own interactive eBooks about how technology is changing ecosystems, combining facts, persuasive arguments, and imaginative scenarios. This project connects directly to the idea that technology can help or hinder ecosystems, as students weigh up real-world examples and dream up future inventions. Students take turns as 'editors', giving feedback to classmates and deciding which books should be published in a digital library for the school community. The final artefact is a collection of multimedia eBooks, complete with student-recorded audio, clickable links, and comic-style illustrations. Book Creator's comic templates and embedded audio features allow students to go beyond text, making their arguments come alive. They finish empowered as authors and advocates, ready to share their ideas for a better world.

Students use Delightex to design and build interactive 3D models of an ecosystem before and after a technological change, such as the introduction of a new machine or method. This activity spotlights how ecosystems adapt and evolve, letting students experiment with adding or removing species and technologies to see the ripple effects. For a fresh angle, students become 'virtual tour guides', recording a walkthrough of their model to explain the choices they made and the consequences for each part of the ecosystem. The final artefact is a narrated 3D ecosystem tour, ready to be shared with families or even played for a visiting environmental expert. Students harness Delightex's advanced animation and layering features to show changes over time, not just static scenes. They emerge as creative systems thinkers, confident in using digital tools to model and explain complex ideas.

Students design and build their own imaginative 'techno-bugs' using recycled materials like egg cartons, pipe cleaners, cardboard, and bottle caps, combined with simple motors or battery-powered movement kits. Each student invents a bug that could help an ecosystem (like cleaning up litter or watering plants), decorating it to show its function and role in the community. They then test and refine their bugs' movement through a collaborative, student-made habitat, reflecting on how technology and nature can work together. This project links directly to the unit's exploration of systems, change, and the impact of technology on living things.

ci: People and the planet are reliant on different energy sources.
lo: Energy types (electricity, fossil fuels, solar); Energy helps us in daily life; Energy transformation; Responsibility to conserve energy and find sustainable sources

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students become animated energy experts using the Animate from Audio feature in Adobe Express (https://new.express.adobe.com/home/tools/animate-from-audio). Each child records their voice explaining how a chosen energy source?like solar panels, wind turbines, or fossil fuels?helps people in daily life and what it looks like up close. The teacher helps students select or design a character avatar that lip-syncs to their narration, turning their explanation into a lively, talking guide. Students add labels and facts to their animated scene, making each video tour unique and personal. The final artefact is a series of animated 'virtual tours' featuring student voices and characters, ready to share at assembly or on the class blog. This process builds confidence and excitement as students see themselves as real experts, making energy concepts accessible for younger peers.

With Puppet Pals, students will script and animate a lively debate between characters who each rely on a different type of energy?imagine a solar-powered robot, a coal train, and a windmill all arguing their case! This playful storytelling approach dives into the line of inquiry about responsibility: should we keep using old energy sources or look for more sustainable ones? Students flip the script by letting one character change their mind mid-story, sparking a conversation about what makes people rethink their choices. The final product is a short, shareable animated video featuring their own voices and creative puppets, perfect for screening at a family energy night or uploading to Seesaw for parent feedback. Using Puppet Pals' custom photo import, students can turn their own artwork or classroom photos into characters and backgrounds, making each debate truly personal. By animating different perspectives, students learn that real change starts with listening?and sometimes, changing your mind.

Students will invent their own 'energy transformation machines' using Makey Makey, turning everyday objects?like fruit, foil, or playdough?into working switches that light up or make sounds. This hands-on challenge brings the idea of energy transformation to life, showing how energy moves and changes form all around us. Students take on the role of inventors at an 'Energy Fair', where they must explain to visiting teachers and families how their machine works and why it matters for a sustainable future. Their final artefact is a working interactive display, complete with a student-made info card and a demonstration video for the school website. They'll harness Makey Makey's key mapping feature to create custom controls and chain reactions, going beyond the usual banana piano. The thrill of making something physical respond to their touch gives students a sense of agency?and a new appreciation for the magic of energy in the real world.

Students use ChatterPix Kids to bring animals or plants from the St Kilda ecosystem to life, giving them a voice to share how energy and technology affect their habitat. Each student draws or photographs a local species?like a penguin, possum, or native plant?then records a short message from that organism's perspective. Using the app's mouth animation and stickers, they animate their character to explain how changes in energy use or pollution might help or harm their home. The final artefact is a gallery of talking ecosystem characters, which can be played for the class or shared with families. This activity encourages empathy and helps students connect scientific concepts to real-world impacts. By speaking as the living things they study, students deepen their understanding of adaptation and environmental balance.

Students will document a week-long 'Energy Detective' mission, snapping photos and recording voice notes about every way energy is used (or wasted) at home and school. This real-world investigation gets students thinking deeply about their responsibility to conserve energy and spot sustainable solutions in everyday life. They take on the role of sustainability reporters, interviewing family members or staff and sharing surprising energy-saving hacks discovered along the way. The final artefact is a multimedia Seesaw journal?complete with annotated photos, audio reflections, and even persuasive messages for the school newsletter?ready to inspire the wider community. Seesaw's drawing and annotation tools allow students to circle, label, and highlight the most important parts of each photo, making their detective work easy to follow. By seeing themselves as change-makers, students realise that even small actions can add up to a big difference.

Students work in teams to design and build mini playground models using cardboard, paper rolls, fabric scraps, and recycled materials, then wire up simple solar-powered circuits (with teacher support) to add moving features like spinning merry-go-rounds or seesaws. They'll test how their playgrounds work under sunlight or a lamp, exploring how solar energy powers movement. This project links energy sources and technology to real-world fun, encouraging students to consider eco-friendly designs that minimize harm to local ecosystems. The Design Cycle guides them from sketching ideas to hands-on building, testing, and sharing their solar-powered creations with classmates.

ci: To sustain life, people and environments depend on one another.
lo: Interdependence of people and environments; How people's wants and needs affect the land; Responsibility to use sustainable resources; Connection between fossil fuels and environmental impact

s.d: Students design a living map where BeeBots navigate between different habitats, collecting and delivering 'resources' to show how people and environments depend on one another. By programming routes that mimic the interdependence of ecosystems, learners explore how wants and needs can shape the land and resource use. Each student adopts the role of a local species, advocating for their own survival as BeeBots interact with environmental challenges like droughts or pollution patches. The final artefact is a collaborative, evolving map with coded BeeBot journeys, shared in a video walkthrough with Year 1 students to spark discussion about caring for natural spaces. Using BeeBots' sequence-and-repeat function, students create loops that represent sustainable resource cycles?letting them model renewal versus depletion in real time. This activity empowers young thinkers to see themselves as stewards of interconnected systems, ready to take real action in their neighbourhood.

Students invent an interactive poster that teaches others about the interdependence of people and environments, using everyday objects as touchpoints. This hands-on project explores the vital connections between humans and their ecosystems, drawing on the central idea that life depends on these relationships. To flip the script, students design their posters for the Prep classes, turning themselves into sustainability mentors for younger learners. The final product is a working poster?touch a leaf, a rock, or a water droplet and hear a student-recorded fact or story play through the Makey Makey. By wiring up their poster and programming sound triggers, students use Makey Makey's capacity to turn anything conductive into a digital button. They finish with the confidence to combine technology and creativity for real-world teaching and advocacy.

Students use Seek by iNaturalist to identify and photograph living things in the schoolyard or a nearby natural area, focusing on how people and environments depend on each other. They record which plants, insects, or birds they find and discuss how these living things contribute to a healthy environment. Students then create a visual 'web of life' showing the interdependence between people, plants, and animals, and brainstorm ways to use resources more sustainably. This activity makes the concept of interdependence tangible and encourages students to think about their responsibility to the environment. Teachers can guide students in reflecting on how their actions affect local habitats. The web of life can be displayed as part of a sustainability project.

Students create digital murals showing the impact of fossil fuels versus renewable choices on local habitats, layering before-and-after scenes in their artwork. This visual storytelling links directly to the inquiry into the connection between fossil fuels and environmental impact. Students work as environmental artists, curating a virtual exhibition to spark conversation at a class 'gallery walk' for parents and peers. Each digital mural features interactive layers?tap to reveal how a landscape changes with different human choices. Brushes Redux's layering and opacity tools allow students to overlay habitats, pollution, and restoration effects, giving them control over visual storytelling. Students leave with the creative confidence to use art and technology as a force for awareness and change.

Students program Sphero Indi cars to navigate a course representing the journey of a resource (like water or food) from its natural source to people, highlighting the steps and choices along the way. This playful coding challenge explores the interdependence of people and environments by making students think about all the stops, obstacles, and helpers a resource encounters. Acting as urban planners, students must design detours for pollution or waste, and brainstorm ways to make the journey more sustainable. The final artefact is a physical map with coded routes, where Sphero Indi cars follow colour-coded paths that students have programmed. Indi's sequence-and-repeat tiles let students build complex journeys with cause-and-effect, not just simple routes. Kids walk away with a hands-on understanding of systems thinking and how small changes can make a big difference.

Students work in teams to design and build imaginative vehicles from recycled materials?think bottle-cap wheels, cardboard chassis, and fabric flags?tasked with carrying 'precious planet resources' (represented by small objects) along a custom obstacle trail. Using simple programmable Sphero Indi cars, students attach their creations and code routes, navigating through zones themed around sustainable choices, resource sharing, and environmental challenges. This hands-on project sparks creativity and problem-solving as students prototype, decorate, and iterate on their designs, reflecting on how technology and innovation can help us move resources responsibly and care for the planet together.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Journeys can lead to challenges and new understandings.
lo: Types of journeys (physical, learning, cultural); Challenges encountered on journeys; New understandings gained through journeys

s.d: Students become time travellers, capturing immersive 360? videos of real or imagined journeys around the school or local neighbourhood to launch the theme of 'Journeys can lead to challenges and new understandings.' This hands-on experience brings the line of inquiry about 'Types of journeys' to life, as students step into the shoes of explorers, migrants, or family members moving through places past and present. By swapping their 360? journeys with a buddy class, students see how perspectives change when someone else walks your path?even if it's just around the playground or through a cultural storybook setting. The final artefact is a collection of interactive 360? videos, each annotated with student voiceovers describing obstacles, discoveries, and emotions along the way. Students use the camera's hotspot feature to embed clickable fact bubbles or questions within their virtual journey scenes. After this, students are ready to ask deeper questions about the paths people take and the new ideas they bring home.

Students compose soundscapes that represent the emotional highs and lows of different journeys?think stomping beats for tricky mountain climbs, gentle melodies for peaceful moments, and surprising sounds for cultural celebrations. This musical adventure connects directly to 'Challenges encountered on journeys' as students translate struggle, surprise, and accomplishment into music. To push creative boundaries, students swap their soundtracks with another classmate and try to guess the journey story behind each one, opening up conversations about empathy and interpretation. Their final artefact is a digital 'soundtrack gallery' played at assembly or shared with families, offering a window into how journeys feel from the inside. Students harness GarageBand's Live Loops and automation features to layer complex sounds and trigger changes that mirror turning points in their journey stories. They'll leave with a new confidence in using music to express emotion and a fresh way to tune into the stories of people on the move.

Students create vibrant digital collages that map out the steps, surprises, and special artefacts from a family or cultural journey, using photos, drawings, and found images. This brings the 'New understandings gained through journeys' line of inquiry into living colour as they sort through memories, symbols, and discoveries. Each collage is designed as a 'mystery journey' challenge for another group?peers must interpret clues and try to reconstruct the story, sparking conversations about how we decode the past. The finished collages are printed as a giant wall display or shared in a digital gallery for families to explore together. Students stretch their thinking with PicCollage's cutout tool and layered backgrounds, allowing them to blend past and present in surprising ways. The project helps students see family history and new cultures not just as stories, but as living puzzles they can piece together themselves.

Students design obstacle courses for Sphero Indi robots that represent the twists and turns of a real or imagined journey?each obstacle or colour-coded tile symbolises a challenge or learning moment. This playful coding adventure links directly to 'Challenges encountered on journeys,' as students must plan, test, and troubleshoot routes that echo the unpredictability of moving through new places or ideas. To flip the script, students invite a Year 1 buddy to try their courses and offer feedback, building leadership and communication skills. The final showcase is a 'Journey Carnival' where families and other classes race Indi through student-created paths, discovering stories along the way. Students tap into Indi's sequence-and-repeat coding to create branching choices and surprise outcomes, mirroring the unexpected nature of real-life journeys. In the end, students gain the confidence to see obstacles not as dead-ends, but as puzzles waiting to be solved.

Students become journey detectives, curating a virtual anthology of picture books and nonfiction stories from Epic that spotlight diverse personal, family, and cultural journeys. This activity shines a light on 'Types of journeys' by inviting students to compare and contrast real-life and imagined paths across places and times. To deepen the experience, students record short audio reviews recommending books to their peers, explaining what challenges and discoveries stood out most and why. Their final artefact is an interactive digital bookshelf, complete with student reviews and a 'choose your journey' reading map for families and other classes. Epic's collections and read-to-me audio feature help students access stories beyond their reading level, opening doors to new voices and experiences. Students leave with a sense of agency as book curators and a toolkit for spotting the big ideas behind every journey they encounter.

s.t: Journey Map Movers: Rolling Story Trails
s.d: Students design and build a 3D rolling map that traces a personal or family journey using large sheets of cardboard, recycled tubes, craft paper, and found materials to create mountains, rivers, and landmarks from their stories. They craft a 'journey cart' or small vehicle from bottle caps and boxes, then use simple push-and-go Sphero Indi robots to help their carts travel along the map's path. As they build, students decorate key stops with artefacts and story prompts, connecting physical movement with narrative milestones. This hands-on adventure helps students reflect on how journeys shape identity and place through collaborative making and imaginative storytelling.

ci: The way we interact with others is influenced by who we are
lo: Personal identity and strengths; How self-regulation supports learning; Building resilience through knowledge of ourselves

s.d: Kick off 'Who We Are' by inviting students to map their personal identity using Freeform, drawing, doodling and clustering words, images and emojis that show what makes them unique. This visual brainstorm directly explores the line of inquiry around personal identity and strengths, helping students see themselves as more than a list of favourites. To turn the usual sharing upside-down, let students anonymously swap their Freeform boards and try to guess whose map belongs to whom?sparking conversations about what we notice about others and ourselves. Each digital canvas becomes a vibrant, one-of-a-kind identity map, ready to display around the room or share in a class gallery walk. The Infinite Canvas feature lets children stretch, zoom and link ideas in ways paper never could, with colour-coding and sticky notes for extra flair. Students discover that their identity is layered, surprising and worthy of celebration, building confidence to express who they truly are.

Help students create their own 'calm down' audio tracks in GarageBand, composing short musical pieces designed to help manage big emotions. This activity brings the 'how self-regulation supports learning' line of inquiry to life?students literally build tools for their own resilience. Linking music with well-being, invite a local music therapist (in-person or virtually) to share how sounds can affect our mood and focus. Each student produces a personalised track or soundscape, which can be shared with classmates or played during mindfulness time. The Live Loops and sound effects library in GarageBand let even beginners experiment with layering calming beats, ocean waves or gentle melodies, making each piece feel professional. Students walk away knowing they can actively shape their emotional world?one beat at a time.

Students use ChatterPix Kids to transform a self-portrait or favourite object into a talking character that shares a personal strength or calming strategy. After snapping a photo, each child draws a mouth and records a short message, such as 'I am brave when I try new things' or 'Taking deep breaths helps me feel calm.' The app animates their voice, making the image come alive with personality and humour. These talking portraits can be compiled into a digital class gallery or played during morning meetings to spark conversations about resilience and self-awareness. ChatterPix Kids' simple interface empowers even the youngest students to become confident storytellers. The result is a joyful celebration of individuality and practical strategies for well-being, voiced by the students themselves.

Invite students to script and perform digital puppet shows in Puppet Pals, acting out scenarios where friends face tricky choices or bounce back from setbacks. This hands-on storytelling task tackles 'building resilience through knowledge of ourselves', letting children step into someone else's shoes and rehearse real-life strategies. To spark empathy, have students base their characters on a mix of their own experiences and stories collected from classmates or family. Their finished show is a lively, voiced-over video, ready for a mini film festival shared with Year 1 or shown at a school assembly. Using Puppet Pals' custom photo feature, students can insert their own faces or classroom props as characters and backdrops, making every show personal and hilarious. Through performance, students gain courage to try new solutions and see themselves as problem-solvers?not just in stories, but in everyday life.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students use the Animate from Audio feature in Animating a Character with Adobe Express (https://new.express.adobe.com/home/tools/animate-from-audio) to bring their personal strengths or calming strategies to life as talking characters. Each child records their voice sharing a tip for staying calm or a story about a time they showed resilience, then selects or customises a character to lip-sync their message. The teacher guides the process, helping students choose expressive avatars and backgrounds that reflect their personality. These animated clips can be compiled into a class 'Resilience Gallery' for families or played during circle time to spark discussion. The automatic lip-syncing makes every student feel like a confident storyteller, even if they're shy about presenting live. This activity turns self-reflection into a creative, empowering performance that celebrates each child's unique voice.

Students design and build a personalised 'Me-Bot'?a simple moving creature that represents their unique feelings, strengths, and calming strategies?using recycled boxes, craft materials, coloured paper, and markers. Each Me-Bot features a 'mood meter' dial and interchangeable face plates or accessories that students create to show different emotions or resilience strategies. Using Sphero Indi cars as the 'engines,' students test and refine how their Me-Bots move along a path they design, symbolising their personal journey and self-regulation choices. This hands-on project weaves together creative crafting and basic robotics, helping students explore and express 'Who We Are' in a playful, memorable way.

ci: Methods of communication have different features which impact their effectiveness
lo: The forms of verbal, non-verbal and visual communication; How the correct form enhances the effectiveness of a message; How people interpret messages and bring their own meaning to interactions

s.d: Students become roving reporters, recording a podcast series called 'Ways We Communicate' that dives into how people share ideas across cultures and time. This hands-on investigation brings the unit's central idea alive by comparing the effectiveness of spoken stories, interviews, and even coded messages like Morse or Braille. Each episode features students interviewing family members, staff, or community guests about the most powerful way they've ever received a message?and why it stuck. The final product is a polished podcast series, shared on the school website and with families, sparking conversations at home. Students use the podcast equipment's multi-track recording and real-time sound-mixing features to layer in music, sound effects, and even snippets of Auslan or other languages for added depth. By stepping into the shoes of real communicators, students gain the confidence to choose the right method for every message?and see themselves as voices worth listening to.

Students design a visual 'Message Decoder' poster series in Canva, exploring how colour, symbols, and layout change the meaning of a message. This creative challenge links directly to the line of inquiry about how visual communication can enhance or confuse what we want to say. To make it real, students build posters aimed at helping new students or families from different backgrounds understand school signs, emojis, or digital cues. The finished posters are displayed in the school foyer and shared digitally with the wider community, inviting everyone to consider how they interpret signs around them. Canva's 'Magic Write' feature lets students generate catchy headlines and experiment with language tone, making their posters pop. Students walk away with the power to make their own messages clearer?and a new appreciation for the hidden language all around them.

Students become silent film directors, creating short iMovie scenes that tell a story using only facial expressions, gestures, and music?no words allowed! This dramatic experiment brings the line of inquiry about non-verbal communication to life, showing how body language and sound can speak louder than speech. Students work in teams to storyboard, act, and film their stories, then swap with another group to interpret the action?sometimes with surprising results! The final silent movies are screened at a 'Red Carpet Premiere' for families and younger classes, sparking laughter and lively debate about what the actors really meant. IMovie's split-screen and picture-in-picture tools let students show two perspectives at once, or reveal a character's secret thoughts alongside their actions. By mastering the art of silent storytelling, students realise how much we say?even when we say nothing at all.

Students curate a global gallery of communication methods using Padlet, collecting examples of greetings, symbols, and gestures from around the world. This interactive wall ties into the line of inquiry about how people interpret messages and bring their own meaning to interactions. Students invite family members or friends from other countries to contribute photos or voice notes, turning the project into a living, multicultural resource. The completed Padlet is shared at assembly and linked in the school newsletter, allowing everyone to explore and comment on the diversity of communication styles. Padlet's map view feature lets students pin each contribution to its country of origin, making global connections visible at a glance. Students leave with a deeper respect for cultural differences?and the skills to decode messages wherever they go.

Students compose original soundtracks in GarageBand to express emotions or stories without using any spoken words, experimenting with tempo, instruments, and effects. This musical adventure highlights the power of non-verbal and auditory communication, directly connecting to the unit's exploration of how different forms shape the effectiveness of a message. Students swap their tracks with classmates, who interpret the mood or story and then compare notes?sometimes discovering wildly different perspectives. The final compositions are played for families and the school community at a 'Feelings in Sound' listening party, with QR codes linking to each student's artist statement. GarageBand's Live Loops feature empowers students to build complex layers and experiment with soundscapes that go beyond simple melodies. By expressing themselves through music, students learn that sometimes, a tune can say what words never could.

s.t: Secret Message Quest: Build & Break the Code Trail
s.d: Students design and construct a hands-on 'communication obstacle course' by creating physical stations?each featuring clues or challenges using different forms of coded expression, such as Morse code, Braille, pictograms, and gesture symbols. Using recycled boxes, cardboard, string, craft sticks, clay, and markers, they craft tactile puzzles or interactive props (e.g., a Braille message hidden in clay dots, a string-and-bead Morse code bracelet, or a pictogram decoder wheel). Incorporating simple robotics like Bee-Bots or Sphero Indi, students program paths that reveal or unlock hidden messages as bots travel between stations. This project immerses students in the evolution and diversity of communication, making them code-makers and code-breakers while emphasizing creativity, teamwork, and the power of expression.

ci: Ethical decision making supports online choices.
lo: How choice of action and reaction affects others online; How informed choices can make a positive difference; Our right to feel safe online and the responsibility to make ethical decisions

s.d: Students use Padlet to create a collaborative digital debate wall where they post real-life online ethical dilemmas, such as cyberbullying, privacy breaches, or digital kindness challenges. They design persuasive posts that include arguments, counterarguments, and evidence about how different online choices affect others. Using Padlet's threaded comments, students respond thoughtfully to peers, suggesting more ethical or empathetic reactions and reflecting on the impact of digital decisions. They curate a rich collection of scenarios and reflections that highlight the importance of safe and responsible online behaviour. This interactive platform encourages students to critically analyse actions and reactions in online communities, fostering their role as ethical digital citizens. The final artefact is a dynamic, peer-reviewed debate wall that showcases their understanding of ethical decision making in digital spaces.

Students will author an interactive eBook titled 'Our Rights and Responsibilities Online,' weaving together stories, advice, and digital pledges. This activity brings to life the line of inquiry around our right to feel safe online and the responsibility to make ethical decisions. Students will interview staff, classmates, or even family members about their own online choices, adding authentic voices and perspectives. The finished eBook will feature clickable pages, embedded audio interviews, and student-drawn illustrations, ready for sharing at a digital safety assembly. By using Book Creator's built-in audio recording and comic templates, students can combine narrative, dialogue, and visual storytelling in ways that make abstract values concrete. Students become advocates for digital wellbeing, building a guide that can empower the whole school community.

Students will design branching scenario games where players must navigate tricky online situations and see the consequences of their choices unfold. This directly addresses how choice of action and reaction affects others online by letting students script and visualise the ripple effects of every decision. Each group will take on the role of game designer, crafting scenarios that challenge players to weigh empathy, honesty, and safety in digital interactions. The finished product is an interactive, web-based simulation that peers and families can play, sparking real conversations about ethical decision-making. Delightex's advanced branching logic feature allows students to build complex, multi-path stories where every click matters. By stepping into the shoes of both storyteller and player, students gain a deeper appreciation for the impact of their online actions.

Students will curate a digital portfolio of 'Ethical Online Choices' moments, capturing screenshots, reflections, and even role-play videos that show both positive and negative digital behaviours. This activity brings to life the idea that informed choices can make a positive difference, as students analyse real and hypothetical online interactions. By sharing their portfolio with a buddy class in Year 2, students take on the role of digital mentors, modelling safe and respectful online conduct for younger peers. The final artefact is a multimedia journal, combining annotated images, voiceovers, and peer feedback, which can be showcased at a parent cyber safety night. Seesaw's drawing and voice annotation tools allow students to explain the 'why' behind every choice, not just the 'what'. Students develop a sense of agency as digital role models, seeing themselves as contributors to a safer online world.

Students will create and host a live Kahoot quiz on digital ethics, challenging classmates and even teachers to make quick decisions in realistic online scenarios.
