This directly supports the central idea that ethical decision-making underpins safe online choices by testing real-world judgement under time pressure. Each student team will research current online trends and dilemmas, crafting questions that spark debate and reveal hidden assumptions. The final artefact is a competitive, interactive quiz event that can be run at assembly or shared with families via a Kahoot challenge link. Using Kahoot's 'poll' and 'multi-select' question types, students can go beyond right-or-wrong answers to explore shades of grey in digital dilemmas. Students become confident facilitators and critical thinkers, realising their power to shape digital culture through thoughtful questioning.

Students design and build a vibrant, walkable 'park' using cardboard, recycled materials, and craft supplies, where each pathway represents different online choices and their outcomes. Along the paths, students place interactive QR codes (created on iPads) that link to short, student-made videos or comics about safe and ethical online behaviour. Sphero Indi cars are programmed to follow chosen routes through the park, visually demonstrating how each decision can lead to positive or negative scenarios for digital citizens. This hands-on project helps students physically map out the impact of online actions, reinforcing their responsibility to make ethical choices and keep themselves and others safe online.

ci: Materials behave and interact in certain ways, which poses challenges and solutions
lo: The three states of matter and their properties; How matter changes states depending on particles, temperature and energy; Responsible and ethical use of materials like glass and plastic

s.d: Students will step into the world of Minecraft with the 'Its Good To Be Green' lesson (https://education.minecraft.net/en-us/lessons/its-good-to-be-green) to design and explore buildings made from different materials, investigating how their choices affect a city's resilience and sustainability. This hands-on adventure lets students see firsthand how the properties of glass, plastic, and other materials shape the way communities adapt to challenges like natural disasters. Acting as eco-architects, students must balance creativity with responsibility, making tough decisions about which materials are best for people and planet. Their finished worlds will be shared as a virtual gallery, where families and other classes can tour their sustainable cities and vote on the most innovative design. Using Minecraft's Redstone circuits, students can even add working features?like automatic doors or emergency lighting?that show how materials perform in real situations. They leave with the confidence to imagine a better world and the skills to build it, brick by digital brick.

Students will become science explainers by creating animated, interactive diagrams that show how water changes between solid, liquid, and gas. This activity brings the 'three states of matter and their properties' line of inquiry to life, letting students visualise invisible particle movement and temperature effects. Each student will record a short segment as if they are reporting live from inside a raindrop, narrating what happens as it melts, evaporates, or freezes. The final product is a narrated video lesson, which can be shared with Year 2 classes as a fun way to spark curiosity in younger students. By using Explain Everything's infinite canvas and layering tools, students can animate particles and temperature arrows moving in real time. They'll walk away with the power to teach complex science ideas in ways that make sense to everyone.

Students will design bold infographics in Canva to compare how glass and plastic are made, used, and recycled, diving deep into the ethical choices behind everyday materials. This project connects directly to the unit's focus on 'responsible and ethical use of materials like glass and plastic,' challenging students to weigh up environmental impacts and community needs. Instead of just listing facts, students will take on the role of campaigners, creating persuasive posters that could convince their local council to make greener choices. Their infographics will be printed and displayed at the next school assembly, sparking real conversations about sustainability. Canva's Magic Write tool lets students generate catchy slogans and clear explanations, making their message pop. They'll finish with the creative confidence to speak up for the planet and inspire change beyond the classroom.

Students become disaster-resilience planners by building an annotated map that shows how St Kilda could prepare for hazards such as flooding, severe storms or extreme heat. They activate MapMaker's geographic layers, add plotted locations and annotate vulnerable places, including low-lying roads, parks and busy community areas. Teams then mark possible responses such as evacuation points, shaded refuges, water stations and buildings made with durable or responsibly sourced materials. Their finished GIS-style map includes a legend and concise evidence notes explaining how each proposed adaptation could protect people and places. Students compare maps to identify where material choices and city planning decisions produce different outcomes. A council-style gallery walk concludes with each team defending one priority action for a safer, more sustainable St Kilda.

Students will use Micro:bit to build simple temperature sensors, collecting real-time data as they investigate how heat changes the state of everyday materials. This activity brings the 'how matter changes states depending on particles, temperature and energy' concept into their own hands, making science visible and measurable. Students will act as lab technicians, testing materials like ice, chocolate, or wax and recording exactly when changes occur. Their data will be displayed on the Micro:bit's LED screen and then shared as a digital chart with the school science fair. By programming the Micro:bit to trigger alerts at specific temperature thresholds, students explore coding and real-world measurement all at once. They walk away knowing how to turn curiosity into evidence?and how to use technology to answer their own questions.

s.t: Matter Morphers: Transforming Transport Rescue Bots
s.d: Students design and build their own rescue vehicle using recycled materials (boxes, bottle caps, straws, fabric scraps), exploring how different states of matter (solids, liquids, gases) could affect its function during a simulated natural disaster. They'll integrate simple robotics by attaching a Sphero Indi or similar programmable base, coding it to navigate a handmade disaster obstacle course (e.g., 'flooded' zones with blue cellophane, 'earthquake' rubble from foam blocks). This hands-on project connects science concepts of matter and responsible material use with practical engineering and digital skills, challenging students to iterate their designs for real-world resilience. The result is a creative, memorable blend of physical making and tech that brings disaster adaptation to life!

ci: People can respond to natural disasters with resilience
lo: The causes and types of natural disasters (tectonic events, weather events); How natural disasters impact the environment and people; How humans respond with resilience and connection

s.d: Students bring natural disasters to life by designing interactive 3D scenes on Merge Cubes, letting them literally hold an earthquake, cyclone or flood in their hands. This hands-on AR experience gets students thinking deeply about the causes and types of natural disasters, as well as their impact on the environment and people. Imagine students working as museum curators, crafting virtual disaster exhibits for a Year 2 audience to explore in a 'pop-up' classroom event. Each student creates a cube that visually shows the disaster's progression, key facts, and a personal story of resilience from someone affected. Using Merge EDU's layered object and annotation features, students can embed audio explanations and clickable hotspots for a truly immersive experience. They walk away with the creative confidence to explain complex events in a way that younger students and families can actually see and feel.

Students become disaster investigators, using National Geographic MapMaker to plot real-world locations of recent natural disasters and trace their effects across continents. This activity dives into the line of inquiry about how natural disasters impact people and the environment, making global events feel immediate and real. Students work in teams as 'newsroom geographers', debating which disasters to feature and how to show the ripple effects on communities, wildlife and infrastructure. The final product is a collaborative, interactive map filled with annotated routes, before-and-after satellite images, and student-recorded voice notes explaining the stories behind each pin. By harnessing MapMaker's drawing, layering, and multimedia annotation tools, students go far beyond simple pins?each map becomes a living storybook of resilience. The experience gives students a sense of global connection and the power to see patterns and human stories behind the headlines.

Students become filmmakers, crafting stop-motion videos that dramatise how communities respond and rebuild after disasters like bushfires, floods, or earthquakes. This taps directly into the theme of resilience and connection, showing how people work together to recover and adapt. To add a fresh perspective, students can choose to tell their stories from the viewpoint of a rescued animal, a child evacuee, or even a community helper, exploring empathy and different experiences. The final videos, complete with voiceovers and sound effects, are screened at a 'Resilience Film Festival' for families and the school community. Stop Motion Studio's onion-skinning and frame-by-frame editing features help students create smooth, professional-looking animations that capture both chaos and hope. Students leave with storytelling skills and a new appreciation for the many ways people support each other in tough times.

Students step into the shoes of journalists, using Adobe Express to create digital front pages or mini-magazines reporting on a natural disaster and the resilient responses that followed. This project brings the 'how humans respond with resilience and connection' line of inquiry to life, as students research real events and highlight stories of hope and ingenuity. Students can choose to focus on a local disaster or one from another part of the world, sparking conversations about fairness and global responsibility. Their finished artefacts combine headlines, survivor interviews, infographics, and powerful images, ready to be shared with the school community or published in the digital newsletter. By exploring Adobe Express's Animate from Audio feature, students can turn their written interviews into animated, talking portraits for an extra layer of engagement. They finish the project with the skills to inform, inspire, and amplify voices that matter.

Students become environmental engineers, using Sketchbook to design and illustrate blueprints for disaster-resistant homes or community shelters. This creative challenge pushes students to think about how humans can minimise the effects of natural disasters, blending science, art, and empathy. To spark real-world thinking, students can compare their designs with traditional Indigenous Australian structures or famous global examples, debating what makes a building truly resilient. Their blueprints, annotated with design choices and material lists, are displayed in a virtual 'Resilient Design Expo' for families and peers to vote on. Sketchbook's symmetry and layering tools let students experiment with complex structures, cross-sections, and even overlay before-and-after scenarios. Students finish with the confidence to imagine?and communicate?practical solutions for safer, stronger communities.

s.t: Rescue Rally: Rapid Response Robot Race
s.d: Students will design and craft a model landscape featuring a community struck by a natural disaster (such as flood, earthquake, or cyclone) using recycled materials, cardboard, and craft supplies. They will then build and decorate 'rescue vehicles' (using Sphero Indi or similar simple robots) to navigate the terrain, delivering tiny relief packages to marked 'safe zones'. The project challenges students to prototype both resilient structures and clever pathways, applying their understanding of disaster impacts and community response. Through testing and refining their creations, students explore teamwork, empathy, and how innovative design helps people share and protect our planet in times of need.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Many factors shape the development of cities.
lo: The essential features of a city; The function of a city; The development of cities through time

s.d: Students become city detectives by building a layered investigation map that asks why Melbourne grew where it did and how transport, water, coastline, parks and services shaped the development of cities. Their map directly explores the essential features of a city, with each layer revealing a different factor that helps a place function for people. Students compare St Kilda with another world city and begin to notice that a tram stop, a harbour, a river or a public square can quietly change the future of a whole community. The final artefact is an annotated 'City Factors Atlas' with symbols, labels, measurement notes and short evidence captions, ready to display for families or another Year 3 class as a guided map walk. National Geographic MapMaker's layer controls, measurement tool and annotation markers let students switch city systems on and off like real urban planners testing what matters most. They leave seeing maps not as flat pictures, but as civic decision-making tools that help communities imagine fairer, smarter cities.

Students enter Minecraft Education as junior urban designers and construct two versions of the same city block: one from the past and one redesigned for a future Melbourne community. This makes the development of cities through time visible, because students must show how buildings, roads, transport, green space and services change as people's needs change. Each team receives a different citizen card, such as an elderly resident, a shop owner, a child cyclist or a visitor with a disability, so the city is judged by how well it works for more than one kind of person. The final artefact is a walkable before-and-after city model with signs explaining design decisions and a short in-world guided tour for another class. Minecraft Education's NPC characters, camera and portfolio features allow students to embed citizen voices, capture evidence and export a design record without leaving the world. Students begin to feel that city-making is not just building taller towers, but listening carefully and designing places where people can belong.

Students build a pocket 'city comfort tester' with Micro:bit to investigate how light, sound and movement patterns influence where people might want to gather in a city. The investigation deepens the function of a city by asking how streets, parks, crossings and public spaces support comfort, safety and connection. Acting as council researchers, students test different classroom 'city zones' and debate whether a place can be technically useful but still feel unfriendly to its citizens. The final artefact is a working Micro:bit prototype that displays icons or scores for calm, busy, bright or safe zones, accompanied by a class demonstration to inform a model city redesign. Micro:bit's built-in light sensor, accelerometer, LED matrix and variables let students collect simple environmental data and turn it into visible feedback. Students discover that data can give young citizens a voice in decisions about the places they use every day.

Students use Dollar Street to investigate how city life looks different when homes, streets, shops and services are viewed through the everyday objects of real families around the world. The activity examines the essential features of a city by asking which features are universal, which are unequal and which depend on history, wealth, climate or culture. Students become museum curators who choose a small set of images that challenge the idea that all cities develop in the same way or offer the same opportunities. The final artefact is a curated 'Windows into City Life' gallery, where each chosen image carries a student-written curator label comparing needs, functions and development factors for families. Dollar Street's income slider, country filters and object categories allow students to sort visual evidence by lived experience rather than by tourist landmarks. Students grow the civic habit of looking beyond skylines and asking whose city story is being seen, supported or overlooked.

Students create a living city data dashboard in Microsoft Excel to test how numbers can tell stories about why cities grow, stretch and change. Their spreadsheet investigates the development of cities through time by comparing data such as population, transport choices, green space, housing types or class survey results about what a city needs. Students take on the role of data journalists, turning raw numbers into a headline that could influence a mayor's next decision. The final artefact is a one-page interactive dashboard with tables, charts, colour-coded insights and a short written recommendation for the Wesley community or a mock city council. Excel's recommended charts, conditional formatting and sort/filter tools help students spot patterns that would be almost invisible in a list of numbers. Students learn that evidence can become a form of civic voice when it is organised clearly and used responsibly.

s.t: Time-Travel City Layers: Light-Up Mini Metropolis
s.d: Students use the Design Cycle to investigate how cities grow, then design, build, test and improve a stacked 3D 'city through time' using cardboard, popsticks, recycled packaging, clay, foil, fabric scraps and paper roads. Each layer shows a different stage of city development, such as early settlement, growing town and modern city, with essential features like homes, transport, water, green spaces, markets and community buildings. They add simple paper circuits with copper tape, coin batteries and LED lights to highlight important city functions, then compare how the lights and layouts change as needs change over time. The final build becomes a hands-on timeline model that helps students explain where people live, why cities are built, and how place changes across time.

ci: Health and wellbeing are impacted by the choices we make
lo: How our body systems connect and function; How our choices affect physical, emotional and mental wellbeing; Strategies to measure and maintain the health of the human body

s.d: Kick off the 'Who We Are' unit by letting students design and host their own Kahoot quiz about healthy choices and body systems, flipping the script so they become the experts. This activity brings the central idea?how our choices shape health and wellbeing?alive as students research, select, and debate which questions will really challenge their classmates. Invite the school nurse or a PE teacher to join as a guest player, sparking cross-campus conversation and showing students their new knowledge matters. The final artefact is a high-energy, student-led quiz event that can be shared with other classes or even families at home. Using Kahoot's question logic branching, students can create adaptive quizzes that respond differently depending on the answer, making every round unique. Students walk away with real confidence as health communicators and a sense of ownership over their learning.

Students become wellbeing campaigners by creating a series of eye-catching digital posters in Adobe Express, each spotlighting a different body system and a daily habit that keeps it healthy. This directly explores the line of inquiry into how our choices impact physical, emotional, and mental wellbeing. Challenge students to design their posters for a real audience?Year 1 students?meaning they must simplify complex ideas and use creative visuals. The finished posters are printed for display in the junior school corridor and published in a digital gallery for families. By using Adobe Express's Animate from Audio feature, students can bring their posters to life with their own recorded voices, making the information memorable and fun. They'll gain persuasive communication skills and learn how to turn science into action for younger peers.

Turn your classroom into a living wellbeing lab by having students track and reflect on their daily health choices using Padlet's timeline view. This activity supports the line of inquiry into strategies for maintaining and measuring health, as students record meals, exercise, screen time, and sleep over two weeks. For a fresh angle, students swap anonymous timelines and write encouraging feedback to each other, building empathy and practical goal-setting skills. The final artefact is a class-wide interactive timeline, full of real-life stories and tips, that can be shared at a parent open night. Padlet's timeline feature lets students see progress and patterns over time, making abstract habits visible and actionable. They'll leave with a toolkit for self-reflection and the confidence to set and reach their own health goals.

Invite students to become animated science explainers by making interactive videos in Explain Everything, modelling how different body systems work together during a favourite activity like running or dancing. This brings the line of inquiry about the connection and function of body systems to life, helping students see the body as a team rather than separate parts. Students work in pairs, taking on the role of sports commentators narrating the 'play-by-play' of what happens inside the body. Their final artefact is a narrated, interactive video that can be shared with the school community or even used as a resource in PE lessons. Explain Everything's live annotation and zoom features allow students to highlight, draw, and spotlight key moments in real time, making their explanations vivid and memorable. They'll walk away with creative confidence and a deeper understanding of how their bodies support everything they love to do.

Challenge students to curate a digital wellbeing bookshelf on Epic, selecting and reviewing fiction and non-fiction texts that explore health, emotions, and resilience. This activity supports the line of inquiry into emotional and mental wellbeing by encouraging students to see reading as a strategy for self-care and growth. Students act as librarians for a week, recommending books to classmates and justifying their choices in short video or written reviews. The final artefact is a class bookshelf with peer-reviewed recommendations, accessible to families and other classes. Epic's collection feature lets students build and share themed book lists, and the built-in quiz and review tools allow for interactive engagement. Students finish as empowered readers and wellbeing advocates, ready to support themselves and others through stories.

s.t: Body Systems Superheroes: Wearable Tech Workshop
s.d: Students design and build their own wearable 'super suit' accessories that represent and support a healthy lifestyle?think heart-rate monitor wristbands, lung-power capes, or balanced diet badges. Using recycled cardboard, felt, LED stickers, Velcro, and craft supplies, each student chooses a body system to highlight and integrates simple tech like Makey Makey or micro:bit for interactive features (e.g., a button that lights up when 'exercising'). Throughout the Design Cycle, students research their chosen system, prototype their wearable, and reflect on how their creation supports wellbeing. This project empowers students to express 'Who We Are' through imaginative, hands-on making that links body systems, wellbeing, and personal agency.

ci: The creative process involves understanding and applying artistic elements to communicate ideas and emotions across disciplines
lo: How colour, movement and music communicate character and mood; The creative process of making a multi-disciplinary presentation; The effort and commitment required to produce a live performance

s.d: Students will create unique soundscapes that express the personalities and emotions of Beijing Opera characters, exploring just how much music alone can tell a story. This activity brings to life the inquiry into how music communicates character and mood, using GarageBand as a creative playground. Imagine students collaborating as composers, debating whether a minor key or tempo shift better brings a mischievous mask to life?every choice becomes a conversation about artistic intent. The final audio tracks are showcased in an interactive listening gallery for families and younger students, challenging visitors to match sounds with character masks. Students will unlock GarageBand's automation feature to carefully fade, swell, and layer sounds for dramatic effect, moving far beyond basic loops. After this, your class won't just recognise music's mood-setting magic?they'll be confident sound designers, ready to shape emotion with every note.

Students become both directors and actors as they record and edit dramatic scenes that reveal the transformation of a character from mask design to live performance. This directly explores the creative process of blending visual arts and drama into a seamless story, as called out in the unit's central idea. By taking on film crew roles, students experience the challenge of capturing movement and emotion, just like professional filmmakers do?watching each other's rushes and offering feedback is all part of the process. The finished videos will be screened at a 'Red Carpet' celebration night, complete with popcorn and Oscars for Best Character Arc. Students will use iMovie's split-screen and picture-in-picture features to interweave rehearsal footage, backstage moments, and final performances, creating a behind-the-scenes documentary. They'll leave with a filmmaker's eye for storytelling and a new appreciation for the teamwork behind every live show.

Students curate a digital gallery of mask designs and performance ideas, inviting anonymous positive critique and suggestions from the wider school community. This taps into student agency and peer feedback, making reflection a two-way street and bringing in fresh perspectives on colour, movement, and mood. As curators, students create guiding questions for visitors, sparking discussion about artistic choices and cultural influences?suddenly, feedback becomes a living, collaborative artwork. Their Padlet will be shared with another campus, uniting creative voices across Wesley and inspiring a real sense of artistic exchange. They'll master Padlet's 'columns' feature so they can organise galleries by emotion, colour palette, or character type, helping even the youngest visitors make connections. By the end, students will see themselves as both artists and critics, ready to express their ideas clearly and receive feedback as a gift.

Students will use Sketchbook to design Beijing Opera masks, experimenting with digital brushes and colour blending to evoke specific moods and personalities. This is a hands-on dive into how colour and line communicate emotion, deepening their understanding of artistic elements. They'll play the role of professional designers, crafting mask concepts for a hypothetical modern production?pushing tradition with their own creative twists. Their digital portfolios will be displayed in a virtual exhibition, with each design accompanied by a student-voiced audio reflection. They'll use Sketchbook's symmetry and custom brush features to achieve intricate, authentic patterns that would be tricky on paper. Students will come away with a designer's toolkit for expressing ideas visually and the guts to reimagine tradition in bold new ways.

Students step into the role of set designers and performers by building immersive 3D virtual stages for their live performances, using Delightex. This activity brings the line of inquiry about the creative process of making multidisciplinary presentations to life, letting students blend visual, spatial, and dramatic thinking. They'll debate how lighting, backdrop, and digital props transform mood and character?sometimes discovering that a shadow is more powerful than a spotlight. Their finished virtual stages will be explored by families on iPads during open night, allowing visitors to 'walk' through and experience each performance space firsthand. Students will dive into Delightex's texture mapping and interactive hotspot tools, enabling them to add movement or sound triggers for a truly multi-sensory stage. They'll finish the project with the confidence to tell stories in any medium?real or virtual?and an eye for the details that make a performance unforgettable.

s.t: Mask Makers' Puppet Parade: Stories on Strings
s.d: Students design and craft vibrant, expressive puppets inspired by Beijing Opera masks and their own cultural identities using cardboard, fabric scraps, yarn, and recycled materials. They integrate simple movement mechanisms?like hinged jaws or movable arms?using popsticks, split pins, and elastic bands, then embed a micro:bit or similar device to trigger light or sound effects that match their puppet's mood. Working in teams, students script and perform short scenes that showcase how colours, movement, and digital elements communicate stories and emotions. The project fuses physical making with coding, performance, and reflection, encouraging deep exploration of personal and cultural expression.

ci: Not-for-profit organisations exist to respond to a variety of needs within our community
lo: The function and purpose of not-for-profit organisations; How not-for-profit organisations respond to community needs; Our responsibility to take action and make a difference

s.d: Students consult a teacher-created Wise Discussion chatbot using the Project Ideation scenario, meeting 'Amira Patel, a community partnerships coordinator' who challenges them to plan a realistic not-for-profit event. Teams ask questions such as 'Which roles would help our fundraiser run fairly?' and 'How could we respond if volunteers or supplies were unavailable?' They compare Amira's advice with their research into local organisations, then assign leadership, communication, finance and logistics responsibilities. Each team produces an event proposal outlining the community need, audience, resources, timeline and measures of success. They revisit the chatbot to test assumptions and refine weak parts of the plan. A class pitch session concludes with peer feedback on how responsibly and effectively each organisation could operate.

Students become investigative journalists, using Explain Everything to create an interactive documentary exploring how not-for-profit organisations operate and make a difference in Melbourne. This deep dive brings the line of inquiry about the function and purpose of not-for-profits to life, as students research real organisations and the needs they address. By interviewing a local charity worker via video call or email, students get an insider's perspective on the challenges and rewards of community action. Their final product is a dynamic, clickable presentation with embedded interviews, voiceovers, and annotated diagrams, ready to be showcased at assembly or shared with families. The magic happens with Explain Everything's live collaboration and interactive hotspots, letting students co-create and link to actual websites or donation pages. Students finish with the confidence to see themselves as active participants in their community, not just observers.

Students become advocacy designers, crafting bold infographics in Canva that spotlight the impact and inner workings of not-for-profit organisations in our community. By visually mapping how these organisations respond to community needs, students dig deeply into the line of inquiry exploring the function and purpose of not-for-profits. Each group chooses a real local charity, then interviews a staff member or volunteer via video call to capture authentic perspectives for their designs. The finished infographics are printed as giant posters for the school foyer and digitally shared with the featured organisations, giving student voices genuine reach. Canva's Magic Write tool empowers students to generate compelling copy and data visualisations that elevate their message beyond a basic poster. Every child walks away realising their creative communication can inspire real-world action and ripple outward far beyond the classroom.

Students step into the shoes of not-for-profit campaigners, using Adobe Express to design a powerful digital poster or social media story advocating for a cause they care about. This activity brings the line of inquiry about taking action and making a difference into the digital age, as students learn how visual storytelling can inspire real change. Students pair up with Year 2 buddies, teaching them about advocacy and co-creating mini-campaigns for younger audiences. The final artefact is a shareable digital campaign?animated, colourful, and ready to be displayed on the school website or sent to a partnering charity. Students unlock the Animate from Audio feature, letting their own voices narrate their message and bring their posters to life. They leave knowing how to amplify their ideas and rally others for a cause.

Students become digital connectors, building a collaborative Padlet wall that maps out all the not-for-profit organisations impacting their community and the issues they tackle. This activity shines a light on the line of inquiry about the structure and function of organisations, as students discover the web of support that exists around them. To add depth, students invite local not-for-profit representatives to leave voice notes or comments on the Padlet, creating a living, interactive resource. The final artefact is a multimedia map filled with photos, links, interviews, and student reflections, which can be shared with new families or featured at open days. Padlet's shelf view lets students organise organisations by type (e.g. Environment, health, social justice), making patterns and gaps easy to spot. By the end, students see themselves as part of a wider network, ready to spot where their own action is needed.

s.t: Pop-Up Pantry Planners: Build & Code a Community Food Network
s.d: Students design and construct a 3D model of a community food support network using cardboard, recycled boxes, string, and art supplies to represent local food banks, community gardens, delivery routes, and collection stations. Teams use Ozobots or Sphero Indi robots, programmed via color codes or block coding, to simulate the movement of food supplies between their crafted locations, solving challenges like efficient delivery and equitable access. This project immerses students in the organisational roles, teamwork, and logistics that not-for-profits use to respond to real community needs. Through the Design Cycle, students prototype, test, and refine both their physical models and robot solutions, reflecting on leadership, resource allocation, and collaborative action.

ci: Engineers design and build structures using specific features and materials to make them strong, stable and fit for purpose
lo: Different types of bridges and their design features; How materials and engineering principles contribute to structural strength and stability; Testing and refining designs through experimentation

s.d: Students become bridge engineers, designing and building their own imaginative bridges in a custom Minecraft world that challenges their understanding of strength, stability, and purpose. This hands-on digital construction directly explores how engineers use materials and design features to make structures that last. By working in teams and swapping roles as architects, builders, and testers, students experience the real-life collaboration of engineering firms. Their final product is a virtual bridge tour, complete with signs explaining their design choices and a walkthrough video to share at assembly. Using Minecraft's Redstone mechanics, students can add working drawbridges or moving parts to demonstrate engineering innovation. They leave with the confidence to see themselves as real-world problem-solvers who can shape the built environment.

Students will build and program physical model bridges using Lego Spike Prime, then test their strength and stability under load. This activity brings the line of inquiry about how engineering principles and materials affect structural strength to life. Students take on the role of design consultants, presenting their bridge solutions to a 'city council' made up of classmates and teachers. The final artefact is a functioning Lego bridge with coded sensors that trigger alerts or lights when the bridge is overloaded, showcased in a live demonstration. Spike Prime's data logging feature lets students collect and graph real-time load and stress data as weights are added. They gain a first-hand understanding of how engineers use testing and iteration to create safe, reliable structures.

Students become bridge detectives, creating interactive infographics in Canva to compare famous bridges around the world and the unique features that make each strong and stable. This investigation dives deep into the line of inquiry about different bridge types and their design features. Students must include a 'design fail'?a real bridge that collapsed?and analyse what went wrong, linking history and engineering. Their finished infographic is published to the school website and displayed at the library for families to explore. Canva's Magic Write tool helps students generate catchy headlines and clear explanations, making their work pop. They walk away with the skills to communicate complex ideas visually and a critical eye for design decisions.

Students create stop-motion animations that bring the story of a bridge's construction, testing, and refinement to life, using Stop Motion Studio. This creative project connects directly to experimenting with and improving designs through hands-on trials. Students take on the role of science communicators, scripting their animations as if they're explaining the process to a younger class or a TV audience. The final artefact is a short, narrated animation that can be screened at a whole-school STEM showcase or shared online. Stop Motion Studio's onion-skinning and voiceover features let students add smooth movement and engaging commentary, pushing their storytelling skills. They finish with a sense of pride in making engineering concepts accessible and fun for others.

Students use National Geographic MapMaker to plot the locations of iconic bridges worldwide, annotating each with its engineering features and the materials used. This mapping activity ties into the inquiry about how materials and environment influence bridge design and purpose. Students act as travel planners, recommending which bridges to visit for a 'World's Strongest Bridges' tour and justifying their choices based on geography and engineering. Their interactive map, complete with custom labels and photos, is shared with families and included in the year-level newsletter. MapMaker's annotation and layering tools allow students to compare bridge types and materials across continents in a way that's visually powerful. They leave with a global perspective on engineering and the ability to connect local learning to the wider world.

Students work in teams to design and construct model bridges using materials like popsticks, string, rubber bands, and recycled cardboard, focusing on stability and innovative structures. Once built, they mount their bridges onto a simple, student-made 'shake table' (crafted from cardboard, marbles, and rubber bands) and use an iPad to record slow-motion videos of their bridge during simulated earthquakes. Teams analyse footage to identify design strengths and weaknesses, then iterate their creations for improved resilience. This immersive project connects engineering, material science, and real-world problem-solving, making the forces that shape our world tangible and memorable.

ci: First Nations people have a deep connection to Country, language and culture
lo: The diversity of language and culture across First Nations communities in Australia; The significance of connection to Country as custodial responsibility; Listening to and learning from Indigenous perspectives

s.d: Students become digital ecologists, using the Field Guide to Victoria app to discover and profile local species that are significant to First Nations communities. Exploring the diversity of language and culture, they investigate how different animals and plants are woven into stories, art, and daily life across Indigenous nations. To deepen the experience, students act as junior rangers, creating short video field reports for a virtual exhibition shared with families and local Elders. Each group curates a multimedia species profile, blending photos, field notes, and voice recordings that highlight cultural connections to Country. By leveraging the app's interactive species identification and audio features, students can embed authentic calls or sounds into their reports. They walk away with a sense of place and a new appreciation for how deep knowledge of Country is passed down through generations.

Students author interactive digital storybooks that weave together Indigenous perspectives on water, land, and sustainability. This project invites them to listen to and retell stories from First Nations voices, exploring custodial responsibility for Country. Each student takes on the role of a cultural storyteller, crafting a narrative that could teach a younger class about respect for the environment. The final artefact is a vibrant, multimedia eBook, rich with embedded audio, video interviews, and original illustrations, ready to be showcased in the school library or shared with families. Book Creator's comic templates and audio hotspots let students layer in dialogue, soundscapes, and even language snippets from different First Nations communities. By publishing for a real audience, students gain creative confidence and a deeper respect for the wisdom held in Indigenous stories.

Students become data detectives, gathering and analysing class-wide data on water use, waste, or biodiversity in their own school environment. This hands-on investigation connects directly to the line of inquiry about how human actions impact ecosystems and how we can act as custodians. They take on the challenge of presenting their findings to the school council, advocating for a new sustainability initiative based on their evidence. Their final product is a set of dynamic, colour-coded graphs and charts that reveal patterns and spark real conversations about change. Using Excel's conditional formatting and chart creation tools, students turn raw numbers into persuasive visual stories. They finish the project with a sense of empowerment?knowing their voice, backed by data, can help protect Country.

Students create reflective audio journals in Seesaw, capturing their evolving thoughts as they learn from Indigenous guest speakers, virtual excursions, and class discussions. This activity embodies the line of inquiry about listening to and learning from Indigenous perspectives. Students step into the shoes of environmental journalists, recording questions, insights, and 'aha' moments to share with a partner class in another part of Australia. The finished artefact is a timeline of voice recordings, photos, and drawings, easily shared with families and even local community members. Seesaw's voice annotation and timeline features allow students to layer personal reflection with images and text, making their learning journey visible and meaningful. They leave with stronger listening skills and a deeper understanding of how stories shape our connection to Country.

Students become cultural geographers, using National Geographic MapMaker to create annotated digital maps showing the diversity of First Nations languages and cultural regions across Australia. This hands-on mapping task brings to life the line of inquiry about the incredible diversity of language and culture within Indigenous communities. To broaden their perspective, students compare their maps with those from other classes and discuss why boundaries and names might differ depending on whose story is told. The final artefact is an interactive, layered map with custom markers, pop-up facts, and embedded links to stories or language samples, ready for display at a school assembly. MapMaker's drawing, annotation, and layering tools let students build maps that are as rich and complex as the cultures they represent. They finish with a new respect for the importance of place, perspective, and the living legacy of Country.

s.t: Water Wise Wonderland: Interactive Creek Quest
s.d: Students design and build a flowing creek ecosystem using cardboard, recycled materials, natural elements (pebbles, sticks, leaves), and craft supplies, creating habitats for native animals and plants. They embed Ozobot robots decorated as 'water droplets', programming them to travel along painted or marker-drawn water pathways, simulating the journey of water through different habitats and human interventions (like dams, pollution, wetlands). Along the route, students engineer interactive features?liftable floodgates, filtering stations, and bridges?using simple mechanisms and recycled parts. This hands-on project blends environmental science, First Nations water knowledge, and creative engineering, helping students understand sustainable water management and the importance of caring for waterways.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Exploration and discovery have led to changes that shape the world we live in
lo: The age of exploration and the reasons explorers set out on their journeys; How Australia changed through European arrival; Different perspectives on the consequences of exploration

s.d: Students will design and code interactive 3D artefacts that bring to life a moment of exploration or first contact, viewable in their hands using Merge Cubes. This hands-on AR experience immerses students in the line of inquiry on 'different perspectives on the consequences of exploration', as they visualise both Indigenous and European viewpoints. Students step into the role of museum curators, crafting digital objects that can 'tell' their own stories when viewed by classmates or families at home. Each student's final artefact is a shareable AR object complete with embedded text, audio, or images, transforming a static cube into a mini time-capsule of Australian history. Using Merge EDU's embedded 3D annotation tools, students can layer explanations and alternate perspectives directly onto the surfaces of their digital cubes, revealing new depths with every rotation. This empowers students to become creators of immersive historical narratives, building empathy and digital storytelling skills that reach beyond the classroom walls.

Students will become time-travelling radio hosts, producing a podcast series called 'Explorers' Debates' where they interview characters from both European explorer and Indigenous perspectives. This directly addresses the line of inquiry about different viewpoints on the consequences of exploration, inviting students to wrestle with fairness, change, and cultural impact. To deepen the experience, students can invite local elders or historians as guest voices, blending real community connections with their creative scripts. The finished podcasts are published on the year level's online hub, ready for families and the wider school to tune in. Advanced use of the podcasting equipment's multi-track recording lets students layer interviews, sound effects, and music for a polished, professional sound. Students walk away with the power to amplify unheard voices and the skills to tell complex stories in their own words.

Students will design and 3D-model artefacts or tools inspired by those used during the age of exploration, from navigation instruments to symbolic Indigenous objects. This taps into the line of inquiry about how exploration led to technological and cultural change, letting students see how invention shaped lives. Students swap digital designs with a partner and annotate each other's work from a different perspective?European or Indigenous?highlighting how meaning and usefulness shift with context. The final artefact gallery is shared as a virtual showcase, with interactive 3D models and student voice explanations embedded for the community to explore online. Tinkercad's 'Send To' feature allows students to export their models for AR viewing, so families can place artefacts in their own lounge rooms. Students finish with creative design confidence and a sense of how technology and culture intertwine.

Students step into the shoes of early explorers and Indigenous Australians by designing immersive 3D scenes that capture pivotal moments of encounter and change in Australian history. By actively shaping environments that reflect different perspectives on the consequences of European exploration, they grapple with the complexities of the line of inquiry around multiple viewpoints. Each group takes on the role of museum curators, crafting virtual exhibition rooms where visitors experience the emotions, challenges, and hopes of people from the Age of Exploration?including both explorers and those whose worlds were transformed. Their final artefact is a walkable, interactive 3D space that can be toured by peers and families, offering an emotional and spatial journey through key moments of discovery and cultural collision. Delightex's collaborative multi-user editing allows students to co-construct their scenes in real time, layering soundscapes, historical artefacts, and dialogue for a richer, more authentic experience. This process fosters empathy, critical thinking, and a sense of agency as students become storytellers who bridge the past and present through digital creativity.

Students use Explain Everything to create interactive timelines that trace key events and figures from the age of exploration, such as voyages by European explorers and Indigenous responses to these encounters. They design slides combining images, maps, and text annotations to show causes and effects of exploration on Australia's landscape and peoples. Using the app's drawing and voice recording features, students narrate different perspectives, including those of explorers and Indigenous leaders, fostering empathy and critical thinking. They embed questions and prompts on slides to encourage peer discussion and reflection about fairness and cultural impact. The final product is a multimedia timeline presentation that captures the complexity of exploration and discovery. Students share their timelines with classmates for collaborative review and debate, deepening understanding through interactive storytelling.

s.t: Exploration Adventure Automata: Moving Moments Diorama
s.d: Students work in teams to design and build a kinetic diorama that brings a key moment from the Age of Exploration or early Australian encounters to life. Using recycled cardboard, popsticks, gears, cams, craft materials, and simple motors or hand-cranked mechanisms, they create a scene where explorers, Indigenous peoples, and landscapes physically move to tell their story. Students integrate a micro:bit (or similar) to trigger sound effects or light signals that enhance the narrative, blending historical research with creative engineering. This project encourages deep understanding of multiple perspectives and the impact of exploration, while making history literally move before their eyes.

ci: Leaders can help a group to function effectively
lo: Roles and responsibilities of effective leadership; Purpose of leadership; The strengths and qualities of a leader

s.d: Students use Padlet to create a collaborative leadership debate wall where they post questions, arguments, and examples about what makes a group function effectively. They design posts exploring roles and responsibilities, leadership qualities, and ethical challenges leaders face, using Padlet's multimedia features to embed images, short videos, and links to biographies of famous leaders. Students respond to peers' posts with evidence-based comments, building a dynamic conversation that deepens their understanding of leadership purpose and impact. This interactive platform encourages critical thinking as students challenge ideas and propose alternative leadership approaches. The final artefact is a rich, threaded discussion that captures diverse perspectives on leadership strengths and challenges. Teachers can export the Padlet as a PDF or share the live wall for whole-school assemblies or newsletters.

Students become biographers, crafting interactive digital books that profile inspiring leaders from their community or the world. This ties directly to exploring the strengths and qualities that make a leader effective. Students are encouraged to include interviews with family members or local leaders, turning their books into living documents that connect classroom learning to real lives. The finished books feature audio recordings, video clips, and clickable timelines, making them perfect for sharing with families or at a school exhibition. Book Creator's embedded multimedia and comic strip templates let students blend storytelling and factual research in creative ways. By the end, students see themselves as authors with a voice, able to recognise and celebrate leadership qualities in others?and maybe themselves.

Turn the classroom into a leadership quiz show, where students design and host their own Kahoot games about the roles and responsibilities of leaders in different settings. This hands-on approach lets them dive into the nuances of leadership roles, testing not just memory but the ability to think on their feet. For a fresh angle, students swap roles with teachers or even invite parents to play, flipping the traditional classroom dynamic. Their final product is a custom Kahoot quiz with scenario-based questions and real-time feedback, which can be shared with other classes or uploaded to the school intranet. Kahoot's advanced question logic and poll features allow students to create branching scenarios?'What would you do if...?'?that spark lively discussion. Students leave with the confidence to lead, question, and collaborate, knowing their ideas can energise a whole group.

Students become campaign managers, designing vibrant digital posters that champion the leadership qualities they believe matter most?creativity, empathy, resilience, or something entirely their own. This creative project links beautifully to the line of inquiry about the strengths and qualities of a leader. To make it real, students pitch their posters to a panel of younger students, collecting feedback and revising their message for maximum impact. The final artefacts are eye-catching, animated posters using Adobe Express's Animate from Audio feature, ready to be displayed on digital screens around the school. By exploring advanced animation and voiceover tools, students learn to communicate a message powerfully and persuasively. They walk away knowing how to inspire others with their vision and how digital media can amplify their voice.

Invite students to co-design a 'Leadership Village' in Minecraft Education, where each group builds a community structure (like a council hall, school, or sports club) and defines the leadership roles needed for it to thrive. This immersive build connects to the purpose of leadership and how different roles help a group function effectively. Students rotate leadership positions within their Minecraft teams each session, reflecting on how different styles and decisions shape the group's success. Their finished world is a collaborative Minecraft map with signposted leadership stories and challenges for visitors to try, which can be toured by other classes or parents. Using Minecraft's in-game camera and book-and-quill tools, students document leadership dilemmas and solutions as part of the village tour. They gain hands-on experience in teamwork, flexibility, and seeing how leadership isn't about one 'boss', but about helping everyone shine.

Students design and construct a 3D maze representing their unique leadership journey, using cardboard, recycled boxes, string, and craft materials to build pathways and obstacles that symbolise personal strengths and challenges. They then code a Sphero Indi or similar robot to navigate the maze, with each section representing a leadership quality or decision point. Students decorate their maze with symbols, photos, and words that reflect their identity and leadership style, creating a physical and digital narrative of 'Who We Are'. The project integrates hands-on building, creative self-expression, and basic coding, making leadership personal, memorable, and interactive.

ci: Social norms and stereotypes can influence the way people express themselves
lo: How stereotypes and social norms form and persist in society; The impact of discrimination, prejudice and assumptions on individuals and communities; How people overcome stereotypes to express themselves and inspire change

s.d: Students become digital myth-busters by unearthing everyday stereotypes and social norms through a collaborative Padlet wall. Tackling the question of how stereotypes form and persist in society, they hunt for examples in media, sports, fashion and even their own schoolyard. To flip the script, they anonymously post moments when they or someone they know broke a stereotype, and then comment on each other's experiences from fresh perspectives. The end result is a living, interactive gallery of stories, images and voices that challenge assumptions and spark debate?not just a static list. Padlet's colour-coded columns and comment threads make it easy to track which social norms get challenged most and which voices spark the biggest conversations. Students leave with the courage to recognise, question and reshape the invisible rules shaping our world.

Students design a series of bold digital posters that expose, challenge, or flip stereotypes using Canva. This ties directly into the impact of discrimination, prejudice and assumptions on individuals and communities, giving students a visual voice. Each group takes on a real-world audience?posting their best designs in the school foyer or online, inviting peers and families to vote for the poster that inspires the most change. The finished posters burst off the screen with striking images, slogans and even QR codes linking to personal stories or action ideas. Students experiment with Canva's Magic Write to brainstorm edgy slogans, then perfect their layouts using the background remover and animation features. This process empowers students to turn frustration into creative activism, and to see themselves as change-makers, not just bystanders.

Students step into the studio as podcast hosts, interviewing classmates, family members or community figures about times they've overcome stereotypes to express themselves. They dig into the line of inquiry about how people push through barriers and inspire change, learning to ask questions that reveal hidden stories and unexpected journeys. Students research a public figure who broke a social norm and create a 'mini documentary' episode, blending their own narration with real interviews. The resulting podcast series can be shared via the school website or played at assembly, amplifying voices that might otherwise go unheard. They master advanced audio editing on the school's podcast equipment, layering in soundscapes, music, and voice effects to make each episode shine. Students walk away knowing how to give others a platform?and how to tell their own story with confidence.

Students become 'identity inventors' by designing a 3D symbol or wearable badge in Tinkercad that celebrates a part of themselves that defies stereotypes. This activity directly explores the line of inquiry about how people overcome assumptions to express who they really are. For an extra layer, students swap designs anonymously and reflect on what the symbol says about identity and belonging, sparking empathy and new conversation across the year level. Their final 3D creations can be printed and worn, displayed, or gifted to someone they think needs a confidence boost. Tinkercad's Shape Generator lets students combine unexpected forms and engrave empowering words or images, pushing their design thinking beyond the obvious. They leave with not just a badge, but a deeper sense of pride in what makes them?and everyone else?unique.

Students become virtual exhibition curators, building immersive 3D museum rooms in Delightex that showcase how artists, activists or everyday people have challenged stereotypes through their words and actions. By diving into how social norms are formed and broken, they curate digital artefacts?artworks, video clips, quotes, or recreated objects?that tell a story of change. They take on the real responsibility of designing an experience for the public, inviting parents or another year level to 'walk through' their virtual space and leave feedback. The completed exhibitions become interactive journeys, where visitors click on hotspots to unlock hidden stories or questions that prompt deeper reflection. Delightex's multi-user collaboration allows students to co-design in real time, debating which stories deserve the spotlight and how to spark curiosity. Students finish with the skills to shape narratives, challenge assumptions, and make their voice felt in both digital and physical spaces.

s.t: Wearable Voices: Message Maker Fashion Lab
s.d: Students design and construct expressive wearable art pieces?such as hats, capes, or badges?using recycled fabrics, LEDs, conductive thread, and simple microcontrollers (like Micro:bit or Circuit Playground Express). Each wearable broadcasts a personal or social message through patterns, scrolling text, or light effects coded by the students, reflecting their identities or challenging stereotypes. The project fuses hands-on sewing, crafting, and circuitry with digital coding, empowering students to literally 'wear' their stories and beliefs. The final showcase invites peers to decode each other's wearable messages, deepening understanding of how fashion and tech can be powerful tools for self-expression.

ci: Goods and services are exchanged within a marketplace
lo: The production of goods from raw materials through manufacturing to consumer; The exchange of currency for goods and services in a functioning economy; Ethics and responsible decision-making in the marketplace

s.d: Students become economic detectives by mapping out the journey of a product from raw material to store shelf using Explain Everything's interactive whiteboard. This brings to life the unit's exploration of how goods are produced, manufactured, and finally reach consumers. Instead of just learning, students play the part of investigative journalists, interviewing 'stakeholders' (played by classmates) at each stage?farmer, factory worker, truck driver, shopkeeper. The finished result is an animated, voice-narrated storyboard video that follows one everyday item (like a chocolate bar or t-shirt), with each student narrating a different stage. By layering video, hand-drawn sketches, and voiceover on Explain Everything's timeline feature, students can create dynamic, branching stories instead of a flat presentation. They finish the project seeing how every simple purchase is part of a much bigger web?and that they have the power to ask better questions about where things come from.

Challenge students to step into the shoes of ethical entrepreneurs by designing a live Kahoot quiz called 'Would You Buy It?' that tests classmates on tricky real-life marketplace dilemmas. This tackles the unit's deep question about ethics and responsible decision-making in the marketplace. Students can consult with a local business owner or school canteen manager to get real examples of dilemmas?like choosing cheaper packaging versus eco-friendly packaging. The final artefact is a student-designed, rapid-fire Kahoot quiz, complete with images, explanation slides for each answer, and built-in discussion prompts for each scenario. By using Kahoot's question randomiser and poll features, students can spark debate and see how opinions shift in real time. They end up not only thinking about what they would do, but also realising that the 'right' answer in the marketplace is often more complex than it seems.

Invite students to create a digital 'Marketplace Guidebook' in Book Creator, where each page profiles a different currency, trade tradition, or marketplace from around the world. This directly explores the unit's line of inquiry into the exchange of currency for goods and services in diverse economies. Students act as travel writers, sharing marketplace stories or interviews from family heritage or overseas friends, making the guidebook truly global. The finished artefact is a multimedia ebook, with audio recordings, hand-drawn diagrams, and clickable links to short video interviews or local market sounds. By using Book Creator's embedded audio and video recording features, each student's page becomes a vibrant, sensory experience?far beyond just text and pictures. Students finish with a tangible sense of how different cultures organise trade, and the confidence to think globally about money, value, and fairness.

Students turn into delivery robots, coding Sphero BOLT to navigate a mini 'city' marketplace and simulate the path goods take from warehouse to consumer. This hands-on activity models the organisation and flow of goods and services within a functioning economy, as outlined in the unit. Layer in some maths by challenging students to optimise their robot's delivery route for time and distance, or to avoid 'traffic jams' and obstacles representing real-world supply chain hiccups. The final artefact is a recorded Sphero journey?complete with route maps, time trials, and a student-created 'delivery log' explaining every decision. Sphero's live data streaming and sensor graphing let students compare routes and tweak their code for maximum efficiency. By the end, students don't just understand how goods travel?they've experienced the thrill (and frustration!) of running a real supply chain.

Students become global trade cartographers by building detailed, annotated maps of historical and modern trade routes using National Geographic MapMaker. This fuels their inquiry into how goods and services are exchanged within marketplaces across time and cultures. Students can take on the role of museum curators, preparing a map-based exhibit for a school open night, complete with stories and artefacts about the journeys of key products. Their end product is an interactive, layered map featuring student-made icons, pop-up facts, and lines tracing the flow of spices, gold, or tech gadgets. MapMaker's layering and annotation tools empower students to visualise overlapping routes and the ripple effects of trade?like cultural exchange and resource scarcity. Students leave with real mapping skills and the ability to tell big stories with place and movement, not just words.

s.t: Supply Chain Showdown: The Automated Assembly Line Challenge
s.d: Students work in teams to design and build a miniature, multi-stage assembly line using recycled materials, cardboard, LEGO, and simple robotics (such as Sphero Indi or Ozobot) to transport and transform 'products' across stations. Each team creates stations (e.g., manufacturing, packaging, quality control, distribution) with physical mechanisms like ramps, levers, conveyor belts (rubber bands, popsticks, pulleys), and programs robots to move goods between them. Students must budget for materials, negotiate resource trades with other teams, and reflect on ethical dilemmas (e.g., fair wages, sustainable sourcing) as their assembly line grows. This hands-on project brings economic systems, supply and demand, and marketplace ethics to life through dynamic prototyping and collaborative problem-solving.

ci: Inventions and initiatives are a response to the changing needs of society
lo: How inventions have changed over time to meet the demands of society; The UN Sustainable Development Goals and the global problems they address; Using the design thinking process to create innovations that respond to real-world needs

s.d: Students become curators in Minecraft's Hall of Inventions (https://education.minecraft.net/en-us/challenges/the-hall-of-inventions), where they explore a virtual museum, discover gaps in history, and then design and build their own invention to fill a missing spot. This hands-on world launches the big idea that inventions are always a response to changing needs, directly linking to how innovations evolve over time. To shake things up, students invite a real-world inventor or grandparent to visit their virtual museum and offer feedback on their creations. Their final artefact is a fully realised 3D invention, complete with a digital plaque explaining the social need it answers, ready for a virtual showcase to the school community. The lesson leverages Minecraft's in-game Book & Quill, letting students write and embed detailed origin stories for their inventions right inside the world. Students leave with the confidence to see themselves as inventors who can shape the future, not just study the past.

Armed with Micro:bits, students become energy detectives, gathering real data about electricity use around the school and brainstorming ways to make Wesley more sustainable (https://microbit.org/teach/lessons/?selected=energy-awareness). This activity brings the UN Sustainable Development Goals to life, challenging students to use technology to address global problems like energy consumption. Students take on the role of sustainability consultants, presenting their findings and recommendations to the campus facilities team. The final artefact is a set of interactive data visualisations and prototype energy-saving devices, showcased at the Future Thinkers' Forum and shared with the wider school. By using the Micro:bit's data-logging feature, students can collect, process, and analyse real-time energy data?a step beyond simple coding. They walk away knowing they can use technology to spot problems and take action for a greener world.

Students become innovation storytellers by crafting animated explainer videos in Adobe Express, each one spotlighting a breakthrough invention and the social challenge it addressed. This directly explores how inventions have changed over time to meet society's evolving demands. Students work in pairs to 'remix' their videos for a younger audience?Year 2 or 3?making big ideas accessible and fun. The finished product is a polished, voice-narrated animation, complete with dynamic transitions and custom illustrations, which can be screened at assembly or shared with families online. Students harness the 'Animate from Audio' feature to bring their narration to life with expressive, AI-powered character movement. They leave the unit with the confidence to explain complex ideas clearly and creatively to any audience.

Students step into the shoes of real-world engineers, designing and programming a Lego Spike Prime robot to solve a challenge linked to the UN Sustainable Development Goals?like building a prototype for cleaning up ocean plastic or transporting clean water. This hands-on build connects directly to the inquiry into using the design thinking process to create innovations for real-world needs. Students swap roles and become judges, evaluating each other's solutions for effectiveness and creativity, just like a panel at Shark Tank. Their final artefact is a working robotic prototype, demonstrated live at the Future Thinkers' Forum, with a short pitch explaining the problem it solves. By using Spike Prime's data-logging and sensor integration features, students can test, tweak, and optimise their designs based on real performance feedback. They finish with not just a model, but the problem-solving mindset and teamwork skills of tomorrow's inventors.

Students author interactive digital books in Book Creator, each one tracing the journey of an invention from its earliest origins to its modern-day impact. This project ties directly to the inquiry into how inventions evolve to meet society's changing needs. Students take on the perspective of a time-travelling reporter, interviewing 'inventors' from different eras and weaving in voices from both history and the future. The final artefact is a multimedia eBook, packed with audio interviews, clickable timelines, and embedded video demonstrations, published to the school library's digital shelf. By using Book Creator's comic templates and audio hotspots, students can make their stories truly immersive and accessible to all readers. They leave knowing how to combine research, creativity, and technology to bring history?and their own ideas?to life.

s.t: Inventors' Circuit Carnival: Power Up Your Problem-Solver
s.d: Students design and build imaginative, hands-on carnival games that solve a real-world challenge (e.g., recycling, clean water, renewable energy) using a mix of recycled materials, cardboard, motors, LEDs, and conductive tape. They sketch ideas, prototype physical game mechanisms, and wire up simple circuits with Makey Makey or micro:bit boards to add interactive features like buzzers, lights, or digital scoring. Throughout the process, students follow the design cycle to iterate and improve their inventions, learning how past innovations inspire creative solutions for today. The final 'Circuit Carnival' lets students showcase and explain their powered-up games, linking invention, play, and the impact of design on society.

ci: Communities interact with the environment in different ways
lo: How community values shape the management of the natural environment; The need for conservation and environmental stewardship; Ways in which First Nations land management practices can drive positive environmental change

s.d: Students will step into a sustainable building in Minecraft and explore what makes it eco-friendly, using this immersive world as a launchpad to rethink how communities interact with their environment (https://education.minecraft.net/en-us/lessons/its-good-to-be-green). This hands-on adventure brings to life the line of inquiry about how community values shape the management of the natural environment, letting students see green design in action. They'll take on the role of sustainability consultants, debating the merits of different features and proposing changes to improve the building's impact. Their final artefact is a virtual guided tour, where each group records a walk-through of their upgraded design, narrating the environmental choices they made. By using Minecraft's in-game camera and book-and-quill, students create illustrated digital field guides to share with families and other classes. Students finish with the confidence to spot ? and suggest ? sustainable solutions in the real world, not just in the digital one.

Students become local biodiversity detectives, investigating native plants and animals in their own neighbourhood using the Field Guide to Victoria app. This activity puts the spotlight on the need for conservation and environmental stewardship, as students uncover which species are thriving and which need protection. They'll connect with a local Landcare or Indigenous ranger via video call, learning first-hand how traditional and modern knowledge combine to care for Country. The final product is a digital field guide entry ? complete with photos, species facts, and a 'threats and actions' section ? published to a class website or printed for the school library. The app's advanced 'compare species' feature lets students spot subtle differences between similar animals, deepening their observation skills. Students walk away as citizen scientists, ready to advocate for the living things that share their place.

Students will script and animate a stop-motion story that shows how First Nations land management practices can drive positive environmental change. This creative task brings to life the line of inquiry about Indigenous perspectives on stewardship, letting students visualise cultural burning, seed dispersal, or waterway care through hands-on storytelling. They'll work in small groups, each taking on the role of filmmaker, narrator, and set designer, and consult with local Indigenous resources to ensure cultural respect and accuracy. The finished artefact is a short stop-motion film, complete with voiceover and sound effects, premiered at a school 'Film Festival for Country'. By using Stop Motion Studio's onion-skinning and frame-by-frame editing, students can craft smooth, expressive animations that rival professional shorts. This experience gives students the creative confidence to tell powerful stories about real-world change.

Students will design and 3D model their own conservation toolkit ? a set of imaginative, student-invented devices that communities could use to protect local habitats. This hands-on engineering challenge dives into the line of inquiry around conservation and environmental stewardship, asking how technology and creativity can support sustainable action. Acting as real-world inventors, students will pitch their toolkit ideas to local experts or First Nations community members for feedback, considering whose needs are being served. Each toolkit is rendered as a full-colour, labelled 3D model with moving parts or modular elements, ready to be showcased in a virtual exhibition for families and the school community. Leveraging Tinkercad's built-in Circuit Assemblies and hinge functions, students can prototype interactive elements (like a sensor-based animal deterrent or a foldable seed spreader) directly within their digital designs. By imagining themselves as problem-solvers whose work could make a tangible difference, students grow as empowered stewards of the environment.

Students will design and build interactive 3D models of local habitats using Merge Cubes, letting classmates explore ecosystems from every angle in augmented reality. This hands-on creation links to the central idea by showing how communities ? human and non-human ? interact with their environment in complex ways. Students become museum curators, adding pop-up facts about threats, species relationships, and human impacts, then challenge visitors to spot hidden connections. The final artefact is a virtual 'Habitat Cube Exhibition', where families and other classes can scan and explore the models using iPads. Merge Cube's custom annotation and layering features let students embed sound bites, quizzes, and video, making each model a multi-sensory learning hub. Students finish with a sense of pride in their ability to bring invisible worlds to life ? and inspire others to care.
