Teachers help children arrange their photos side-by-side, adding stickers, speech bubbles, or simple captions to highlight what has changed. During a gallery walk, siblings or older buddies play 'photo detectives'?guessing which current photo matches each baby photo. The finished collages are displayed at transition events for the school community, sparking conversations about growth and identity. Children walk away with a sense of pride in their journey and the realisation that change is something to celebrate.

Children will bring their favourite toy or comfort object to life, giving it a talking mouth with ChatterPix Kids and recording a message about starting prep or learning something new. This playful activity taps into the experience of life transitions, helping children process big emotions through imaginative role-play. By flipping the perspective?letting the toy give advice or encouragement?kids find it easier to voice their own hopes and worries. The finished artefact is a class video montage of talking toys, shared with families and next year's kinder group to support others facing similar changes. ChatterPix Kids' animated mouth feature lets even the shyest child see their words come alive in a safe, silly way. Children discover that their feelings are normal and that they can help others with their stories.

Children will create digital self-portraits on Brushes Redux, layering colours and shapes to show how their identity has changed from babyhood to now. This creative process connects to discovering who we are through our experiences, as kids reflect on new skills, friendships, and interests. To spark deeper thinking, teachers prompt children to add 'future me' layers?drawing themselves as they imagine growing up or starting school. The final artwork is printed as a fold-out 'Me, Then, Now, and Next' booklet for each child to take home. Brushes Redux's layering function allows kids to toggle between different stages of their self-portraits, making change visible and exciting. Children leave with a sense of continuity and optimism about who they are becoming.

Children will embark on a story adventure using Book Creator, choosing from a selection of picture books about change, family, and growing up to read aloud as a class. After listening, each child draws or dictates a page about a special memory or a time they felt brave during a change, which teachers help add to a collaborative digital class book. Families are invited to contribute a photo or story from their own childhoods, building a shared digital bookshelf that celebrates diversity and belonging. The class book is published as a QR code poster for the family picnic, so everyone can explore the stories together. Book Creator's audio recording and drawing tools mean even pre-readers can participate fully, adding their voice or illustrations. Children gain empathy, vocabulary, and the comfort of knowing that everyone experiences change in their own way.

s.t: Journey Jars: My Story in a Bottle
s.d: Children will create their own 'Journey Jar' by decorating a large plastic jar or bottle with fabric scraps, tissue paper, and stickers to represent their personal story. Inside, they will place soft, tactile objects like cotton balls, ribbon pieces, and photos (or drawings) of important moments, people, and places in their lives. Using a Bee-Bot, children will then create a simple map on a large mat, guiding the robot from one jar to another to share and hear each other's stories. This hands-on project helps children explore their identity, life transitions, and sense of belonging through creative building and collaborative storytelling.

ci: People express themselves in diverse ways, shaped by their imagination, culture, and personal experiences.
lo: How imagination and creativity influence the ways we express ideas; How materials and techniques help us share personal and cultural experiences; How we interpret and respond to expressions from ourselves and others

s.d: Children invent playful sound sculptures by connecting everyday objects?like fruit, playdough, or foil shapes?to a Makey Makey board, turning them into touch-activated musical instruments or storytelling buttons. With teacher guidance, each child chooses objects that represent their favourite things or family traditions, then records a short sound, word, or song to match. As classmates tap each object, they hear a burst of laughter, a greeting in a home language, or a snippet of a favourite tune, sparking conversations about how sound and touch can express who we are. The interactive soundboard is set up for families to explore during pick-up, letting children proudly demonstrate their inventions. Makey Makey's simple alligator clips and conductive materials make the magic feel tangible and accessible. Children leave with a sense of wonder at how technology can turn their ideas and memories into something everyone can experience.

Children become storytellers by acting out their favourite cultural tale or home tradition, while the teacher records short video snippets using Seesaw. This activity brings the line of inquiry 'how materials and techniques help us share personal and cultural experiences' to life through dramatic play. Families are invited to send in special objects or costumes from home, so children can see how their own backgrounds add colour to the class story. The final video playlist is shared privately with families, sparking conversations at home about culture and creativity. Seesaw's drawing-on-video feature lets children add colourful marks or stickers to their scenes, making every performance pop with personal flair. Children gain confidence in sharing who they are, and learn that everyone's story is worth celebrating.

Children explore the textures and colours of their world by collecting natural materials?leaves, pebbles, petals?and arranging them into creative patterns, which the teacher photographs and uploads to PicCollage. This hands-on activity connects to the line of inquiry about how materials and techniques help us share experiences, as children discover how arranging real objects can tell a story or express a feeling. Children vote on a theme for each collage?like 'joy', 'family', or 'my favourite place'?and discuss how different choices change the mood. The finished collages become a digital gallery, sent home to families and displayed on the classroom screen. PicCollage's cut-out tool lets the teacher crop each child's arrangement into playful shapes, highlighting their creative decisions. Children walk away seeing that expression can start with their own hands and the treasures they find outdoors.

Children experiment with Brushes Redux by mixing digital paints and using their fingers to create swirling, colourful self-portraits. This links directly to exploring how imagination and creativity influence the ways we express ideas, as children choose wild colours or shapes to show how they feel inside. For a fresh angle, children swap portraits and guess each other's emotions or stories, learning how art can be interpreted in many ways. The final digital gallery is printed as a class book for the art corner and shared as a slideshow with families. Brushes Redux's layering feature lets the teacher help children add backgrounds or patterns behind their faces, making every portrait a burst of personality. Children discover that art can be a window into both themselves and their friends.

Children bring their clay sculptures or painted creatures to life by giving them a voice with ChatterPix Kids, recording a short message or song that matches their creation's personality. This joyful activity explores how we interpret and respond to expressions from ourselves and others, as children imagine what their artwork might say if it could talk. To mix things up, the class votes on which sculpture should tell the day's story, and children listen for feelings or messages in each other's recordings. The final talking-art video is played at assembly or sent home, letting families hear the magic too. ChatterPix Kids' sticker and filter features let the teacher add silly hats or backgrounds, making every creation even more unique. Children leave with the confidence that their ideas can leap off the page and make others smile.

Children design and craft their own unique puppets using socks, fabric scraps, felt, yarn, buttons, and paper cups, expressing their feelings, stories, and cultural backgrounds through imaginative character creation. With teacher support, they use a simple programmable Bee-Bot as a 'parade leader,' decorating a large parade path on the floor with colourful paper, markers, and collage materials. Each child programs the Bee-Bot to guide their puppet along the parade route, introducing their character and sharing a story or feeling as their puppet 'marches.' This playful project blends hands-on making with basic robotics, celebrating diverse ways we express ourselves and connect with others.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time

ci: Human interaction with the natural world causes change.
lo:
The natural world
Human interaction with nature
Changes people can make

s.d: Children become nature detectives, using Seek by iNaturalist with teacher support to identify plants, insects, and birds in the Elsternwick campus garden. This hands-on adventure sparks curiosity about the natural world and how humans interact with it every day. By inviting a local gardener or Indigenous knowledge holder to join the walk, students connect their discoveries to real community stories and cultural perspectives on caring for Country. Their discoveries are captured as a class photo journal, with each image showing the child who found it and the name Seek provided, to be displayed in the foyer for families. The 'Nearby Species' feature encourages children to notice patterns?like which creatures are found close to the playground versus the veggie patch. This experience builds wonder, observation skills, and a sense of stewardship for the living world right outside their classroom door.

Children become environmental helpers, using Sphero Indi and colour tiles to guide the robot through a 'nature rescue' obstacle course they build from natural materials. This playful journey invites them to explore how human actions?like clearing paths or planting seeds?can change the environment for animals and plants. Each child takes on the role of a different animal, advocating for safe passage or new habitats as the Indi navigates through their collaboratively designed terrain. The final artefact is a class video (teacher-recorded) of the robot's journey, narrated by students in character, and shared at assembly. Indi's programmable colour sensors allow children to experiment with cause-and-effect, discovering how different tile sequences create new outcomes for their animal friends. This empowers even the youngest learners to see themselves as problem-solvers and caretakers of the world.

Children transform leaves, rocks, and sticks into talking characters using ChatterPix Kids, animating voices for nature's treasures. This creative storytelling brings the line of inquiry 'changes people can make' to life, as each object shares a wish for how humans could help or harm its home. Children imagine themselves as the voice of a tree asking for less rubbish, or a worm hoping for more healthy soil, deepening empathy and environmental awareness. The finished talking photos are curated into a digital 'Nature Speaks' gallery for families to enjoy on Seesaw. ChatterPix's ability to add silly stickers and effects invites playful experimentation, making each message memorable and unique. Students walk away knowing their voices?real or imagined?can inspire others to care for the planet.

Children co-author a tactile class book in Book Creator, documenting their collective journey as 'Planet Protectors' through photos, drawings, and dictated stories. This project celebrates their growing understanding of human interaction with nature, highlighting small changes they can make?like picking up litter or watering plants. To make the book truly special, students invite their families to contribute a photo or story about caring for nature at home, weaving school and home life together. The final eBook is projected at a school showcase and sent home as a digital keepsake. Book Creator's built-in audio recording lets each child narrate their own page, so their voices and accents become part of the story. This collaborative process nurtures pride, belonging, and the belief that even little hands can make a big difference.

Children step into the shoes of animals, plants, and people using Puppet Pals, creating short digital puppet plays about sharing resources and making choices in nature. The activity invites them to dramatise scenarios?like animals searching for water, or people planting trees?and explore the consequences of different actions. By inviting a buddy class from Year 1 to watch and give feedback, students experience the thrill of being storytellers who can influence others' thinking. Their puppet shows are exported as short movies and played on the foyer screen for the whole school community. Puppet Pals' customisable backgrounds and characters let children blend their own artwork with digital puppetry, making each play a unique expression of their ideas. This builds confidence, communication skills, and the sense that their stories can spark real conversations about caring for the Earth.

s.t: Little Habitat Heroes: Animal Homes Build & Explore
s.d: Children will work together to create cozy animal homes using big cardboard boxes, fabric scraps, leaves, and soft materials, building nests, burrows, and dens for plush animal toys. After building, they'll use a simple child-friendly camera or tablet to take photos or short videos of their creations, narrating who lives there and how we can help animals share the planet. This hands-on project lets children explore the idea of habitats and caring for living things, while developing empathy and teamwork. Teachers guide the building and tech use, ensuring a safe, playful experience.
